ASRS:1795172.n: On the above mentioned date and time, I was the designated Pilot Flying. Descending through the Los Angeles area on vectors I was instructed to descend from 4,000 feet to 2,600 feet. I was overflying the city of Los Angeles on vectors to HHR. Autopilot was engaged, 2,600 feet was set in the altitude pre-selector and I began my descent. Another pilot reported to ATC that they flew past a drone off their right wing around 4,000 feet on approach into LAX. That would put the drone in our proximity off our right wing as well. Both the Pilot Monitoring (PM) and I were looking for that drone. I had mentioned to the PM that I have never been this low over the city of Los Angeles and we need to pay close attention to our surroundings. Through the distraction of trying to identify the drone, I descended through 2,600 feet to 2,400 feet before being advised of my altitude by ATC. I immediately disconnected the autopilot and corrected to the assigned altitude of 2,600 feet. No further issues occurred and no near misses were experienced to my knowledge. I was not informed by ATC of any possible pilot deviation nor given a contact number to call. Corrective action was taken to resolve the altitude discrepancy, and I have discussed with my crew and maintenance facility the possible reason why altitude was not captured by the autopilot. As Pilot in Command, I fully take responsibility for the actions on this day, both negative and corrective, and have discussed our safety procedures with my crew. I am filling out this report as I feel aviation is founded on safety and I strive to improve on every aspect of my piloting safety, skills and knowledge. Thank you for your time and consideration.
ASRS:1795172.s: The Pilot Flying descended below the assigned 2,600 feet to 2,400 feet while distracted by a reported drone near Los Angeles. The pilot immediately corrected the altitude after ATC advisement, attributing the deviation to distraction and a potential autopilot capture issue.

ASRS:1795174.n: Lost power at approximately 1,000 feet toward end of climbout to remain in pattern for touch and go's was probably 1/4 to 1/2 mile beyond end of runway, turned back to runway and informed Tower I had lost power and needed to land. I checked for any remedial problems and saw none, but noticed my prop was not turning. I proceeded to land back on runway and coast to a stop on the taxiway. I was able to hand push the plane to the fuel pumps and added fuel and the plane then restarted. the puzzle being the plane only took approximately 26 gallons when the tank holds 36, though only 32 usable, so I think there is some chance I might have had a vacuum created in the fuel tank. I do run un-vented fuel caps per a notice regarding the Aeronca sedans because with vented caps there had been some incidents of planes running out of power attributed to the wing at higher pitch up creating a vacuum at the tank. The Aeronca Sedan has a belly vent that faces forward to pressurize the fuel tanks, or I could just have not realized how low the fuel was and it lost power because of the pitch up for climb then couldn't restart because the prop stopped turning i.e. I didn't pitch down aggressively enough.
ASRS:1795174.s: The pilot of an Aeronca Sedan lost power at 1,000 feet during climbout, likely due to fuel starvation from a tank vacuum or low fuel, and executed a safe landing. The aircraft restarted after refueling, though the pilot noted the propeller had stopped turning and the tank accepted less fuel than expected.

ASRS:1795179.n: Had irregular engine parameters on departure. At cruise had a START VALVE OPEN light on and ran the QRH and following the QRH shut the left engine down. We continued on to ZZZ and did not request priority handling, but did tell ATC we had shut one engine down. We were closer to ZZZ1 airport but deemed higher to descent so continued on to ZZZ. QRH says to land at 'NEAREST SUITABLE AIRPORT.' Landed in ZZZ with no further issue and company is now saying we should have diverted to ZZZ1. There was no smoke, no fire, the RIGHT engine seemed to be running normal so there was not an urgent need to get on the ground. If I were the Captain I would have requested priority handling, but the Captain was worried about FAA inspections and company fallout with a priority request. I however would have also elected to continue to ZZZ as suitable to me also implies maintenance.
ASRS:1795179.s: The crew shut down the left engine at cruise due to a START VALVE OPEN light and irregular parameters, continuing to ZZZ instead of the closer ZZZ1. The reporter believes the decision was correct as there was no fire or smoke, though the company now claims a diversion to ZZZ1 was required.

ASRS:1795193.n: I was practicing air taxiing and quick stops with a 31-hour student pilot on a taxiway. During the recovery phase of the quick stop, the student did not raise enough collective to arrest the descent. I took controls at around 30 feet AGL and increased the collective to our 5-minute limit, but we continued to descend and impacted the ground hard enough to spread the skids. A piece of non-structural sheet metal detached from the underside of the helicopter and landed beside the taxiway. I reported what happened to the tower and they sent someone to retrieve the sheet metal. I flew the helicopter back to the flight school's ramp and did not observe any damage other than the spread skids. I should have taken the controls earlier and not allowed the descent rate to develop to an unrecoverable state. I was trying to talk the student through the correct control inputs when I should have just abandoned the maneuver and recovered.
ASRS:1795193.s: An instructor and student pilot hard-landed a helicopter on a taxiway during a quick stop training exercise when the student failed to arrest descent. The instructor took control at 30 feet AGL but could not prevent skid spreading and sheet metal detachment, attributing the incident to delayed intervention.

ASRS:1795196.n: GPS system went into Dead Reckoning mode, but we did not notice right away. After about 5 minutes, it found the aircraft position again and updated, showing the aircraft track about a mile further west than it had displayed before. We were traveling north just outside of the ZZZ Class Bravo. We do not believe we penetrated the edge of the airspace at any time, but once the GPS came back online and updated, we were substantially closer than we had been believed based on the previous, ambiguous, nav data.
ASRS:1795196.s: Pilots reported that their GPS entered Dead Reckoning mode while flying north outside ZZZ Class Bravo airspace. After five minutes, the system updated showing the aircraft one mile further west, placing them closer to the airspace boundary than previously indicated by the ambiguous navigation data.

ASRS:1795200.n: On date, our aircraft took necessary evasive action to avoid a Near midair collision while on an IFR Flight Plan in Night-time Visual Meteorological Conditions. Our aircraft was descending to an assigned altitude 7,000 feet while established on an assigned heading of 220 degrees. While descending through approximately 7,700 feet, at approximately 17.5 DME from BAPPA Intersection (Initial Fix for RNAV approach Runway 19 at GEU) approximately 229 degrees bearing to the fix, the onboard TCAS System issued a 'Traffic-Traffic Advisory'. About one second later the approach Controller issued a 'traffic alert' in conjunction with an 'immediate left turn' heading assignment of 170 degrees. After hearing the tone in the Controller's voice, I immediately complied with the Controller's (initial) request. As I glanced over to the TCAS portion of the screen, the conflicting traffic and our aircraft appeared to be converging, almost touching our aircraft's position on the screen. Scaled down to lowest distance ring/range, I estimate the distance between aircraft was less than a mile and the traffic was at about our twelve to one o'clock position. The traffic's altitude indicated 700 feet below our current altitude while we were descending before I looked away from the screen. I believe the traffic continued on a converging trajectory relative to our position prompting the Controller to re-issue the traffic alert combined with the immediate left turn heading assignment. I am not sure if the Controller did not receive our first acknowledgement of their Traffic Alert or if it was the fact the Controller saw our targets practically merge on their scope, but the tone in the Controller's re-issuance of the clearance convinced me the conflicting traffic had closed the distance between our aircraft and I was more focused on flying away from the traffic than verifying our distance by staring at the screen. My copilot confirmed the altitude separation was as little as 400 feet on screen and the traffic's position along with our position had merged on screen. At first glance, our distance to the conflicting aircraft appeared so close, I didn't have enough time to try to gauge the aircraft's performance or our convergence trajectory on screen. At that moment I felt there was not enough distance between us to wait for a Resolution Advisory from our TCAS System either. I discontinued the descent and level-off assignment of 7,000 and initiated an immediate power and pitch up maneuver. As a result, I climbed about 1,000 feet about our then current altitude of approximately 7,700 to an altitude of approximated 8,700 and the speed of our aircraft increased by about 30 knots from approximately 250 knots to approximately 280 knots indicated airspeed. When I was clear of conflict, I resumed the descent to 7,000 feet, resumed normal speed and complied with the Controller's new clearance. I am convinced the Controller's immediate left turn heading assignment alone was not sufficient to avoid the conflict. While performing the evasive maneuver, I heard the Controller correcting another aircraft on frequency advising them of a possible pilot deviation by that aircraft, however I don't recall if the term 'Pilot Deviation' was actually used and am not sure if that aircraft the Controller corrected was the same aircraft that caused our Traffic Alert/ Traffic Advisory. The Controller seemed extremely busy at this time, so we opted not to query the Controller on frequency regarding our near-miss. The area in which this occurred lies just north of DVT airport near a practice area, an area notorious for intensive pilot training. The brightly lit city lights on a clear night sky while descending may have masked the exterior lights of the conflicting aircraft just ahead and below us, as we never caught a visual of the aircraft.
ASRS:1795200.s: The pilot of an IFR aircraft descending to 7,000 feet at night reported a near midair collision with traffic 400 feet below and less than one mile away. The pilot executed an immediate climb to 8,700 feet and speed increase after determining the controller's left turn clearance was insufficient to avoid the conflict.

ASRS:1795210.n: Upon second lap around the pattern on ZZZ, I heard Aircraft Y calling 5 miles away with intend to join pattern behind downwind traffic in sight. That radio call came right came in between my Student Pilot call from crosswind to downwind. And there was another aircraft that was just passing the numbers. I made a second left downwind RWY XX call in case my Student Pilot's position call wasn't heard.I was passing mid-runway point and couldn't see the airplane that was joining pattern. Aircraft Y reported 45 degree entry , left downwind [Runway] XX behind downwind traffic. After I passed the abeam point, I instructed Student Pilot to not turn base nor descend until ahead traffic passed our wing, in which we had momentarily lost sight as they were doing a very wide pattern. At that moment, Aircraft Y and I were about to collide. Aircraft Y was positioned/ entering traffic on left base instead of downwind, behind us, as they called previously. I took controls from Student Pilot executing an evasive maneuver, steep left turn from base to final, while trying to not collide with aircraft on final that had just passed us. Aircraft Y made a turn to their right. No one was hurt nor lost aircraft control.
ASRS:1795210.s: The pilot and student on a second pattern lap at ZZZ nearly collided with Aircraft Y, which entered left base instead of the reported downwind. The pilot took controls and executed a steep left turn to avoid the conflict, resulting in no injuries or loss of control.

ASRS:1795211.n: Another aircraft was cleared through ZZZ airspace en route to ZZZ1 and was approved to do so via ZZZ Tower, which indicated that it did not have a visual on that aircraft. ZZZ does not have radar.I was cleared for takeoff on ZZZ Runway XX around the same time. Tower gave a frequency change to the other aircraft approximately one minute later and advised them of the aircraft taking off (me). The other aircraft responded that they were looking for traffic. Tower gave me a frequency change one to two minutes after that and advised me of the other aircraft.I was unable to spot the aircraft, but saw them on my traffic system and used the visual display and audio traffic alerts to avoid the other aircraft. I kept searching for the plane, climbing away from their flight path during this time, but even so, the traffic system indicated that we came within 100 vertical feet of each other.I believe that ZZZ Tower should have visually identified the transiting aircraft prior to clearing me for takeoff, or required me to identify the other aircraft prior to clearing me for takeoff. Both aircraft were in ZZZ airspace at the time of the event, and yet I am fairly certain that the controller did not have a visual on either of us (but certainly not on the other aircraft).If in this situation in the future, I will delay my takeoff until I have identified any aircraft that could become a hazard during my takeoff and climb-out. In addition, I will execute a turn away from the other aircraft, even when in controlled airspace.
ASRS:1795211.s: The pilot reported a near-miss during takeoff at ZZZ Tower, a non-radar facility, where a transiting aircraft was cleared without visual identification. Relying on traffic alerts, the pilot avoided the other aircraft, which came within 100 vertical feet, attributing the risk to the controller's failure to visually identify traffic before issuing clearances.

ASRS:1795220.n: During an aerial survey flight at approximately 16,500 feet the flight crew observed a drone pass 1 to 2 feet over the left wing tip of the aircraft. The drone was estimated 3 to 5 feet in diameter. It appeared to be a white color. It happened too quickly to describe the shape and dimensions with any degree of accuracy. Same goes for the direction of the craft. There would have been absolutely no chance of taking evasive action given how fast the event occurred. Same company has observed a drone at 15,500 [feet.] with a similar size and a near miss within 20 feet in the past.
ASRS:1795220.s: During an aerial survey at 16,500 feet, the flight crew observed a white drone pass 1 to 2 feet over the left wing tip. The event occurred too quickly for evasive action, and the crew noted a similar near miss by the same company at 15,500 feet in the past.

ASRS:1795234.n: I was pilot in command of a tail wheel airplane. The purpose of the flight was to maintain tail wheel proficiency. I was seated in the forward pilot station with a passenger seated in the aft pilot station. We departed to proceed to ZZZ with the intention of performing upper airwork maneuvers enroute to a landing at ZZZ to exchange pilot stations. Winds at takeoff were reported SW at 6 knots.On our arrival at ZZZ the automated weather was reporting winds as SW 8G16. The main Runway XX/XY [at] ZZZ is closed for resurfacing and the taxiway 'A' is marked as the temporary runway. The midfield windsock indicated the winds were generally SW 8G16 with some intermittent change to W and continuing intermittent gusts. On final approach to Runway XX the apparent winds were significantly more westerly. The aircraft touched down on the right main gear first. I used forward elevator to keep the horizontal stabilizer and rudder in an airflow that kept them aerodynamically effective. As the left main gear touched down I applied additional right aileron to arrest sideway drift and left pedal to maintain runway longitudinal alignment. As the tail wheel was about to touchdown the rudder became ineffective for maintaining runway alignment I applied left braking action but was unable to maintain runway heading and the nose of the aircraft yawed right and the aircraft exited the runway. As the aircraft weathervaned further nose right it slid sideways a short distance and the left wing tip contacted the ground. The aircraft was partially on the runway. Both tires were inflated and there was no apparent damage to the left wing. I elected to apply power and maneuver the aircraft clear of the runway and taxi into the ramp area of ZZZ to secure and inspect the aircraft.
ASRS:1795234.s: The pilot in command of a tailwheel aircraft exited the runway during landing at ZZZ due to ineffective rudder control in gusty crosswinds. The aircraft weathervaned right, causing the left wingtip to contact the ground, but the pilot maneuvered it clear with no apparent damage.

ASRS:1795238.n: I filed IFR flight plan. The flight was uneventful. I was cleared by ZZZ Center to descend to 10,000 feet MSL. I confirmed that clearance. I descended and was level for a minute or so when the Controller said to climb back up to 11,000 feet which was the altitude to which Controller cleared me. That was incorrect and would have been the wrong altitude for that direction of flight. The Controller admitted on the radio [to] working six frequencies at once. There was no traffic conflict. I think it is unfortunate that the Controller was so busy and the transmissions revealed Controller was very new on the job but the Supervisor should have helped out. Controller cleared me to 10,000 feet about a minute after Controller told me to climb up to 11,000 feet. Controller was clearly confused.
ASRS:1795238.s: The pilot reported that ZZZ Center initially cleared a descent to 10,000 feet but then incorrectly instructed a climb to 11,000 feet due to the controller managing six frequencies and being new. The controller later corrected the clearance to 10,000 feet with no traffic conflict.

ASRS:1795274.n: Aircraft X was descended to 3,000 feet by the trainee with control from the adjacent TRACON sector. We didn't talk to him soon enough to offer a 30 degree intercept for the RNAV Approach. We vectored him back around after requesting control from the other TRACON again. We were discussing assigning 2,000 feet to Aircraft Y landing at a different airport. The trainee turned Aircraft X heading 340, which I questioned and suggested heading 270. When the trainee issued the amended heading, she also descended Aircraft X to 2,000 feet. I did not catch it as during the same time, the trainee had released Aircraft Y off one airport and Aircraft Z off another airport, who were in conflict, in addition to an air carrier departure requesting practice approaches. I took over the frequency, and noticed Aircraft X already at 2,000 feet but he was not quite established on the approach and therefore, assigned an altitude below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude. When doing something out of the ordinary the controller trying to help could also put the aircraft on a better heading to intercept especially when we never approved the aircraft descending to 3,000 feet. Offer Aircraft X a different RNAV approach or offer to run the approach for the lows. The Low Altitude Alert never alarmed.
ASRS:1795274.s: A trainee controller descended Aircraft X to 2,000 feet below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude while managing multiple conflicting aircraft and a departure. The supervising controller took over after noticing the unauthorized descent, noting the Low Altitude Alert failed to activate.

ASRS:1795292.n: Sat in ZZZ for hours for a delayed flight coming from ZZZ1. During the swap, the outgoing Captain informed me that the Crew that brought the aircraft into ZZZ1 said that upon landing the right thrust reverser malfunctioned. The delay was due to Contract Maintenance MEL'ing the right thrust reverser. During pre-flight I checked the logbook, Release, and stickers as well as looked up the MEL on my EFB. During this time the 'A' Flight Attendant informed me that a passenger was refusing to wear their mask and creating a scene and that the CSR had been called. Eventually the passenger was removed and an updated report was sent to the aircraft. During the distraction I neglected to click on the hyperlink in the MEL in the Maintenance portion labeled MEL SP#XX Thrust Reverser System. If I had I would have noticed on that a Circuit Breaker for the #2 Engine should have been pulled and collared. Upon landing in ZZZ2 I informed the outgoing Captain of the MEL. During my commute home I received a text from said Captain that he found the wrong CB had been collared and that he had written it up and ZZZ2 Maintenance was fixing the issue. Upon reviewing the SP#XX I can only assume that the CB for the #1 Engine had been pulled instead. Inbound Captain advised that they had received the aircraft late in ZZZ due to Thrust Reverser MEL applied in ZZZ1 on previous flight and then further delayed on their flight due to a Passenger refusing to comply with mask requirements.In reviewing the logbook I found that the MEL sticker in the front of the logbook was not completed. The MEL number was not entered, the Special procedures performed were not entered and the circuit breakers pulled and collared were not entered. When I reviewed the logbook entry, the special procedures were references SP-XX. I also observed C/B's #2 Engine TR Sync Lock and #2 Engine TR INTLK pulled and collared.I then reviewed the MEL and SP-XX and discovered the following errors.1. SP XX calls for the #2 Engine TR Sync Lock c/b and the #2 Engine TR Control c/b to be pulled and collared. the Control C/B was NOT collared as prescribed in SP XXnd the INTLK c/b WAS collared contrary to SP XX2. There was no MEL sticker placed on the Inoperative TR lever.3. There was no MEL sticker placed above the respected N1 gauge.I contacted Maintenance Control to confirm my understanding of the MEL regarding the incorrect Circuit Breakers and they confirmed the wrong circuit breaker had been pulled. Notified ZZZ2 Maintenance and entered the discrepancy in the logbook. ZZZ2 Maintenance arrived and corrected the circuit breaker configuration and signed off the discrepancy I had entered. Missing information on the logbook sticker was also corrected.I have long felt that our MEL is VERY inadequate when it comes to circuit breaker identification. In this particular instance the nomenclature is correct and was just applied incorrectly by the Mechanic, but if the C/B locations were included it would have been much more apparent to the Mechanic as well as flight crew that the two C/B would not be immediately adjacent to each other. I have brought this to the attention of Flight Ops previously with regards to other MEL's and have been advised that changes are slated for a future revision that has been delayed due to aircraft out of service returns, COVID and other issues. I also feel it should be reinforced to flight crews that MEL compliance is not solely the responsibility of the Maintenance department and that we should always verify (to the limits of our abilities) those aspects of MEL compliance which we have ready access to on each airplane we accept regardless of previous crews acceptance of the aircraft.
ASRS:1795292.s: The pilot reported that a mechanic incorrectly applied a thrust reverser MEL by pulling the wrong circuit breakers and failing to complete logbook stickers. The pilot discovered the error during pre-flight, notified maintenance at the destination, and noted that the MEL documentation lacks sufficient circuit breaker location details.

ASRS:1795315.n: About XX minutes after we reached our cruise altitude, my FO (First Officer) and I observed the level on our #2 Oil Qty gauge go from 11 to Y then Z, then blank rather quickly. It had been normal up until then, we just caught the decrease at 11. After checking the QRC and QRH for Low Oil Qty to no avail, we noticed our #2 Oil Pressure dropping. It stabilized at 29 psi but fluctuated from XX to XY with 29 being the median amber band. This continued for the remainder of the flight until TOD (Top of Descent). I referenced the Engine Low Oil Pressure Checklist in the QRH on Page X.XX. It states that if the oil pressure is at or below the redline: Go to the Engine Failure or Shutdown checklist on Page X.XY. The oil pressure never reached the redline, so the checklist stops there. All other engine parameters were normal with no vibration. My FO (First Officer) continued to fly and talk with ATC while I set up a phone patch with our Dispatcher as I decided that there was too much information to use ACARS. I told them what was going on and that we were continuing on to ZZZ but we were also prepared to divert if need be later on. They were in agreement as there was no need or requirement at this time to shut the engine down or divert. I talked with the Flight Attendants and we had a good discussion about the situation. I told them that our aircraft was operating just fine and that it seems that we have an indication issue and that I was not going to make a PA. I also asked them if they could discretely look at the aft portion of the right hand engine to see if they saw any oil. My FO (First Officer) and Flight Attendants did a great job along with our Dispatcher and Maintenance Control. Later in the flight, our Dispatcher gave us single engine landing data for ZZZ. Descending into ZZZ when the thrust levers were slowly retarded to idle, the oil pressure and qty actually increased. By the time we were on final approach, the said indications were normal.
ASRS:1795315.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced fluctuating #2 engine oil pressure and quantity indications during cruise, which normalized during descent and approach. They consulted the QRH, coordinated with Dispatch and cabin crew, and continued to the destination without diverting or shutting down the engine.

ASRS:1795347.n: 7 mins after pushback at ZZZ, waiting on the ramp, engines shut down. APU on save fuel for our 20 mins ATC hold. Passenger advised FA they forgot to takeout the spare lithium battery from there valet bag. FA advised CA, Captain called dispatch and advised agreeing we are unable to take flight until the battery is removed from the cargo compartment. We pulled back into the gate found passenger's battery had her remove it. Operation continued as normal after removal.The cause of the event was that Passenger did not advise gate of battery after being asked if there are any lithium batteries in the bag (according to ZZZ manager). Reporter recommends start the [special] tag process prior to boarding and make another announcement making sure there is no batteries in there [special] tag bag. Rethink/possible rewording of battery announcement for more/better clarification.
ASRS:1795347.s: The crew delayed departure at ZZZ after a passenger admitted to leaving a spare lithium battery in a valet bag. The aircraft returned to the gate for battery removal, with the cause attributed to the passenger failing to declare the item during gate screening.

ASRS:1795361.n: I was the First Officer and the pilot monitoring. We were cleared to descend via the ZZZZZX. Approaching FL200 on the descent, I noticed my airspeed start to decrease rapidly without any change in airplane thrust or pitch. I called out 'airspeed' while inspecting the standby and Captain's airspeed indicator. We called unreliable airspeed and started the QRC (Quick Reference Checklist). We followed the QRC followed by the QRH (Quick Reference Handbook). We were able to confirm that the Captain's airspeed indicator was accurate based on the pitch and power settings and correlating with the standby airspeed indicator. The QRH instructed us to reengage the autopilot and change the ALT SOURCE selector to the Captain's side. This allowed my airspeed indicator to correspond with the Captain's and standby airspeed indicator. After we dictated which airspeed was accurate, ATC had given a heading and altitude to continue into ZZZ. I completed the QRH checklist for Unreliable Airspeed but kept the unreliable airspeed tables open to make sure the pitch and power settings correlated with our speed. We continued to fly the ILS approach into ZZZ without any further incident. The Captain notified Maintenance and Dispatch once we were blocked in and the door open. We were unable to conclude the cause that created the unreliable airspeed situation. But, I will become more familiar with the airspeed unreliable checklist and table so that I may refer to it and utilize it more efficiently in the event of another similar occurrence.
ASRS:1795361.s: The First Officer experienced rapid airspeed decay on his indicator during descent to FL200 while monitoring the flight. The crew followed unreliable airspeed procedures, switched the ALT SOURCE to the Captain's side, and completed an ILS approach without determining the specific cause.

ASRS:1795362.n: I was the First Officer and pilot monitoring on this ZZZ to ZZZ1 flight, XXX on [aircraft], arriving into ZZZ1 from the south east, at night, in VFR conditions. Due to the winds out of the north at ZZZ1 (310 at 12 gusting 21), RWY XX was the only landing runway on the ATIS. Upon loading RWY XX, the ZZZZZ [arrival] would not show as an available arrival in the FMC. ATC did not assign the ZZZZZ arrival but instead gave us direct ZZZZZ1 (a waypoint on the ZZZZZ), and then direct to the airport. These ATC instructions were given near ZZZZZ2 [fix] on our flight plan. With the Captains concurrence I executed direct ZZZZZ3. Additionally, the Captain had me select ZZZZZ3/12,000 as a hard altitude in the FMC to help with descent planning (12,000 was a crossing altitude restriction on the ZZZZZ1). I then placed ZZZZZ5 as the waypoint that would follow. As we got closer to ZZZZZ3, Approach directed us to maintain present heading with a further descent to 10,000. This heading did not keep us in a direction tracking the ZZZZZ arrival over the water along [geographic fix 1] , but instead brought us on a more westerly heading over terrain on the southwest side of [geographic fix 1].Approach then directed a descent to 8,000. Then directed a right turn to 250. Then directed a further right turn to 260. And finally, a descent to 7,000. Approach then asked: 'Do you have the field in sight? 2oclock 21 miles' The Captain and the Observer both spoke up to speaking that they could see the airport. I as well saw the lights of the airport and felt comfortable concurring. The Captain said he could accept the visual and so I then relayed this to Approach. Approach than cleared us the visual approach RWY XX. At this point the Captain looking at his descent planning showed us slightly high on the VNAV descent path and started a descent below 7,000. Shortly after this and around 6,200 ft, a GPWS alert 'CAUTION TERRAIN' enunciated. Looking at my Terrain display, the AMBER terrain mapping showed terrain off to our right. The Captain immediately arrested his descent and the Observer and the Captain and I visually confirmed the terrain off to the right of our flight path. Shortly after this ATC further directed us to begin our right turn towards the field. The Captain and I continued to maintain visual separation with the terrain and delayed further descent until comfortable the terrain clearance was no longer a concern. We then conducted an LVSA on the MCP and an uneventful landing in ZZZ1. [Reporter added concerns] accepting a visual approach at night. Although we could see the lighted airport environment ahead, what was not so apparent was the dark terrain just below the city lights that was still ahead and to the right of our flight path. At night, the city lights in the distance can cause night vision to be affected and spotting unlit terrain between your flight path can be potentially more difficult to see. Accepting a visual approach is not something that should be done lightly. The better course of action was to recommend to the Captain we delay accepting a visual until we were closer to the field and the terrain well behind us. ATC did not help matters by asking us to an accept a visual approach as early as they did. A mistaken assumption could be made that the terrain protections of 7,000 was past us and a descent to establish an already slightly high VNAV path to RWY XX could be initiated. Clearly the terrain ahead was much closer to our altitude, we had several miles to go before a descent below 7000 should have been initiated. The GPWS 'CAUTION TERRAIN' was a very clear on this point. The importance of GPWS Terrain monitoring [is that] GPWS is an essential situational awareness tool and one the pilot monitoring only had displayed initially. Had the Captain also had TERR selected this may have mitigated the early descent, but as pilot monitoring I should have done a better job monitoring the TerrainMapping display. Clearly after the 'CAUTION TERRAIN' annunciation appeared, the Yellow Terrain mapping became very clear on both our displays. Additionally, when descending in mountainous terrain it's also important to remember that the GPWS system will only display terrain data that is 2,000 feet below or closer to the aircraft. Depending on your range ring and your location and rate of descent, you can quickly go from no terrain colors to quite colorful ones in short order. Vigilance in monitoring Terrain Mapping along your flight path is key. Lastly, had this situation happened in [different type aircraft], the terrain profile view function would have provided significant situational awareness to the crew on the terrain that was still ahead. [Regarding] RNAV approach to XX, the [company] aircraft behind us had received approval to fly to a point on an RNAV approach to XX, an approach that is currently not available on our aircraft. Had this been available, this would have been a valuable tool providing altitude protections and a significant aid to situational awareness. Even if not an RNAV approach, a visual approach page like the ZZZZZ3 VISUAL Rwy XY that is available in JEPPS would have also aided in better descent planning for the RWY XX visual approach.
ASRS:1795362.s: The First Officer and Captain on an XXX aircraft accepted a visual approach at night, descending below 7,000 feet and triggering a GPWS 'CAUTION TERRAIN' alert due to unlit terrain ahead. The crew arrested the descent, maintained visual separation from the terrain, and completed an uneventful landing after the alert.

ASRS:1795393.n: We conducted the ZZZZZ4 arrival and joined the ILS XX approach from ZZZZZ [Intersection] as briefed. When the Captain contacted the Tower, the Controller cleared us to land XX Right. The Captain read back the clearance. I said, 'Can you confirm Controller wants us to land on the right? We're on the ILS XX Left.' The Captain confirmed with the Controller cleared to land on the right. The Controller responded 'Affirmative. XX Right, Cleared to land.' At the time, we were well above 1,000 feet in visual conditions with the runway in sight and, so I had no objection. I clicked off the autopilot and side-stepped to XX Right and we landed. No issues arose with ATC or any other traffic. The next day, the Captain reached out to me and we spoke over the phone. Captain learned that we had actually been cleared for the ILS XX Right approach and Captain intended to file a report. A couple of days later I was finally able to confirm that this was correct. We aren't able to determine if it was being read back correctly or incorrectly, but there was never a clarification type of response from ZZZ Approach. It's also important to bring up that the Captain was wearing a face mask throughout the flight operations which did contribute to difficulties in communication with myself and with ATC at various times during the trip. This likely was a contributing factor to our deviation. Another contributing factor was the violation of sterile cockpit below 18,000 feet by the Captain and myself. Personally, I was distracted by our conversation as well as the fact that Captain was wearing a mask during the flight.Complacency is also a factor as the ZZZZZ4 Arrival usually results in the ILS or visual to XX Left.I think our company needs to take a harder stance on mask-wearing during flight operations in the flight deck. I recommend that the company forbids the use of masks by pilots during flight operations to ensure that communications are clear and effective. In this case, it can be assumed that the Captain was repeating the clearance saying 'XX Left' but the Controller did not hear it clearly and assumed Captain was saying XX Right. Therefore, Captain was never corrected and we continued with what we had expected in our heads. There were multiple points throughout our trip that ATC did not understand the Captain and asked who was calling or needed clarification on what Captain was saying because it was difficult to understand with the mask. I thought on several occasions throughout our trip that it was the Captain's choice to wear it but if we have an emergency situation that I really hope Captain would take it off so that effective communication could be established and maintained. An emergency situation did not occur, but clearly an issue did arise with our approach to our destination. ZZZ had a broken layer at 1,700 feet and we were expecting to do an approach. Descending into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ4 arrival we had set up for the ILS [Runway] XXL. We were assigned to join the ILS [Runway] XXR at ZZZZZ [Intersection] and then later cleared for the ILS XXR approach. We did not fly the ILS XXR. We flew the XXL approach and when we were on with Tower, we told them we were inbound on the ILS XXL. Tower cleared us to land XXR. By the time we contacted Tower we were out of the clouds and could see the runway. We verified two times that we were cleared to land XXR and not XXL. And Tower confirmed that we were to land XXR. Since we had visual on the runway, we side stepped and landed on XXR. We were probably at 1,500-1,600 feet AFE when we side stepped. We were confused as to why they had changed runways on us, but we knew that XXR was longer than XXL and that the landing speeds were the same and we were familiar with the airport. As we side stepped, I programmed in the ILS XXR so that we had a backup source even though we visually had the airport in sight. Later in the evening it still didn't sit right with me that we had a runway change that late, especially since we had been on an IFR approach. I realized we had in fact been assigned ILS XXR all the way back on with Approach. They never corrected me. So, I either read it back correctly but we were really hearing what we wanted to hear (ILS XXL) or they never corrected me and we all missed it. The approach was stable all the way through for XXL and the sidestep was done in a safe manner.I attribute not being sterile in the descent as a factor even though we were assigned to join ILS XXR at ZZZZZ prior to FL180. I would say complacency and expectancy were the primary factors. XXL wasn't closed and we were set that we would be doing the ILS XXL. It was also the last leg on the last day of our trip and we had had a long day. I had been up since 8 or 9am and we had flown 4 legs. This flight landed around XApm.I can say that I once again am reminded how serious our jobs are and that miss hearing a simple 'L' vs 'R' can be life changing. I can only say that I am thankful that this took place during a low traffic period and that we were able to maintain a safe condition. I'm honestly not too sure how to avoid this situation. I believe that writing down my clearances would assist in allowing me to verify and that maybe I need to make sure to turn my headset up so that I won't miss ATC.
ASRS:1795393.s: The flight crew flew an ILS Left approach instead of the cleared ILS Right, later side-stepping to land on the Right runway after Tower clearance. The deviation resulted from miscommunication due to the Captain's face mask, sterile cockpit violations, and crew complacency regarding the expected runway.

ASRS:1795404.n: On this flight we had to heavily brake for two different tugs that drove out right in front of us on the vehicle road, and four others cut us off close enough that we had to stop and wait for them to clear the aircraft. One of the heavy brake situations, the tug driver ran a stop sign and did not look before he was directly in front of us. This seems to be happening much more regularly in Atlanta recently, I have had multiple instances in the past several weeks. Tug drivers not driving safely and not giving way to aircraft
ASRS:1795404.s: The pilot reported that during taxi at Atlanta, the aircraft had to brake heavily or stop because multiple tugs cut them off or ran a stop sign. The reporter attributes these incidents to tug drivers failing to drive safely or yield to aircraft.

ASRS:1795437.n: The Captain refused to brief me along with other crew members because I asked to maintain the appropriate amount of social distance.Captain told me to go to the back if I didn't want to come closer. Not receiving a crew briefing jeopardizes the entire crew along with the passengers.[Suggest] for the Captain when time permits, to brief the crew or brief us individually.
ASRS:1795437.s: The Captain refused to brief the reporter and other crew members due to a request for social distancing, directing them to the back instead. The reporter stated that missing the briefing jeopardized crew and passenger safety and suggested individual briefings when time permits.

ASRS:1795464.n: After completing a fuel stop at PEO, I taxied from the fuel pump near the FBO to Runway 28 for departure. Prior to taxiing I completed my pre-taxi checks and self announced my taxi on CTAF. The wind was 220@17G23 and I wanted to complete my run up into the wind. Runway 28/10 doesn't have a parallel taxiway to the East requiring a back taxi for approximately the half the runway length. The runway, departure and arrival corridor appeared clear and I announced taking the runway for back taxi with no other traffic heard. I completed a short run up, scanned the runway and announced on CTAF I was taking off Runway 28. I applied power, checked instruments and accelerated down the runway. Shortly I noted something in the distance down the runway, a second later noticed engines rise above the crest of the the runway and I immediately aborted takeoff. I was close to rotation speed, pulled power back and aggressively braked. Once at a safe speed I announced I was aborting and vacating the runway. I was close the the north/south taxi and uneventfully exited the runway at that point. At that time I saw a Falcon jet exit runway 10/28 via the next taxiway about 800 feet down the runway heading to the fuel pumps. I turned my aircraft around announced my back taxi and departure. Concerned that I had an equipment issue or was on the wrong frequency I asked for a radio check while I was departing downwind and received a good check. Due to a significant crown/slope in the runway it is not possible to see the opposite ends of the Runway 28/10. The other aircraft operator should follow the best practices identified in AC 90-66b par 10.1 self-announce their intentions and monitor the frequency for other traffic as well. Additionally, the aircraft was taxiing from the west hangars to the fuel pumps and if there's sufficient wingtip clearance they should use the parallel taxiway instead of the runway as an increased measure of safety.
ASRS:1795464.s: The pilot aborted a takeoff on Runway 28 at PEO after discovering a Falcon jet exiting the runway, caused by a significant runway crown blocking visibility. The pilot attributed the near-miss to the other operator failing to self-announce intentions or use the parallel taxiway.

ASRS:1795472.n: I was taxiing to Runway 12 via taxiway alpha and witnessed a near midair collision. The runway in use at the time was Runway 12 as there was a [Cessna] 172 on final approach and another aircraft at the run up area near Runway 12. A Cessna 172 was on final approach for [Runway] 12 and a Stearnman was taking off on the opposite end of the runway (Runway 30). I witnessed the two aircraft flying right at each other and the Stearnman flew right over the Cessna 172 at approximately 200 feet and then banked to the right. There was an argument over Unicom that occurred between the Cessna pilot and Stearnman pilot. The Cessna pilot was an Instructor Pilot and basically told him the runway in use was 12. The Stearnman pilot was argumentative and suggested he is also an Instructor Pilot and that the pilot determines the runway in use at an uncontrolled airport.I am reporting this because of the safety implications. The Stearnman pilot was clearly in the wrong, but expressed that he was right over radio chatter. My goal here is to initiate the required actions to ensure this never happens again as I do not want to see someone get killed because of an unsafe pilot.
ASRS:1795472.s: A taxiing pilot witnessed a near midair collision between a Cessna 172 on final for Runway 12 and a Stearman taking off from Runway 30 at an uncontrolled airport. The Stearman passed 200 feet above the Cessna, leading to a radio argument where the Stearman pilot incorrectly claimed pilots determine runway usage.

ASRS:1795474.n: I was wrapping up a long training flight with my instructor and we were practicing approaches and landings before wraping up for the day. On the third landing approach there was a Cessna 150 ahead of us in the pattern. I extended the downwind to make room and turned base and final much further out than typical. One of the things we had been practicing is making sure to be low enough on the approach to not overshoot since it is such a short runway. On this approach I was quite low and setup a little low on final when I realized that while I had seen the C150 land I wasn't certain it had cleared the runway. I thought it might still be on there and asked my instructor if we should go around. He said no and to go ahead and land since we didn't see the other aircraft on the runway anymore and we would be landing very short. The previous loop around the pattern I initiated a go around because it didn't feel right but was assured that we were setup just right for landing and should've landed. I think that I was reluctant to do another go around 'for no reason' if I didn't need to according to the instructor.Shortly after landing and rolling out several feet and up the incline in the runway we saw the other airplane at the far end. At just about the same time we heard frantic calls for the other airplane to get off the runway as soon as possible. I was setup for a short field landing and exited the runway after a very short landing roll about 1,700 feet from where the other aircraft had exited the runway. We were shaken from the realization that we had shared the runway and scared the other training aircraft.Contributing factors:1. Fatigue- This was one of the first training sessions after a 4 month break and my instructor and I were exhausted.2. Human Factors - I deferred to my instructors experience and decided against the go around. We have since discussed this issue and agreed that if either of us feel a go around is a good idea we will go around.3. Airport - The runway X landing zone is at a significantly lower elevation than the XX end of the runway. because of the geography is difficult to see aircraft at the other end.
ASRS:1795474.s: A student pilot and instructor landed a training aircraft on a short, sloped runway while a Cessna 150 was still occupying the far end. The near-miss occurred due to fatigue, the student deferring to the instructor's decision to land, and limited visibility caused by the runway's elevation change.

ASRS:1795476.n: My aircraft does not have ADSB. If I depart Merrill to the north and do not receive the Part 93 deviation from ATC, then because of the combination of Part 93 and the ADSB requirement over Anchorage Class C, I am required to fly over Cook Inlet below 600 ft. MSL, which puts the aircraft in a position out of gliding distance to land. Recent local memory has multiple examples of this situation ending in a fatality. There is a large number of general aviation aircraft operating in the Anchorage area that are ADSB negative and that fatal outcome is likely to occur again in the future due to the airspace rule combinations currently in place.
ASRS:1795476.s: A pilot reported that ADSB-negative aircraft departing Merrill northward without a Part 93 deviation must fly below 600 ft MSL over Cook Inlet due to Anchorage Class C rules. This places the aircraft out of gliding distance to land, creating a high risk of fatality for general aviation operators in the area.

ASRS:1795489.n: Approaching the ZZZ airport I was instructed to enter right traffic for[Runway] XXR, #3 following a Cessna on downwind. I acknowledged the instruction, advised I was looking for traffic, and slowed to approximately 70 KIAS.Approaching mid-field downwind I saw a Cessna about 500 ft to my right at the same altitude. I was not able to see the other aircraft initially because it was obscured by my wing. The pilot if the other aircraft announced on the radio the he had a traffic conflict and we both turned opposite directions. The tower controller acknowledged the situation and provided instructions to resolve the conflict. We both landed safely. I believe that this situation could have been avoided if the Tower Controller provided more accurate position reports, and more closely monitored the progress of approaching traffic on radar.
ASRS:1795489.s: The pilot reported a near-midair conflict with a Cessna while on downwind for Runway XXR, caused by the other aircraft being obscured by the wing. Both pilots executed opposite turns to resolve the conflict, landed safely, and the reporter attributed the incident to inaccurate position reports and insufficient radar monitoring by the tower controller.

ASRS:1795503.n: While navigating to a fix ATC inquired as to where we were navigating. I responded direct to the fix ZZZ1. Our FMS showed us 2 miles south. ATC came back and said we were in fact 12 miles from ZZZ1 so at that point I knew our GPS wasn't working. I asked for vectors to the airport and they were provided. Upon an uneventful landing our GPS still showed us 34 miles from the airport when we were sitting on the ramp.
ASRS:1795503.s: The pilot reported a GPS failure during the approach phase while navigating to fix ZZZ1, where the FMS displayed incorrect distances compared to ATC radar. After receiving vectors for an uneventful landing, the GPS continued to show erroneous position data on the ramp.

ASRS:1795514.n: I was the Pilot Monitoring (PM) on the flight to ZZZ. Descending on the ZZZZZ FIVE arrival heading to the ZZZZZ1 fix. Approximately 20 miles from the ZZZZZ1 fix ATC called and revised the fixes after ZZZZZ1 but told us to comply with all the restrictions. The ZZZZZ1 fix includes a crossing restriction of 27000 feet. I read back the new clearance and confirm it with the Captain/PF. Done, then I went heads down to re-program the FMS including changing the landing runway.As I transfer my eyes back to the PFD to continue with the PM duties, I noticed the altitude at approximately 25,000 feet. I pointed the deviation to the Captain who stopped the descent. No traffic conflict was issued by ATC and we continued with the arrival using the depicted profile. While I have the primary duty of PM there are additional duties such as the checklist, FMS Programing, radio calls etc., that can distract us at important times. Compounding the situation was long days with five legs and 10 plus hours of duty. On top of that, due to the COVID crisis, we are operating with reduced staff and salary freeze creating additional stress and fatigue. I think prioritizing the duties is important and an art. Yet sometimes we reach limits and we don't recognize it.
ASRS:1795514.s: The Pilot Monitoring on a flight descending on the ZZZZZ FIVE arrival missed a 27,000-foot crossing restriction at the ZZZZZ1 fix while reprogramming the FMS. The Captain stopped the descent at 25,000 feet after the PM noticed the deviation, attributing the error to distraction, fatigue, and operational stress.

ASRS:1795543.n: Aircraft X was IFR inbound to ZZZ requesting the LOC RWY XX, however, the tower still on their COVID hours closes early. When the tower closed they put the localizer on RWY YY so the LOC RWY XX was unavailable. Due to winds Aircraft X was unable RWY YY. They requested the RNAV Y RWY XX. I had traffic for Aircraft X as they were approaching ZZZZZ with the crossing altitude of 051 and the traffic at 047 I gave a restriction for traffic. This confused the pilot so I went back and cancelled the approach clearance and told the pilot to expect clearance at ZZZZZ1, but this was a mistake, what I meant to say was ZZZZZ. The pilot did not question me but did seem confused. Rightfully so. When Aircraft X was clear of the traffic they reported that they were direct ZZZZZ. I then cleared Aircraft X to cross ZZZZZ at 5,100 cleared straight in RNAV Y Rwy XX approach. Aircraft X appeared to over shoot ZZZZZ before turning to ZZZZZ2. I questioned the pilot that the next fix past ZZZZZ was ZZZZZ2, is that where they show their self going. The pilot stated they just passed ZZZZZ2 and I can't quite understand what they said after that. But at the time I thought they said going to ZZZZZ3 the next fix on the approach. While this was going on I had a couple other aircraft waiting and another facility call me for point outs. When my attention took me back to Aircraft X their path appeared off and had began a go around and the moment they called me I issued the low altitude alert and an immediate climb. They attempted the approach and landed safely on the second attempt. My initial reaction to this approach was that something was off, which is when I questioned the pilot. I gave them the benefit of the doubt and hoped that they had corrected the overshoot at ZZZZZ and was properly on the RNAV Y RWY XX at ZZZ. However, I should have just gone with my gut and broke the aircraft off the approach when I noticed the error and vectored back around for a second attempt. Hindsight when you look back is always better. We try to not delay aircraft and hope that they are truthful when we question them about approaches. However, safety is our number one priority and concern and I did feel like there was something not right and looking back I wish I would have just broken the aircraft off the approach and re-sequenced. It is always easier to watch a replay to see how we can improve, but that is important so we do not repeat our mistakes.
ASRS:1795543.s: An air traffic controller issued a confusing clearance and failed to break off Aircraft X from an RNAV approach after noticing an overshoot, leading to a low altitude alert and go-around. The aircraft landed safely on a second attempt, though the controller admitted they should have vectored the pilot away earlier upon detecting the error.

ASRS:1795554.n: Takeoff rejected due to autothrottle disengagement. Throttle advanced normally, then paused, then reduced to idle at 30 knots. Cleared runway. We were cleared for takeoff. Upon power up, we received an Autopilot Disconnect Alert and we rejected the takeoff well below 80 knots.
ASRS:1795554.s: The crew rejected takeoff below 80 knots after the autothrottle disengaged and throttles reduced to idle at 30 knots. This occurred following an Autopilot Disconnect Alert received upon power up, prompting the crew to clear the runway.

ASRS:1795573.n: FL350, the Auto Controller number 2 went INOP and the red Cabin Alt light illuminated. We ran the checklist and did a phone patch to [Name]. We elected to continue to ZZZZ. After fifteen minutes, the Cabin Altitude controller number 1 was not controllable. We switched to manual controller. We ran the Cabin Auto Inop checklist. Called Dispatch and returned to ZZZ. We did [advise ATC] and descended to FL250. We ran the diversion guide checklist. First Officer flew the aircraft to a great landing into the sun. She was very professional the entire flight and I am thankful she was my partner. She made many suggestions. Flight departed ZZZ with no issues. About 1 hour into the flight, Flight Attendant reported losing the galley ovens. About 1:30 into the flight we got a Cabin Altitude Warning. Ran the QRH and switched from Auto 2 to Auto 1 controller. The cabin altitude went back down from 10,000 to about 8,000 and seemed stable. We contacted Dispatch and [Maintenance Control] and everyone agreed it was safe to continue to ZZZZ. After about 15 minutes the cabin altitude started increasing again and right before it hit 10,000 we switched to the Manual controller per the QRH. The cabin altitude was controllable again but we [advised ATC] and opted to turn around and go back to ZZZ. Completed the diversion checklist. We also felt more comfortable at a lower altitude and descended to FL250. Landed in ZZZ without any issues. Captain was very professional and as cool as the other side of a pillow during the entire event.
ASRS:1795573.s: The crew experienced a cabin altitude warning at FL350 due to inoperative auto controllers, requiring a switch to manual control. They descended to FL250 and diverted back to ZZZ, landing safely after consulting Dispatch and Maintenance Control.

ASRS:1795635.n: Uneventful flight to ZZZ. On final ILS XXR at ZZZ, below 2,500 feet, inside ZZZZZ but prior to ZZZZZ1, LOC and GS Captainured, flaps 20 set, Captain called for leg gear down and disconnected AP and A/T. At this moment, the L HYD SYS PRESS Master Caution Lt illuminated. At first I thought the light was associated with the AP and A/T being disconnected. It took a couple seconds to recognize that it was the HYD pressure light. At this time also we were checking in with XX_1 r outside ZZZZZ1 and were cleared to land. Very shortly after I accepted the leg clearance, the Captain alerted to Go Around and made the Go Around call to Tower. We accomplished the normal go around procedure and shortly received a LDG GEAR DISAGREE caution as the gear did not retract due to the initial emergency. We repositioned the gear handle to the down position and that caution extinguished. After reaching 3,000 feet and completing the GA procedures, the Captain continued to fly the AC and I accessed the Non Normal procedure through the FM on my EFB. The HYD section has a large index and initially I inadvertently selected the HYD SYS PRESS L and C non-normal and after the first two steps realized we were in the wrong checklist and switched to the HYD SYS PRESS L (only) Checklist. I ran the checklist aloud as the Captain continued to fly. Step 7 instructed not to use auto brakes. When completing the deferred items, the flaps and gear were already in the proper configuration and due to the post Go Around altitude and box pattern vectors, though not unduly rushed, I inadvertently failed to re-run the descent checklist as part of the deferred items, missing the last reminder to not use autobrakes. We did run the deferred landing checklist, and the Captain flew the approach to landing. After touchdown the auto brakes engaged firmly and the Captain immediately moved the speed brake lever slightly fwd to disengage the autobrakes and proceeded to manually brake the AC along with use of the RT engine reverser. We slowed to a gentle stop with approximately 1,500 feet remaining on Runway XXR. Due to the lack of runway steering we remained on the runway, coordinating with ground personnel, and monitored brake temps. After an initial external check by ground personnel, we secured the engines, remaining on APU power for the remainder of the ground ops evolution and tug to our gate. Communicating with ZZZ approach on the ILS XXR to ZZZ between ZZZZZ and ZZZZ1, with the flaps at 20 and after lowering the landing gear, we received an EICAS message L HYD SYS PRESS. I was Pilot Flying, hand flying with the A/P and A/T off. The First Officer was Pilot Monitoring. At ZZZZZ1 we switched to ZZZ Tower and informed them we would abandon the approach. We were given a northerly heading and a climb to 3,000 [feet]. I decided to abandon the approach using V/S mode as we were at approximately 1,600 feet, and to reduce my workload, engaged the right autopilot. I inadvertently called for 'Gear Up' which did not occur due to the loss of the left system. We realized this error when a 'GEAR DISAGREE' EICAS message appeared and returned the gear handle to the down position. The gear remained down from the prior approach through the eventual landing.I stated the I had the airplane and the radios and directed the First Officer to run the L HYD SYS PRESS non-normal checklist.We also pulled up the status page and noted the loss of quantity from the left system, less than .2 with RF showing.We initially started the L and C HYD SYS PRESS checklist but caught the error when the checklist called for an action regarding the center system.We then proceeded to run the L HYD SYS PRESS checklist, but made an error, missing the 'do not use autobrakes' step. I would eventually select Autobrakes 4 for landing.ATC asked me at this point if I needed the equipment standing by and I declined.Upon completion of the checklist up to deferred items, I [advised] with ATC.ATC asked us which runway we would like, and I inquired about [Runway] XYL. ATC said it would be available as a visual approach. I decided to re-use the ILS to XXR as we were set up for it already, would benefit from the precision guidance at night, and it had an approach light system that [Runway] XYL did not. The length of [Runway] XXR provided our required landing distance, with margin, plus around another 4,000 feet.I sent a brief ACARS message to Dispatch stating I had [advised with ATC] and would be landing in ZZZ. I should have included the nature of the [event] and our need of a tow in the body of the message. Despite being somewhat concerned about the time available as I was stuck in a high drag configuration, I still had enough time to send a more complete message and should have done so- it would have been a few more keystrokes. I also had enough time to re-run the non-normal checklist. Doing so would have caught the autobrake restriction. The First Officer and I discussed this in our debrief.I then briefed the purser using the TEST acronym, advising that we would NOT need to prep the cabin for evac.I do not recall asking for the equipment to be standing by, other than stating we would need to be towed off the runway. The equipment was in fact standing by for us at landing and detected hydraulic fluid that contaminated the runway.ATC had provided a modified box vector for us, and as we were approaching base I exchanged roles with the First Officer and assumed aircraft control as Pilot Flying. I called for the deferred items. Another opportunity exists in the deferred items with a descent checklist step stating the autobrakes should be off. In our debrief, we discussed that the were a number of items in the deferred items checklist that were not applicable to our situation such as alternate gear and flap extension. This may have led to the error and missing the descent checklist step. We committed to running future checklists step-by-step.The flaps 20 approach was uneventful, and I used the autopilot and autothrottle until short final. Approach had given us a discrete frequency for ZZZ Tower and the rescue equipment. At landing, I felt a sensation similar to anti-skid activation and immediately disengaged the autobrakes by slightly advancing the speed brake lever, and came to a stop using the operable reverser and manual braking.ZZZ Fire and Rescue assessed our aircraft and we set up for a tow-in. ZZZ Fire and Rescue noted hydraulic fluid contaminated the runway.We proceeded under tow to gate. At the gate, I discussed the event with Dispatch and the [Chief Pilot].In my debrief with the First Officer, we went through the debrief card. The items that seemed to go well included workload management, automation management, and our planning and decision making. The humbling items that could have gone better would include my monitoring and cross check of the items on the non-normal checklist. In a future event, with time available, one of us will independently re-run the non-normal checklist before committing to the approach. Calling for the gear up as we abandoned the approach was a rote response. With a hydraulic issue on arrival in the terminal area, next time we will maintain the existing configuration unless performance reasons dictate otherwise.Communication with Dispatch should have been more thorough, next time I will spend an extra two minutes to send a more informative message to Dispatch.
ASRS:1795635.s: During an ILS approach to ZZZ, the crew encountered a left hydraulic system pressure loss, executed a go-around, and later landed with auto-brakes engaged due to a missed checklist step. The aircraft stopped safely with manual braking and reversers, but required a tow after hydraulic fluid contaminated the runway.

ASRS:1795680.n: Prior to performing the engine start checklist, we noticed the main cabin door was not indicating closed. We asked the Flight Attendant to try to reopen and close the door and after multiple attempts it would not show closed so we called Maintenance. To my surprise, they offered to defer it under MEL52-3-1 without sending Maintenance to the aircraft. In my experience, mechanics have always gone over to the aircraft whenever there are issues relating to the main cabin door so I found this a little odd. We reviewed the MEL and Maintenance Control asked about nuisance messages which did not exist at the time, so we put the MEL in the logbook but shortly after I realized that we did not have any nuisance messages because we did not have engine 1 running which would prompt a Master Warning MAIN DOOR OPEN. We went back to Maintenance Control and discussed how the maintenance action required to remove the micro switches was required because once we start engine 1 the system logic will generate a MAIN CABIN DOOR EICAS warning. They argued that was not a 'nuisance' because it was only going to triple chime once and not continuously and I had to reiterate multiple times that a Master Warning EICAS being displayed is inappropriate and a distraction/nuisance. I was passed over to the Maintenance Supervisor, and another Maintenance Control person who all seemed generally confused with what I was talking about. I suspect they misunderstood the system logic or which door we were deferring because they said they issue this MEL '2-3 times a week' which I highly doubt. Eventually, we told them they need to send a mechanic out because we had already made a PA that the aircraft would need to be inspected by Maintenance. A mechanic came out and removed the micro switches faster than it took to stay on that circular conversation with Maintenance Control. Shortly after applying the MEL and pushing back, we started engine 1 and MAIN DOOR OPEN EICAS warning presented. This was extremely confusing because that message should not appear when the micro switches are removed, similar to when they perform that same procedure on the bag door micro switches. Additionally, when a message is going to be displayed after an MEL is applied it usually includes that information as a note on the MEL, like with MEL 21-13. I called a friend in Flight Technical for some clarification on why that message appeared and he agreed it should not be present and it was possible the maintenance action was not done appropriately because an Embraer manual shows the need to remove 4 micro switches but the AMM Task only has the Mechanic remove 2. I called Maintenance Control again and explained the situation, and the supervisor was adamant the AMM Task was completed correctly and only required the removal of 2 micro switches and reiterated multiple times that the message should be displayed because the micro switches were removed. At this point, we had been racing against a DOT 3 hour limit clock and an FAR 117 max duty time limit, so we elected to take the aircraft because the supervisor confirmed all maintenance actions required of this MEL had been completed, we verified compliance with the MEL, and we knew why that message was presented.Either there is a discrepancy with the AMM that doesn't tell them to remove all of the required micro switches or the MEL should include a note that says the Master Warning displayed. Accepted aircraft after confirmation from Maintenance Control Supervisor that there was no other option to make the EICAS Master Warning extinguish. First of all, is this an MEL we really want our planes flying multiple days with? The aircraft flew an entire day the following day, so this MEL was not applied to get the aircraft to a maintenance hub. If we had an RTO (rejected takeoff), how would I know which door is really opened and closed? That's literally why we have the door pages up during takeoff. Next, the company needs to investigate the inconsistency withthis MEL not saying the EICAS warning should be present or the improper maintenance action that caused it to appear.
ASRS:1795680.s: The flight crew and maintenance personnel encountered a main cabin door indication issue prior to engine start. After deferring the fault under MEL 52-3-1, a Master Warning EICAS message appeared upon starting engine 1, which the crew attributed to a discrepancy between the AMM task and the required micro-switch removal.

ASRS:1795726.n: Upon departure from ATL Runway 8R, we encountered severe wake turbulence passing through 600 feet AGL until about 1,000 feet AGL. Momentary full left aileron deflection was necessary to maintain directional control. Three large rolling moments were experienced over a span of approximately 10-15 seconds. The preceding aircraft was an A321.A321 wake turbulence, light quartering crosswind kept the wake over the runway centerline.Realize that wake turbulence is not always directly related to weight and small airbus aircraft are very heavily loaded on a small wing.
ASRS:1795726.s: The crew encountered severe wake turbulence from a preceding A321 between 600 and 1,000 feet AGL after departing ATL Runway 8R. Light quartering crosswinds kept the wake over the centerline, requiring full left aileron deflection to maintain control during three rolling moments.

ASRS:1795783.n: Captain advised we had a maintenance issue to have checked out before boarding our return flight to ZZZ. I believe pilots saw something had leaked under the engine, observed by FO walk around. Mechanic looked for AC left engine fuel leak suspected by pilots, after a period of time (I do not recall) mechanic could not find leak, he signed off on logbook. Pax began boarding, entry door was closed, on push back, FA's were doing safety demo when FA 4 was called over by passenger sitting in right window seat a few rows aft of the wing. Passenger stated something was dripping from wing. Demo was almost complete, FA 4 continued with demo then looked out to see pax concern. Upon seeing fluid dripping from several places along the underside of the wing, she went to get another FA to see the issue. FA 4 took FA 3 to see the dripping. FA 4 and 3 went to the forward entry area to inform FA 1, I was working FA 4 and standing next to FA 1 so I was also informed at this time. FA 1 called Captain (CA) to advise. Several minutes later we were notified by CA that we were going back to gate and need to disarm doors. Same mechanic (only one I saw) returned. Passengers remained onboard while he checked the issue further. It is my understanding he reported he still found no leak. Sometime later CA advised crew and passengers via PA that we would be starting engines at the gate to further troubleshoot the problem, he advised passengers to remain seated. I was told this test was done at the Captain's request, not the instruction of this mechanic. Engine test was completed, seat belt sign turned off, more time passed and it was decided to deplane passengers. While crew waited on the AC for info from the company as to our schedule and whether this plane was going to be able to be repaired, our FO showed CA a video of the fuel leak while the engine test was running. I saw this video, fuel was pouring from the engine like a running garden hose. CA stated he had no confidence in this mechanics ability to perform his job as he appeared that he had no idea how to handle it. While I was discussing this with CA he told me he asked the mechanic earlier to call Company Maintenance base for instruction. The mechanic told CA yes he did call Company. CA told me he was angry with this mechanic because he himself called Company and was told mechanic did not contact them. Aircraft was taken out of service hours later. Upon arrival at Gate 1 in ZZZ, ground personnel connected to headset after engine shutdown to report a fluid leaking from number 1 (left) engine. He smelled his fingers, reported that it smelled like fuel, and asked me to investigate the fluid. The First Officer and I both investigated, and felt, to the best of our knowledge, that the fluid smelled like fuel. At that point, there was a puddle under the #1 engine, 3 feet in diameter, and fuel was dripping at a rate of 2-3 drips per second. As we stood there discussing, the dripping reduced to 1 drip every 4-5 seconds. The FO and I agreed that we were unfamiliar with any allowable drips on the 737 MAX LEAP engines, and I proceeded to the cockpit to make an entry in the aircraft logbook, dispatch a code in ACARS, and call the Maintenance Control to coordinate for a maintenance technician. The technician arrived and we conferred on the above information, and he proceeded to investigate and coordinate with the maintenance team in Company (my assumptions, although I did hear his telephone conversation at one point). After his investigation, he returned to the cockpit to inform me that he had opened the engine cowl, performed his checks, and found all valves ready for service. He signed off the write up and dispatched the aircraft for service. We boarded the passengers and pushed from the gate at XA:40. Push back was normal, engine start on engine #2 was normal. After push back was complete, we started engine #1. After engine start, and after the push crew had disconnected and given me a salute, ground personnel came back, pointing to the #1 engine. At the same time, the Cabin Crew called to alert me to a passenger that was reporting fluid leaking from the RIGHT side of the aircraft, and a Flight Attendant confirmed that we were leaking fluid. The report that fluid was leaking from the right was incongruous, and caused the FO and I a couple minutes to confer and investigate what that could be. We later found out the leak was in fact from the LEFT side, and was from the #1 engine. I did note in my investigation, that the #1 main tank fuel quantity differed from the #2 main tank fuel quantity by nearly 400 lbs, a discrepancy that didn't exist before pushback as I had noted the fuel during the Before Start checklist. By this time, the same ground coordinator who had reported the previous leak connected to headset and reported that we were again leaking fuel from the #1 engine. His report was that fuel was gushing out from under the engine cowl. The FO and I coordinated and elected to taxi back to the gate to expedite arrival and engine shutdown. The ground crew quickly assembled and we returned to the gate at approximately XA:48, and shut down both engines. I made another logbook entry and called Maintenance Control to inform them that we had returned to the gate and required the maintenance technician to perform more checks before we could depart. The maintenance technician returned, and we performed an engine run at the gate on the #1 engine, which resulted in identifying a large fuel leak, with the technician recording video. At this point the aircraft was taken out of service, and I began coordinating with station personnel and Crew Scheduling for subsequent actions.
ASRS:1795783.s: Pilots and cabin crew reported a fuel leak from the left engine on a 737 MAX during pushback and engine start, despite a mechanic initially signing off the aircraft as serviceable. The aircraft was returned to the gate and taken out of service after a ground run confirmed a large fuel leak, which the captain attributed to the mechanic's failure to properly diagnose the issue or contact maintenance control.

ASRS:1795821.n: My Captain and I were in the descent phase of our flight initially level at 4,000 feet MSL while on frequency with DFW TRACON.My Captain and I both heard the Controller give us a descent clearance to 2,400 feet MSL, we both accepted the clearance and my Captain read back/acknowledged the clearance to ATC.The clearance to descend to 2,400 feet did not seem unusual or out of place as we were approximately 20 NM from the RBD airport, upon leveling our aircraft at 2,400 feet my Captain and I were discussing visually seeing radio towers at our 11o'clock and approximately 10 SM in ahead and to the left of our flight path and we were expecting to be vectored around the obstacles.A few seconds after we had discussed the mentioned radio towers DFW TRACON challenged our altitude of 2,400 feet insisting we were supposed to be at 4,000 feet MSL upon hearing that radio call, and confirming with ATC we expeditiously initiated a climb back to 4,000 feet.At no point in the flight did I feel like we were in danger or in an un-safe proximity to the obstacle radio towers or in the vicinity any other aircraft as we were in VMC conditions, with good visibility.In my perspective, the Controller seemed to be over worked at the time of the occurrence and did not verify with my Captain after his read back to descend to 2,400 feet, indicating we had read back a correct clearance.After completing our flight, getting ready to taxi into parking on the ground at RBD, we were informed there was a similar sounding aircraft call sign on frequency and that the descent clearance to 2,400 feet was for the similar sounding call sign and not for us.We were also informed that we were 'stepped on' during our radio transmission, unknown to us during our read back to DFW TRACON to descend to 2,400 feet. It seems to me DFW TRACON should have confirmed who was supposed to descend to 2,400 feet when they did not receive a clear read back. While descending for landing at the Dallas executive airport, we were given a delayed descent with a crossing restriction which required an expedited descent. We hustled down and made the assigned crossing altitude restriction. Shortly following that, we were assigned a new frequency and cleared to descend to 4,000 feet.
