We initiated a normal descent and almost at the same time we were leveling, we were cleared to descend to 2,400.I acknowledged the clearance to descend on the radio and we initiated a normal descent to 2,400 feet. As we were descending, I pointed out the radio towers at our 11 O'clock position to my co-pilot. My thoughts were that the controller would give us a slight vector to the right, otherwise I would request a turn.Very shortly after that, the Controller challenged our altitude. I replied that we were cleared to descent and that I had acknowledged the descent. The Controller stated that they needed us back at 4,000. We immediately complied.The Controller appeared to be very busy. I tried to keep all communication correct and prompt. In speaking with the ATC person he stated that there was another aircraft with the same registration ending - same letter and that the Controller referred to that aircraft with an abbreviated call sign.In my opinion, if the Controller does not get a clear read back from an aircraft, especially if there are similar call signs on frequency -- then the Controller should state 'That clearance was for N--- only' I have heard that many times.'Contributing to this was the fact that there were several aircraft that the Controller was working and may have been challenged doing so.I never felt in danger at any time as we saw the radio towers and am not aware of any conflict with any other aircraft in our proximity.
ASRS:1795821.s: Pilots descended to 2,400 feet MSL during approach to RBD after accepting a clearance intended for a similar-sounding call sign. The controller challenged the altitude due to a transmission overlap and workload, prompting an immediate climb back to 4,000 feet with no safety conflict.

ASRS:1795837.n: We were 3rd in line for takeoff at ZZZ and it was particularly busy. There was a lot of rotary traffic present in the right pattern as I believe there was a helicopter event present. We had been having breakfast at the cafe and witnessed 4-5 Cessna 172's doing power off approach so they were in the left pattern. When we were holding short of [Runway] XX @ [Taxiway] A we could hear the Controller on tower was busy and we waited for around 10 minutes. In that time, myself and the PIC who was left seat agreed that it was standard traffic pattern, I checked the sectional to confirm. We made a comment that perhaps rotary traffic was using the right pattern for separation. We got called by Tower and the Controller thanked us for our patience and said Runway XX clear for takeoff. We proceeded to takeoff and climbed in the upwind to around 650 feet before making a turn to the left. Whilst we were in the crosswind segment, still climbing we noticed a plane that appeared to be 200-300 feet below us in right downwind for Runway XY off to our left, on its way to pass underneath us. It was probably 600 feet away when we first noticed it and it passed underneath our nose. We were both puzzled as to what they were doing. Once we were clear of them, we made another left turn into left downwind for XX the Controller came on the radio and said to us that we had come very close to 'my' ILS traffic for ZZZ1 and that they had it written down that we had requested right traffic, which was incorrect. Our inactions were verifying left or right traffic, assuming left traffic was standard especially due to all the rotary traffic using the right downwind for XX. The Controller was particularly busy and perhaps as we were heading to ZZZ1 they figured it was more direct to make right traffic. We climbed to 200 feet of TPA [Traffic Pattern Altitude] on the upwind so to make sure we were as close to TPA before being in Downwind at the wrong altitude. We were cleared for takeoff for Runway XX. Prior to takeoff, I was monitoring entry of all aircraft entering the traffic pattern. Helicopters were on right downwind Runway XX, while fix-winged were entering left downwind Runway XX. I never communicated which way I was going to turn crosswind since I was following the other aircraft that have been in the pattern throughout the morning. After departure, I climbed to about 700 feet and started to monitor other traffic in the area prior to making my crosswind turn. I saw a small aircraft to the left of me that was descending about 200-300 feet below. I then started to make a left crosswind turn from XX0 degrees to approximately YY0 degrees. I flew over the traffic and continued heading south for ZZZ2. ZZZ Tower Controller then addressed me on the radio that they had me down for a right downwind turn. I never once communicated I was making a right downwind turn nor heard the Controller mention, 'make right crosswind upon departure'. If I wasn't supposed to make a left crosswind because of other traffic on an ILS for ZZZ1, why didn't the Controller mention that to me prior to departure? I would have gladly complied and made a right crosswind turn and continued my course to ZZZ2.
ASRS:1795837.s: Pilots departing Runway XX at ZZZ made a left crosswind turn, conflicting with ILS traffic on a right downwind. The controller stated they had recorded a request for right traffic, while the pilots assumed left traffic was standard due to observed rotary operations and did not communicate their intended turn.

ASRS:1795852.n: After takeoff, during climb phase, clearance was given from ZZZ Approach [Control] to climb restrict to 12.000 feet direct ZZZZZ intersection. When crossing 10,500 feet, ZZZ Approach instructed to call ZZZ Center on frequency XYZ.AB. I did try to call ZZZ [Center] on XYZ.AB several times, but no contact received. I could listen ZZZ Center very weak on XYZ.AB, and could listen the other aircraft communicating. I tried to ask another aircraft for a relay between me and ZZZ Center, but no answer. No answer from ZZZ [Center] also. I tried to contact back ZZZ Approach and ask for a different frequency, but had no answer from ZZZ Approach also. I started looking on my charts and started calling ZZZ Center on other frequencies, but no answer again. I tried to contact XYX.ZB, but no answer also. This was when I realized that I was facing a communication fail. At this moment, I selected 7600 (communication fail code) on my transponder (squawk). Decided to continue the flight following my flight plan clearance received, towards my destination. Over ZZZ1 tried to call ZZZ [Approach] but no answer. During all time I tried to use different radio equipment on board and also keep trying contact with ZZZ Center, ZZZ1 Approach, ZZZ Tower, another aircraft that sometimes I could listen very weak, but no answer.When approaching ZZZZZ1 intersection, on XYX.ZB I started listening ZZZ Center transmitting blind for me a telephone number for me to call. I also could listen if I received the message to press ident, I did. After that, ZZZ transmitted to me, blind again, to turn left heading 270 and descend to 6,000 feet, and asking me to press ident if I received. I pressed ident, and followed the instruction given. ZZZ [Controller] replied that they see my ident, and weather information for ZZZ [Airport] was given to me, together with a VFR approach and landing clearance on ZZZ3 Runway XX, and ident was requested again. I understood and pressed ident again. ZZZ Center said to me to try contact with ZZZ1 Approach on XCY.DZ I tried, but no answer was received again, and I kept monitoring both frequencies, the reception was very weak and noisy. After few moments I could listen a last transmission saying me the weather and clear to land on Runway XX, after landing try to call ground.I did land on Runway XX, and after landing, vacated the Runway via Taxiway 1, stopped and tried to call Ground. Again, no contact. Decided to turn left on Taxiway 2 and look for a place to park. I couldn't see any signal from Tower or follow me car at that time. When I was closer to the Tower, I could listen to Ground calling me, and I replied back. He said he was receiving me too weak. Instruction was given to continue Taxiway 2, hold short Runway XY. Next instruction, cross Runway XY turn left on [Taxiway] 3 and hold short Runway XX. At the holding, communication was lost again. Parking brakes applied. I took my phone, called ZZZ [Center] and asked ZZZ1 Tower telephone number. I tried to call Tower but phone didn't complete the call. After few minutes, I decided to make a 180 turning back, to not cross the runway. I did it and followed Taxiway 2 back, when I received a transmission on the ground frequency saying to turn left on Taxiway 4 and park. This was what I did. After stopping the aircraft, I didn't move from inside until police and the airport ground personnel came to me and said me that I can leave the aircraft. Before leaving the flight deck, I took my phone and called the ZZZ Tower again and after speaking with [the Controller], situation explained, he asked me to call ZZZ center on phone number given. I did call ZZZ, asked to call with the supervisor. I explained all the situation and the same I am writing here on this report.After all done, I was asked to taxi the aircraft to another apron. I asked to park the aircraft at the hangar, closer to the FBO, where an aircraft technician could help me to troubleshoot and fix the airplane. A follow me car was provided to me and the taxi was done following the follow me car, and aircraft parked in front of the hangar.
ASRS:1795852.s: The pilot experienced a complete two-way radio communication failure during climb and approach after takeoff, likely due to weak signal reception. The crew squawked 7600, followed blind instructions from ATC to land, and eventually parked at a hangar for technical troubleshooting after intermittent ground contact.

ASRS:1795879.n: At Gate XX in ZZZ, I was notified of a Passenger with a lithium-ion powered heart monitor. She told the Flight Attendant that her spare battery was in her checked luggage. I asked the Gate Agent if this was okay. The Agent was not sure but was going to check. I then called Dispatch to check on the battery. Dispatch connected me with someone else in Operations who said it was okay to continue. After talking it over with Operations and Dispatch and having been given the okay to continue, we were on are way to ZZZ1. After landing, I received an email saying that the battery needed to be in her carry-on bag, not in the checked bag. The cabin was notified of a Passenger with a lithium-ion battery powered heart monitor, of which she had her spare battery in her checked luggage. After consulting Dispatch and others at Operations, the Captain was told that this was okay with our policies and procedures. Once we landed in ZZZ1, we were told this was against our policies and procedures.
ASRS:1795879.s: The Captain and cabin crew departed with a passenger's spare lithium-ion heart monitor battery in checked luggage after Operations and Dispatch approved it. Post-landing, the crew was informed the battery placement violated policy, contradicting the pre-flight clearance.

ASRS:1795883.n: After pushback, while centered on Taxiway D8 in the alley between terminals [1 and 2], I noticed multitudes of vehicle traffic (Passenger buses, tugs, fuel trucks, etc.) moving along the edge of the alley. Unfortunately, those Ground vehicles have no defined lane to stay within that guarantees wingtip clearance from taxiing aircraft. As a result, the Ground traffic did not move in a standardized flow/distance from our aircraft in the alley. In fact, depending on size/type of aircraft parked at their gates, the ground traffic was not able to move in a straight line and would move out toward the center of the alley. In my assessment, the risk for misjudging vehicle/aircraft wing tip clearance, by either Aircrew or Ground Personnel, will increase during low ambient light and/or low visibility conditions.Airport Operations should paint a Ground vehicle taxi lane that guarantees clearance from aircraft pushing and entering/exiting the length of the alley between Terminal 1 and 2. Operations should emphasize the higher risk/potential for collision in this area during annual Ground Operator refresher training and initial qualification. At a minimum, update Company bulletin to warn Crews about uncontrolled vehicle movement in close proximity to taxiing/pushing aircraft and the need for increased vigilance.
ASRS:1795883.s: The pilot reported that while taxiing on Taxiway D8 between Terminals 1 and 2, uncontrolled ground vehicles lacked defined lanes, causing inconsistent wingtip clearance. The reporter attributed this collision risk to the absence of painted vehicle lanes and recommended operational updates to mitigate hazards during low visibility.

ASRS:1795884.n: During single-engine taxi out, the A FA called the cockpit, informing us of passengers' non-compliance with the facemask policy. The decision was made to return to the gate. As we taxied back toward the Ramp, I coordinated with the Captain, advising that I felt it was appropriate to perform an After Landing flow prior to returning to the gate. Captain agreed, and I accomplished the flow. While holding for a gate, and on the apron with the parking brake set, the A FA called back to the cockpit, advising that the passengers were now willing to comply and that the three FAs were comfortable with continuing the flight.At this point we re-accomplished a Before Taxi flow (as appropriate for our single engine taxi configuration), then ran a Before Taxi Checklist. We then coordinated with ATC to proceed with a taxi clearance for departure. The Number 1 engine was started and the rest of the taxi and takeoff proceeded uneventfully. Once airborne, I noticed that we had departed with the autobrake selector in the OFF position. As I thought about the sequence of events leading to that I thought of two things: placing that switch to RTO takes place in the Captain's Before Start flow. I also recalled that when I performed the After Start flow (following the Passenger incident), I placed the Window Heat switches to ON, another item that is normally accomplished in the Captain's Before Start flow.Clearly, in our unique situation, a Before Taxi flow, followed by a Before Taxi Checklist was insufficient to reposition all switches to their appropriate positions prior to taxi and takeoff. Of note, neither of us felt rushed, and we both felt that we used good CRM to methodically think through our situation before continuing, yet in the end, something was missing. I've referenced the manuals, looking for a procedure that would have trapped our errors, but am still left wondering. Since we started the original taxi single engine and never shutdown that engine, the procedure in Flight Ops Manual never entered our minds, yet that guidance probably would've caught the error.Non-standard Ops lead to inadvertent takeoff with auto brakes selected off. On taxi out, the A FA called to tell me that there was a family being non-compliant regarding the face mask policy. I made the decision to taxi back to the gate. I asked the FO to complete the After Landing Checklist. While we were waiting for a gate, the FA called to tell us, 'Never mind, the issue is resolved.' At that point, we completed the Before Taxi Checklist and taxied to the runway. After takeoff, the FO pointed out that RTO switch was not re-selected to 'armed.' Our unique situation made it impossible for autobrake re-selection to occur.In this situation, our normal checklist does not catch the error. I should have triple checked everything because our routine taxi out was interrupted.RTO reengage missed during a taxi back to the gate and subsequent cancellation of that.
ASRS:1795884.s: The flight crew returned to the gate due to passenger mask non-compliance, then resumed taxi after the issue resolved. This non-standard sequence caused the crew to miss re-arming the autobrake to RTO, resulting in an inadvertent takeoff with the selector in the OFF position.

ASRS:1795900.n: When reviewing weight and balance takeoff data, the 'Flap Retraction Altitude/Min Cleanup Altitude Engine Out listed for Runway 35R was different from the that listed on Jeppesen 10-7 chart. The aircraft data showed 7,400 ft. as the cleanup altitude while the Jeppesen chart showed 7,187 ft. We checked the Takeoff/Landing Reference section and it also showed 7,400 ft. We remembered reading somewhere that [performance] data supersedes other data if there is a conflict. I checked the [performance data] link on the COS page and under Normal Operations Section, it states 'In the event an Electronic Flight Plan(EFP) instruction differs between sources, use EFP output from ACARS.' It is apparent that the Jeppesen 10-7 chart is then incorrect as the other two sources state the minimum is 7,400 ft. We set 7,400 ft. as the cleanup altitude because of the statement about using ACARS output if different data exists and because it is the most conservative/higher altitude but this needs to be corrected to prevent confusion for Crews in the future. Thanks. Incorrect engine out minimum safe altitude on Jeppesen Chart.
ASRS:1795900.s: Pilots identified a discrepancy between the aircraft's 7,400 ft engine-out cleanup altitude and the lower 7,187 ft listed on the Jeppesen 10-7 chart for Runway 35R. They set the higher altitude based on ACARS performance data, noting the Jeppesen chart requires correction to prevent future crew confusion.

ASRS:1795909.n: We landed [Runway] 26R, and taxied FD NE to hold short [Runway] 26L. A small airplane, a single-engine Piper, was also holding short of [Runway] 26L at NE. As we approached the hold short line at a taxi speed of 2-3 kt, the First Officer asked me if I could see the small airplane ahead of us. We were less than 50 feet away, and I was just starting to see it, but it almost completely blended into the taxiway and surrounding lights. We were configured per Company SOP regarding ground movement, including taxi light on. We were not advised by the Tower Controller of any ground traffic ahead of us. I attached some images that were taken when we were stopped approximately 50 feet away from the small airplane ahead of us.
ASRS:1795909.s: The flight crew approached a Piper holding short of Runway 26L at 2-3 knots but nearly collided due to the aircraft blending into taxiway lights. The Tower Controller provided no traffic advisories, and the crew stopped 50 feet away despite following standard operating procedures.

ASRS:1795920.n: At XA:36, a baggage tug runner with 2 carts crossing the ramp from the X concourse on the interline baggage route (between 1 and 2 on the X and 3 and 4 on the Y concourse) did not yield to aircraft traffic Westbound on the XX line. The Ramp Tower controller alerted the flight crew of the tug and carts, at which time the crew advised they had the tug in sight. The tug, which is supposed to give way to all traffic while using the interline baggage route, did not yield to the aircraft, which had to come to an abrupt stop, less than 25 feet from the cart. The City and County of ZZZ was notified, and Airport Operations was dispatched in an attempt to track down the tug runner, but they were unable to identify the cart and driver. The Ramp Station Operations Supervisor was also notified. The station's camera system was down to start the morning, and did not come back up until XA:37, 1 minute after the incident occurred.
ASRS:1795920.s: A baggage tug runner failed to yield to a westbound aircraft on the XX line, forcing the flight crew to stop abruptly less than 25 feet from the carts. The driver could not be identified because the station's camera system was down during the incident.

ASRS:1795928.n: It was determined that pilot's FAA Medical was updated on 202011 with special Issuance / Expiration date and it was defaulted to the 6-month expiration date in Pilot Records.Due to the high volumes of FAA Medical coming in for the past few months and FAA Medical extensions, this one fell through the cracks.Because of the pandemic last year, pilots were granted FAA medical extensions on their 'Expiration Time', and that may have caused the confusion and to slip by.We are very careful when processing FAA Medicals including other work that we process, and fully intend to process our work as accurately as possible.
ASRS:1795928.s: A pilot's FAA Medical with a special issuance expiration date was incorrectly defaulted to a six-month limit in Pilot Records due to high processing volumes and pandemic-related extension confusion. The error occurred because the specific medical record fell through the cracks during data entry.

ASRS:1795934.n: DFW has an odd system of ground-frequency assignment for the east side of the airport, that has long concerned pilots for the very reason this incident highlighted. Outbounds from the remote, E Terminal spots of XX to YY are often assigned the discrete Ground frequency of 121.80, even though all other east-side operations for the apt are issued 121.65. However, those of us assigned 121.80 are never switched to the 'main' frequency of .65 that everyone else is operating on.On this day, as we taxied out we were assigned 121.80, but the First Officer, to his credit, decided to take the initiative to also pull up 121.65 on the other radio, so we could hear what was being said to and by the other aircraft operating in the same area and taxiways and the same controller. Northbound on Taxiway K approaching Taxiway Z there was a B737 waiting to pull out. Ground issued instructions to them over 121.65 to pull out ahead of us, and then transmitted to us on the same frequency to give way. The only reason we were aware of these transmissions was because we were monitoring both frequencies. We gave way to the B737 without incident and everyone went on their way none the wiser, except us. Had we not been monitoring 121.65 but just on our assigned frequency of 121.80, there's every reason to believe both aircraft would have gotten much closer together before the ground controller might have discovered his error, and ultimately, it was not his error but the assignment of two, discrete frequencies to different aircraft taxiing on the same taxiway.
ASRS:1795934.s: A crew taxiing at DFW on Ground frequency 121.80 avoided a conflict with a B737 by monitoring the alternate frequency 121.65, where the controller issued conflicting instructions. The incident resulted from the airport's practice of assigning discrete frequencies to aircraft on the same taxiway, which prevented the controller from addressing both crews simultaneously.

ASRS:1795943.n: While on the visual approach into HOU on the ILS 4. The FO (First Officer) was Pilot Flying and while he was flying the approach I noticed what I thought were two birds just to the right of the aircraft at around 9 o'clock but outside the course. I made the FO aware of this and continued to keep scanning for more birds in the area since the first one I saw was well clear of our course. However at 2,300 ft. and 0.5NM past ELREN on the ILS 4 the two objects were actually drones that past off our right hand side that were the size of two big birds. I noticed the two were indeed drones because I saw the propellers on two of them and they had a shiny black finish on them. I also checked the TCAS to see if they were there, but it didn't show them on the screen. I relayed this information to HOU tower and told them what altitude and where they were. Upon landing and taxing off the runway and contacting ground, I was given a phone number to call the tower to give them more information on the description of the drones, and where I spotted them on the approach.My suggestion is to always keep scanning the area for any hazards while flying even if the TCAS system doesn't show anything in the area.
ASRS:1795943.s: During a visual ILS 4 approach to HOU, the crew identified two drones at 2,300 ft past ELREN that were not displayed on TCAS. The pilots reported the drone's location and description to HOU Tower and Ground after landing.

ASRS:1795950.n: TA/RA on arrival. Flying the RAVEN6 arrival into BWI, we were level at 5,000 feet when a small aircraft flew beneath us. The aircraft showed to be 400 feet beneath us, and at that time the TCAS RA did not want us to maneuver. Once we passed the traffic, we notified ATC and landed.
ASRS:1795950.s: Pilots flying the RAVEN6 arrival into BWI at 5,000 feet encountered a small aircraft 400 feet below. The TCAS RA did not issue a maneuver command, so the crew passed the traffic, notified ATC, and landed.

ASRS:1795954.n: Pushback was delayed due to catering (and vehicles impeding the catering truck from approaching the aircraft). Following push clearance, the tug began the push but we came to a stop after approx. 15 sec. I thought perhaps something crossed behind us and we would resume the push. But, after a few more seconds, the tug driver said that a catering truck wasn't moving. That seemed odd, and the Captain and I wondered why a catering truck wouldn't clear a moving aircraft. That's when the Captain looked through his side window, over his shoulder and told me, 'THAT'S why the truck isn't moving - it's sitting under our wingtip!' We hadn't felt anything and the tug driver was asked if we were touching. He said that he couldn't tell. A crowd gathered. I informed ramp of our situation and our intent to remain in position to investigate. A maintenance rep came on interphone and let us know it was difficult to determine how close the wingtip was to the roof of the truck. It was judged safe to set brakes. After some time, it was decided to let air out of the truck's tires. Personnel climbed atop the truck and after getting a closer look, the truck was moved. No visible contact/damage was noted but the possibility was mentioned that the winds were moving the aircraft slightly and the wingtip may have bounced off the roof and that may have not been enough to show damage but that an inspection would be the best course of action. We were cleared to be pulled forward to the gate and the aircraft was taken out of service and the crew and passengers deplaned to the aircraft at the adjoining gate. The remainder of the flight was uneventful.Since we were being pushed straight back, we did not see the events leading up to the potential contact. It would seem that a combination of catering truck driver and wing walker inattention may have contributed.[Suggest] Company communications to [the catering company] and maintenance re-iterating the need to be vigilant. About 60 feet into a routine pushback, the aircraft stopped. The Tow Driver told us a 'catering truck driver is refusing to move.' I asked if I should set the Parking Brake. The Tow Driver said 'No.' I looked out the left window and saw a catering truck with no driver in the cab. I called Ramp Control on the radio to report the situation. I looked out the window again to see a Maintenance Technician on the catering truck's over-the-cab loading platform. He was leaning on the railing to look toward the aft-right side of the truck. I opened the aircraft L2 Window to get a better view. I saw the Left Wing apparently resting on the middle, top-right of the back portion of the catering truck. I saw numerous Ground Crew and Maintenance personnel walking around the catering truck gesturing at the apparent contact point. A Maintenance Supervisor saw me looking out the window and got on the Ground Interphone to tell me what was going on. She said they thought there was actually no contact with the catering truck but couldn't be sure until they employed an operable hydraulic work lift - the first one they tried was inoperative. I asked how big/small the gap was. She thought the wing was about an inch from touching the truck, but the wind was causing the aircraft to gently rock, possibly bouncing the wing off the top of the truck. After many minutes, a plan emerged to deflate the tires of the catering truck and tow it out of the way, preventing any possible further contact with the wing as the wind blew. After the catering truck was clear, the Maintenance Supervisor got back on the Ground Interphone to tell us the aircraft was being taken out of service as a precaution and a replacement Ground Crew would tow us back to the gate for deplaning. We were not to set the parking brake until safely at the gate. Company Operations and Maintenance coordinated a different aircraft for us to continue the flight. The tow was uneventful. Once parked, we ran the Shutdown Checklist. Maintenance Technicians boarded and asked us to not shut down the aircraft. They also invited the First Officer and me to go outside and get on the work lift to inspect the wing. To my eye, there was absolutely no indication of any kind that the wing had contacted the catering truck, however, I know that painted panels of modern materials can deform, return to shape, and not show outward signs of damage. Not that it was my decision, but I concurred with Maintenance in taking the aircraft out of service. Passengers and crew boarded the new aircraft and departed uneventfully.Cause Unknown. I would only be speculating on events that occurred out of my view.I can only speculate how this event occurred, so I cannot provide prevention suggestions.
ASRS:1795954.s: During pushback, the aircraft stopped when a stationary catering truck was found under the left wingtip, causing a potential contact incident. Although no visible damage was found, the aircraft was taken out of service for inspection, and passengers were transferred to a replacement flight.

ASRS:1795974.n: BWI Approach Control was vectoring us for a visual to RWY 10 and keeping us at 3,000 ft due to traffic below us at 2,000 ft. Approach turned us in on a short approach between COLUM and JEANS fix to Runway 10 and cleared us to 2,000 ft. On right base we were asked if field was in sight and we acknowledged it was and we were cleared for a visual to RWY 10 and contact tower. Crossing altitude at JEANS is 1,500 ft so pilot flying selected 1,500 to catch the glide path. At 1,800 ft tower said they were getting a low altitude alert and cleared to land. Pilot flying disconnected the autopilot and leveled which was just about on glide path 6.4 miles from runway. We were never below the 1,500 ft min altitude inside of COLUM and joined the glide slope normally and landed. The approach was stable at all times.Possible short approach clearance by ATC.Better vectors by ATC or requesting extended downwind. Possibly alert was issued due to leaving us high and us having to increase rate of descent. On arrival to BWI, the Approach Controller kept us at 3,000 ft due to a Cessna at 2,000 ft. As we were turned toward the final approach segment between COLUM and JEANS on the approach, the controller gave us 2,000 ft and asked if we had the field at 1,230 and 8 miles. We confirmed the airport in sight and we were cleared for the visual approach and told to contact Tower. Crossing alt at JEANS is 1,500 ft. We started to descend to 1,500 as we were rolling into the final at 1,800 ft in the descent the tower called a low alt alert. We leveled the aircraft at 1,800 ft and 6.4 miles from the runway. GS was captured and normal landing accomplished no other coms about low alt alert.We were cleared for a visual approach and were descending to the Altitude at the Marker. Apparently our rate of descent may have triggered the low alt alert. The approach controller could have extended us further out in order to give more time to descend at a slower rate since they had held us up high so long.
ASRS:1795974.s: BWI Approach Control vectored the aircraft for a short visual approach to Runway 10, holding it at 3,000 ft before clearing descent to 2,000 ft. A low altitude alert occurred during the descent to the 1,500 ft JEANS crossing altitude, likely caused by a high rate of descent, but the crew leveled and completed a stable landing.

ASRS:1795990.n: We were on the TIPTOE Visual Runway 28L. We were paired up with a heavy that was on [Runway] 28R. Due to the gusty winds from the north we ended flying on their wake which caused our plane to roll, creating an upset. We followed upset recovery procedures and we aborted landing and went around. Factors are gusty winds from the north and also night time. Being paired with a heavy caused the winds to push the heavy airplane wake in our flight path. During strong winds from the north, they need to provide greater spacing between planes to help mitigate wake. On final approach in SFO we were paired up with a heavy jet on the right side with very gusty cross winds from the north. On 5 mile final we encountered wake from the heavy and it induced a roll upset. The recovery procedure was utilized and aircraft control was regained at which point we encountered the wake again and it induced a second roll upset. Proper upset recovery techniques were utilized and we went around without issue. The cause of this event was due to high gusty winds out of the north and being paired too closely with a heavy jet upwind. The resulting wake was blown directly into our flight path. Having known about the winds and the pairing of the heavy jet closely spaced upwind, I would suggest staying a minimum of 1 dot high on the glide slope and requesting a long landing so as to avoid potential wake in the future.
ASRS:1795990.s: Pilots on a TIPTOE visual approach to Runway 28L at SFO encountered wake turbulence from a closely spaced heavy jet on Runway 28R due to gusty north winds. The resulting roll upsets forced the crew to execute upset recovery procedures and go around.

ASRS:1796009.n: On short final in SFO, while landing on 28R around 400 feet, we encountered severe wake turbulence from a 747 ahead of us landing on 28L. Executed a missed approach.
ASRS:1796009.s: The crew encountered severe wake turbulence from a 747 landing on 28L while on short final to 28R at SFO around 400 feet. They executed a missed approach as a result.

ASRS:1796032.n: In cruise at FL350 a 747 passed right to left 1000 ft above. There was no traffic advisory from ATC, and we did not see the overflying airplane till it was passing. We discussed turning left to parallel the wake or descend to avoid. These options were not possible with the limited time available. The seat belt sign was turned on and moments later we experienced light-moderate wake turbulence. I immediately called to confirm the FAs (Flight Attendants) were ok. They confirmed that although they we standing in the galley they were ok. A passenger who was returning from the lavatory did bump their head on the sidewall as they were taking their seat. FAs reported that they offered ice pack and assistance but the passenger declined. From first sign of overflying plane till we experienced wake was well under a minute. With even an extra 20 seconds we would have had time to avoid the wake. See and avoid or an ATC traffic advisory would have made this easy to avoid.
ASRS:1796032.s: A 747 overflew the reporting aircraft at FL350 without an ATC traffic advisory, causing light-moderate wake turbulence. A passenger bumped their head while returning from the lavatory, though flight attendants remained uninjured in the galley.

ASRS:1796045.n: While performing Removal of MAU (Module Avionics Unit) 2, The first step is to remove the EICC (Emergency Integrated Control Center). The first step in removal of the EICC is to de-energize HOT BUS 1. I performed the procedure of removing battery 1 connector, removing external power and tagging the overhead panel. Ground power cord was removed, and external power door shut and tagged. I removed the rain cover and connectors to the EICC. I was in the process of removing the power and ground feed cables to the EICC at the back of the unit. I backed the ground wire nut most of the way off and started on the battery 1 wire. While removing the nut from the battery 1 cable my ratchet hit the aileron bell crank and an electrical arc occurred. The arc was massive. I than noticed glowing coming from the aileron cable force cables. I ran to the cockpit and removed the fire extinguisher. When I returned to the fwd electronics bay area, the cables were still glowing. I discharged the extinguisher onto the force cables. One quick burst on the captain's side and one quick burst on the co pilots' side. Verifying no more glow, I had co workers go get the lead and sup. I was working off my IPAD.
ASRS:1796045.s: A mechanic performing MAU 2 removal caused a massive electrical arc and fire when a ratchet struck the aileron bell crank while disconnecting the battery 1 cable. The mechanic extinguished the glowing force cables with a fire extinguisher after the arc occurred in the forward electronics bay.

ASRS:1796070.n: I began my pre-flight and noticed that my emergency exit rows were not working. Maintenance came on and they said that all the batteries were dead. The aircraft was brought in from ZZZ1 [airport], so it was not the first flight of the day.
ASRS:1796070.s: A cabin crew member reported that emergency exit rows were inoperative during pre-flight on an aircraft arriving from ZZZ1. Maintenance determined all batteries were dead, noting the aircraft was not on its first flight of the day.

ASRS:1796089.n: Aircraft X migrated from [program] to [program 1] records tracking.Prior to migration, [Logbook Deferral Sheet] 70XXXXXX was issued for replacement of the RH MLG FWD Trunion pin at next gear replacement and [Logbook Deferral Sheet] 70XXXXXY was issued for inspection of the pin each 24 month interval as required per [Repair Document] 32-XX-XX-X. At system migration [Logbook Deferral Sheet] 70XXXXXX was converted to [Logbook Deferral Sheet] 02XXXXX and [Logbook Deferral Sheet] 70XXXXXY was deleted. Therefore, the previous accomplishment history doesn't appear to be available since the [Logbook Deferral Sheet] is no longer accessible in [program]. [Maintenance Operations Manual] 03.XX.X states in part, 'Review all [documentation] for correctness of deferral reference, repetitive and/or terminating action.' During system migration the repetitive action requirements are not being transferred to the surviving [Logbook Deferral Sheet].I just happened to catch this one (and will update with a [Repair Document] revised inspection interval) but it is a systemic issue and virtually every migrated item that previously had a separate [Logbook Deferral Sheet] for an interim inspection will have a high potential of missing a required inspection because the previous tracking items are being deleted without the data being transferred and Maintenance Control not have access to the precious item history. As a side note, when Maintenance Control does a Spec Table update we are required to enter ZZZ (line) for the function to work. This results in the entry appearing as if it was made by a ZZZ line station person instead of coming from Maintenance Control. This is inaccurate.
ASRS:1796089.s: A mechanic reported that during an aircraft records system migration, a repetitive inspection requirement for a landing gear trunion pin was deleted, causing a loss of maintenance history. This systemic error risks missing future inspections because the new system fails to transfer data from deleted deferral sheets.

ASRS:1796105.n: After startup with a student, we performed a brake check, both sides, with a positive exchange of controls and no issues. After receiving our taxi clearance for an intersection departure, I observed my student taxiing faster than usual, and off centerline. I told him to slow down and bring the aircraft back to centerline, and he informed me there was a problem with the right brake. I took control, was unable to slow the aircraft, and with the runway hold short line approaching notified ground of my inability to stop. I swung to the right, and used brake to perform a 180 degree turn at speed, but wasn't able to turn tight enough to avoid crossing. I notified tower of my crossing, and cleared the runway environment. I got a clearance to taxi back to parking, where we ended the attempted flight, and shut the aircraft down until maintenance could diagnose and resolve the issue.
ASRS:1796105.s: A pilot and student taxiing for an intersection departure encountered a right brake failure, preventing the aircraft from stopping before the runway hold short line. The pilot executed a high-speed 180-degree turn, crossed the runway, and returned to parking to end the flight for maintenance.

ASRS:1796107.n: We were returning to ZZZ from ZZZ1 late on the afternoon. The enroute environment was apparently busier than the recent 'new normal' for that time of year as we had been limited in our climb clearances to between one- and three-thousand feet per climb clearance since our departure 25 minutes earlier. Our most recent climb clearance was to FL400 (on our way to our filed FL410). Subsequently, ATC called traffic (I don't recall the model or the horizontal distance away) at '1,000 feet ABOVE YOUR ASSIGNED ALTITUDE' (emphasis mine). I would have replied 'Looking' or some similar acknowledgment. I did look and then subsequently noticed my FO (who was PF and in the left seat) had shallowed our climb to 100 FPM or so out of FL390 -- significantly less than the 5 or 600 FPM I would have expected. We were also very light, so a climb rate that shallow would have soon required a power reduction. At about the same time we got a TA and the Controller asked us to confirm we were level (or leveling?) at FL390. I don't recall the exact exchange, but I would have replied something to the effect that we were climbing to FL400, he would have said something to the effect of maintain FL390. At that point I fully processed what was happening, gave silent kudos to my FO for correctly interpreting the bad direction this was going, and directed him to 'push.' As what we had was a TA, not an RA, the autopilot was left engaged, but he did direct the nose down and I dialed 390 into the ASEL. The Controller asked us to confirm we were at FL390. I interpreted that as him wanting that confirmation on tape and I gave it to him, although we were, in fact, changing our vertical direction from up to down at FL393 at that point.We are a very structured flight department. In order for an airplane to be directed to an altitude during enroute climb or descent, the Controller has to assign that altitude, the PNF has to read it back and dial it into the ASEL, the PF has to verbally and independently repeat that altitude for both of us to hear, and has to acknowledge that he sees that same altitude displayed in front of him. Owing to that routine sequence and cadence of events, we are both 100% certain that we were assigned FL400.That said, I can allow as how I have possibly been wrong at least once in my flying career. My FO was hired on just as COVID came on the scene last year. With the reduced amount of flying we've been doing since, he is still considered 'new' to the operation and as such not fully comfortable with our procedures. By that, I mean that I sometimes sense a hesitation for him to be as assertive as he should be and as assertive as he would be by now had this been a normal year. That notwithstanding, I would expect any pilot in our organization to question, in no uncertain terms, anything they were uncertain about, especially an ATC clearance. Likewise, no one in our organization, from Director of Flight Ops down, would hesitate to ascertain verification of any such uncertainty, no matter who questioned it. That's the way we move airplanes without bending them. I'm still 100% certain we were cleared to FL400.In retrospect, and we observed this at the time, the primary thing that would have alerted us to this unfolding conflict would have been for the Controller to have called the traffic as '...opposite direction at FL400.' That would have raised the hackles on the back of my neck and elicited from me a request to confirm our assigned altitude. There is no error-trapping possible when traffic is called as '1,000 feet above your assigned altitude.'Additionally, and this is not a negative, just observation and fact: we're flying the oldest, and by far the most reliable, airplane in our fleet of four, however, owing to her age, we're looking at a pair of >XX-year-old TCAS displays on dedicated three-inch round screens. There are no course overlays, no distance rings and, especially on the longer ranges (20 and 40 mile), no way to preciselyassess the relative position, direction or closure rate of traffic approaching, especially when doing so nearly head on. Technology is good. Newer technology can sometimes be better.On a positive note, we did visually acquire the traffic while far enough apart that had evasive action been necessary (it wasn't), we would have had plenty of time to take it. We did debrief this incident immediately after its occurrence, replayed the events out loud and decided the error was ultimately ATC's, that we had done everything we could to mitigate the repercussions to the controller and that we were not at fault.
ASRS:1796107.s: During an enroute climb to FL400, the crew received a traffic alert for an aircraft 1,000 feet above their assigned altitude and a TCAS Traffic Advisory. The First Officer shallowed the climb and descended to FL390 after ATC instructed them to maintain that level, which the crew attributed to an ATC error in traffic reporting.

ASRS:1796110.n: While in transit to ZZZ [Airport], with 2 passengers on board and just prior to entering ZZZ1 Center Control airspace, I started getting occasional low pressurization indications that eventually stopped. After and while in ZZZ Center airspace and talking to ZZZ Center Control I was directed to descend from flight level 310 to 270. After setting up my descent I received a low cabin pressure warning indication that prompted me to don my mask and drop the cabin masks as well. My TBM 850 aircraft is equipped with an emergency descent feature in the event of low pressure and that system went into effect turning me 90 degrees to the right and descending me. While descending I requested priority handling and was diverted to ZZZ1 [Airport] where I landed safely.
ASRS:1796110.s: The pilot of a TBM 850 with two passengers experienced low cabin pressure warnings while descending from FL310 to FL270 in ZZZ Center airspace. The aircraft's emergency descent system activated, turning right and descending, prompting a priority diversion to ZZZ1 Airport for a safe landing.

ASRS:1796125.n: We were cruising at FL320 around late afternoon when transmission with ZZZ Center became difficult as we were handed off to the next frequency. ZZZ Center's transmissions were muffled and unreadable at times. Multiple aircraft, including my own, had to ask Center to repeat instruction due to the muffled voice and weak transmission. My belief is that the Center Controller was wearing a mask and that mask was causing the majority of communication difficulty.If true, the use of masks by Center controllers is creating a serious communication and safety issue between pilots and Air Traffic Control. Everything about the national air space system is designed so pilot to ATC communication is to be understood without interference or confusion. The use of masks by ZZZ ATC has the potential to create confusion and ultimately a sacrifice of safety.
ASRS:1796125.s: A pilot reported muffled and unreadable transmissions from ZZZ Center while cruising at FL320, forcing multiple aircraft to request instruction repeats. The pilot attributed the communication difficulty to the controller wearing a mask, warning that this practice creates a serious safety issue.

ASRS:1796133.n: I fly X type missions, for which I'm wearing a mask, which I knew harms the sealing of my active noise reduction headset (and as a result reduces the sound quality, bringing in some ambient noise). It was not until yesterday that I realized how disruptive this is.I was flying on the last leg of my IFR flight plan, from ZZZ to ZZZZZ (from there to my destination - ZZZ1). ATC called me and said something about heading 290 with ZZZZZ in it, I assumed they're telling me I need to fly 290 to ZZZZZ (and from there proceed as usual). That's what I did, ATC got (rightfully) upset and told me that I was asked to fly 290, which I then did and later cleared for a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ1.Listening to the recording on liveatc.net, I could clearly hear the ATC telling me to depart ZZZZZ at heading 290. That 'depart' is the one piece of the puzzle I didn't hear during the flight.On my way back - no passengers, no mask - all of a sudden ATC sounded much clearer. It made obvious to me this has to change, and I need to find a mask that does not interfere with my headset.
ASRS:1796133.s: A pilot flying an IFR mission reported misinterpreting an ATC clearance to depart ZZZZZ on heading 290 due to ambient noise caused by a mask interfering with their active noise reduction headset. The pilot subsequently corrected the heading and completed a visual approach after realizing the equipment issue degraded communication clarity.

ASRS:1796136.n: Upon a smooth touchdown/landing, the nose wheel 'broke off' at a weak point that AutoGyro has designed into the Gyroplane. It appears, not for sure, that the nose wheel shaft (the weak point) had been cracked and finally gave way while I was landing. No damage, no injuries. The weak point fork was replaced.
ASRS:1796136.s: The pilot reported that the nose wheel shaft of an AutoGyro Gyroplane fractured at a designed weak point during landing. The reporter suspects the shaft was pre-cracked, but the incident resulted in no injuries or damage, and the fork was replaced.

ASRS:1796147.n: We were approaching ZZZZZ intersection from the west which is a transition onto the ZZZZZ 3 arrival and had received multiple descent clearances out of our cruising altitude of FL350. Eventually we were cleared to cross ZZZZZ at FL230. Flying the ZZZZZ 3 'as published' we would normally cross ZZZZZ1 at FL230 per the STAR and the FMS altitude crossings were set for this. ZZZZZ is 14 miles prior to ZZZZZ1 so crossing ZZZZZ at FL230 requires a change in the FMS and a steeper descent. We acknowledged the clearance and a few minutes later while performing a challenge and response descent checklist and when flying overhead ZZZZZ I realized that we were still on the original profile descent to cross ZZZZZ1 at FL230 and we were crossing ZZZZZ above our assigned altitude of FL230.I attribute this error to our reduced amount of flying in the past 12 months due to the COVID lock down and to distraction by the descent checklist.
ASRS:1796147.s: The flight crew crossed ZZZZZ intersection above the assigned FL230 while descending from FL350 on the ZZZZZ 3 arrival. The pilot attributed this altitude deviation to reduced recent flight experience and distraction caused by performing the descent checklist.

ASRS:1796173.n: Took off from San Pedro Sula and noticed there wasn't a SID or obstacle departure procedure taking off from Runway 22 into terrain either side of centerline and ahead. There is a SID for runway 4 which is what we took off on. Shouldn't there be some kind of procedure for this runway? I filed a report and got a response back asking me to also fill out this report.
ASRS:1796173.s: A pilot reported that after taking off from Runway 22 at San Pedro Sula, no SID or obstacle departure procedure existed for the terrain ahead and to either side. The pilot noted a SID is available for Runway 4 and questioned why no procedure was published for Runway 22.

ASRS:1796297.n: During boarding a young man stopped right in front of myself and the Purser and had a motorized board he was carrying. The Purser started asking him questions about it like, What it was, how it works, how do you operate it and does it have a battery in it? The Purser wasn't comfortable with it so she messaged the agent about it and requested a CSR come down and ask him further questions. The Purser then informed the Captain about the board and he too was very concerned about it and he went to get a CSR. The CSR came and the customer came up to the boarding door with the board and they began talking about how he was able to get this far with it on an aircraft. He came from ZZZ to ZZZ1 then onto ZZZ2. The customer said he made several phone calls to TSA and [Air Carrier] about bringing the board and was told he could bring it on the aircraft with a lithium battery. The Captain then informed him that it was a prohibited item onboard the aircraft unless he had proper documentation stating that it was OK, to which he did not. The Captain told him he could not go on this flight with the board and had him retrieve his belongings and his traveling partner and exit the aircraft. The customer was very upset and began cussing and raising his voice so much so that everyone on the aircraft heard him about having to get off the aircraft. I only know the customers were in [seat], I do not have names.
ASRS:1796297.s: During boarding, a passenger attempted to board with a motorized board containing a lithium battery. The Captain denied boarding due to lack of required documentation for the prohibited item, resulting in the passenger and his partner exiting the aircraft after becoming verbally abusive.

ASRS:1796355.n: I picked up Aircraft X from [Company] after annual inspection. The flight home was uneventful until reaching pattern altitude. Upon putting down the landing gear I noticed that I only had 2 green lights. The light for the right main gear was not illuminated. I informed Tower of the potential problem and asked for assistance is noting the status of the landing gear. Multiple aircraft, along with Tower, indicated that all landing gear were extended. I extended the flaps fully and continued a stabilized approach. The aircraft was allowed to gently touch down on the mains, at which point a felt the right main begin to give way. I began to slow the aircraft while the right wing tip made contact with the pavement. The drag from the wing pulled me to the right, and I eventually ended up coming to a stop in the grass to the right on Runway XX. I then shut the engine down and exited the aircraft. There was no evidence of any fuel leaks or other problems. Initial inspection of the plane revealed a mechanical failure of a pin that connects 2 portions of the landing gear system. The only known damage was to the right wing tip, right flap, and right side rear door step. A recovery company was contacted, and we moved the plane into my hangar for the night.
ASRS:1796355.s: The pilot experienced a right main landing gear collapse during landing after a post-inspection flight, despite visual confirmation of gear extension. The incident was caused by a mechanical pin failure, resulting in damage to the right wing tip, flap, and rear door step before the aircraft stopped in the grass.

ASRS:1796374.n: We were advised that someone had tested positive for COVID. It had been a long period of time since they were in the building. It was during the mid shift, so they didn't have contact with anyone. The TRACON was shutdown and relocated to ZZZ1 Tower at XA:0L on a weekday. This is a busy day of the week and time for us. The functionality of working from the Tower is limited. It also requires all radar sectors to be combined. The volume and complexity was far too great at this time of day. Even with trying to limit operations the radar scope was too cluttered. There were many uncontrolled VFR's. The data blocks overlapped and the Mode-C was unreadable. Traffic workload was high. We asked ZZZ2 Traffic Management Unit (TMU) for 20 Miles In Trail (MIT), but that was not adhered to. Communications were also difficult. We asked all surrounding facilities to use a single frequency but that was not always followed. VFR's calling for service were using published frequencies.There was no reason to rush this cleaning. Everyone in the facility had already been exposed for hours, if not days. Waiting until XF:00L would have ensured traffic volume and complexity was light enough to work from a reduced area such as ZZZ1 Tower. The rush for cleaning was not worth the safety risk to the flying public.
ASRS:1796374.s: Air traffic controllers relocated to ZZZ1 Tower during a busy weekday due to a COVID-19 cleaning rush, resulting in excessive workload, radar clutter, and unreadable Mode-C data. The facility failed to adhere to requested 20-mile spacing or single-frequency communications, creating a safety risk that could have been avoided by delaying the cleaning until traffic was lighter.

ASRS:1796375.n: I was working Sector X (AOA [At Or Above] FL360) and another sector was being saturated (Y/Z/A combined. Training was being done at this sector), so they split off A to me. There was a lot of traffic and weather in the area. Apparently, restrictions were put in place that aircraft entering ZZZ1 [Center] from us and landing at ZZZ [Airport] needed to be AOB FL260. I was working an Ultra High Sector. When I was given the briefing by the trainee, the trainer ran over to my scope and said that Aircraft X needed to be AOB [At Or Below] FL260. The aircraft was at FL430 and maybe 40 miles from the boundary, on top of same direction and opposite direction traffic. Aside from that there were numerous conflicting aircraft issues already fixing to happen. My EDST [En-route Decision Support Tool] had a bunch of red alerts of which should have been fixed prior to the aircraft entering our area. Again, this was on the sector I was gaining, NOT the one I was already working. I was bit overwhelmed taking the sector just due to the amount of work that needed to be corrected due to the neglect of the training team.I descended Aircraft X to FL390, knowing I would have to move or quickly descend the aircraft through two others converging at FL390 and another directly below at FL380.I assigned the altitude and realized the speed gain was great enough that I could get Aircraft X down to FL360 (base of my stratum) and miss Aircraft Y, heading the same direction at FL380. To ensure I had room and miss opposite direction traffic at FL390, I turned Aircraft X. My turn was a bit too aggressive and in doing so, the wind caused the aircraft to lose a bunch of speed, resulting in the CA going off. I turned Aircraft Y to the left to keep separation, but it was already lost. From my observation, I showed a loss of separation to where they were separated by 4.9 miles and 900 feet vs the 1000/5 I need. I didn't stare too long as I had to go on to other separation tasks that were not completed prior to receiving the additional airspace/traffic.First, splitting sectors at the last minute has become all too common an occurrence with this COVID schedule and working 'more with less.' The whole environment is unsafe and the things we do are dangerous, resulting in issues like the one I had.Secondly, I won't be taking sectors from a person who doesn't have it all figured out, no matter what the Supervisor says.I take pride in what I do and having separation errors is unacceptable. I had the pilot helping me out the best he could and I second guessed myself that the aircraft would descend through the altitudes fast enough in a straight line Aircraft X started to outrun Aircraft Y as he descended. My turn was too aggressive, and I never played it into my head how much the wind would impact the turn. I think just trying to take action to descend the aircraft to meet a restriction overruled my common sense to think how my actions would play out. Solely my fault, but it could have and should have been avoided had other things been done in a timely manner prior to my taking the airspace. It seems to be a trend to do everything last minute, which is what creates such mistakes. Had I worked that aircraft and known of the restriction, Aircraft X would have descended below all my traffic 100 miles prior. Maybe not to FL260 so as to penalize the aircraft, but at least below those who were deviating and being rerouted around the weather.
ASRS:1796375.s: An air traffic controller managing a newly assigned ultra-high sector lost separation between Aircraft X and Y while aggressively turning X to meet a late altitude restriction. The controller attributed the 4.9-mile, 900-foot separation error to their own aggressive maneuvering compounded by wind, but cited unsafe staffing and last-minute sector splits as contributing factors.

ASRS:1796379.n: I was being relieved from the CIC position and opened the X Sector which was combined with the Y and Z Sectors due to volume. At the time of the incident, Henderson Tower requested a release on Aircraft Y on the SCAMR SID with the RASLR transition. They advised they could provide visual separation with the inbound IFR which I approved. At the same time I had a flight overflying HND enroute to VGT and another inbound to HND. Upon departure, I pointed out Aircraft Y to the Y Sector observing Aircraft X on the NIITZ Departure so I could maneuver around inbound and overflight traffic. I observed Aircraft Y above my existing traffic and what appeared to be safely behind Aircraft X as they were approximately 8 miles and 50 KIAS slower than Aircraft X. I shipped Aircraft Y to ZLA just prior to them reaching 12,000 MSL. From replays I observed, the loss appeared to have occurred approximately 15-20 miles down line.We are now approximately 30 days into new Metroplex airspace and this procedure is designed to 'blend in' LAS SIDS. This particular one causes aircraft to unnecessarily fly into each other. ZLA also has control of these aircraft by LOA at 15,000 MSL. A simple turn to the RASLR Fix could have avoided this. I also mentioned the inefficiencies of the new design to our Metroplex team prior to implementation. .
ASRS:1796379.s: An air traffic controller in the X Sector reported a loss of separation between Aircraft Y on the SCAMR SID and Aircraft X on the NIITZ Departure approximately 15-20 miles downline. The controller attributed the incident to the new Metroplex airspace design causing aircraft to fly into each other, noting a simple turn to the RASLR Fix would have avoided the conflict.

ASRS:1796380.n: Aircraft X was inbound to EKO. I issued a descent clearance to 14,000 feet and asked the pilot if he had the weather at EKO and to expect a visual approach. The pilot said he was unable to obtain the weather, so I issued him the current METAR. I also informed the pilot of the airport's location. Moments later, I observed the pilot descending. I immediately issued a low altitude alert since he was in a 13400 ft. MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) and was descending below. The pilot immediately canceled IFR.
ASRS:1796380.s: An air traffic controller issued a descent clearance to 14,000 feet to Aircraft X inbound to EKO. The controller issued a low altitude alert when the pilot descended below the 13,400-foot Minimum IFR Altitude, prompting the pilot to immediately cancel IFR.

ASRS:1796383.n: I just took over the position X. I was briefed that we would be switching from east operations, to west operations because of a wind shift. About 3 weeks ago, we moved scopes and positions around to accommodate increased social distancing. Due to this, there are new macros and procedures that supervisors must adhere to. As our last aircraft landed on the east runways, the Supervisor started to put in new macros. My tags did not acquire, and I had to manually coordinate with the Feeder to let him know when I had radar on traffic. When I was starting to get busy and it was clear the macros being entered were not working, my scope changed from a west operations final pref set to an east operations final monitor preference set. I had to slide over to the adjacent position and work my final off of that scope because mine was completely unusable.This is an absolute safety concern that I have heard has happened before. I recommend they move the scopes back to the normal working configuration because this is clearly not working and is a huge safety hazard and it should concern everyone.
ASRS:1796383.s: An air traffic controller reported that during a transition to west operations, new macros failed to acquire tags and caused their scope to revert to an east operations preference set. The controller had to manually coordinate with the Feeder and work from an adjacent position due to the unusable scope, citing the social distancing layout changes as the cause of this safety hazard.

ASRS:1796396.n: Aircraft X checked on approximately a 6 mile final on the Visual Approach and I cleared him to land. At approximately a 4-mile final Aircraft Y asks for an 'S turn to the North' to which I state 'Approved'. About 30 seconds later, Aircraft X asks for another s-turn to the south to which I also state 'approved as requested' and inform him that there is no traffic in his vicinity and also issued the wind. Aircraft X is now on a 1.5 mile final and well east of the airport and asks 'Tower, Aircraft X we are still plenty high, can we do a left tun and a left 360 around?' I state 'Unable' due to traffic in trail and ask Aircraft X if he needs to go around. Aircraft X replies 'affirmative'.At this point Aircraft Y is approximately 2 miles well east of the airport and it appeared that they were turning toward the airport. Not wanting Aircraft Y to overshoot finals, I issue 'Aircraft Y, fly heading 195, climb and maintain 2,000'. When Aircraft Y becomes established on the heading, I issue 'fly heading 210 and maintain 3,000'. I did this without coordinating with Approach first because things were rapidly developing as Aircraft Y was indicating 190 knots and they appeared to be headed toward terrain east of the airport. I realize that this was a vector below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA). The MVA east of the airport is 2,400 feet but at this point, I wanted to get Aircraft Y away from terrain as quickly as possible without issuing any vague or confusing instructions to the pilot. I did coordinate with Approach with the 210 heading when I got the chance and it was approved.As I stated in my above narrative, I realize that the vector that I issued was below the MVA but from my perspective from the Tower, I needed to get Aircraft Y away from terrain as quickly as possible. This was a unique situation where I had to utilize my best judgment with the circumstances that were presented. I realize that I was breaking the rule of vectoring an aircraft below the MVA but what was the alternative at this point? Let Aircraft Y head toward terrain and possible result in a catastrophe? It was the best of the two bad choices that were presented to me at that point and I had to quickly make a judgment call.
ASRS:1796396.s: An air traffic controller vectored Aircraft Y below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude of 2,400 feet to avoid terrain after the aircraft overshot the final approach. The controller justified this deviation as a necessary judgment call to prevent a potential catastrophe, acknowledging the rule violation but prioritizing immediate safety.

ASRS:1796399.n: Aircraft X was a departure from ZZZ [Airport] enroute to ZZZ1 [Airport]. The aircraft checked on frequency climbing to 14,000. I acknowledged the aircraft, issued them normal airspeed and the local altimeter setting. There was weather south of my sector, but I did not depict any weather along Aircraft X's route of flight. Prior to ZZZZZ waypoint, the aircraft was level at 14,000. I was working a normal amount of departure volume. However, due to COVID staffing, I was working a combined sector. 2 Low Altitude sectors, and 1 High Altitude sector, which has been common during COVID. The difficult part is that we typically work the low altitude sectors on around a 50 mile range, but since we have the high altitude sector, we need to have the combined sector using a 150 mile range. As Aircraft X was right over ZZZZZ, I noticed moderate precipitation was beginning to appear, but I did not have time to issue the weather before the pilot reported turbulence. The pilot stated they were in moderate and basically severe turbulence and asked for a vector or different altitude. I immediately descended the aircraft to 13,000 and coordinated with the next sector, since they had track control. I again asked the pilot if they need anything and they asked for a lower altitude. I coordinated with ZZZ Approach, to point out the aircraft descending to 10,000 due to the turbulence. I then descended the aircraft and asked the pilots if there was any damage or injuries. The pilot stated that he and the other pilot were the only ones onboard and they were not injured and did not suspect any damage to the aircraft. When the aircraft was level any 10,000 and clear of the now depicted weather, I asked the pilot again how they were doing. They said that the ride had improved. A short time later, the weather in that area grew rapidly to moderate and heavy precipitation. I transferred communications of Aircraft X to the next sector. After the incident, I needed to vector numerous other aircraft away from that hazardous weather.COVID schedules, low staffing and long time on position were all contributing factors. My area has been extremely short staffed during our COVID schedule and tonight was no exception. We only had 5 CPCs scheduled for the shift, and also needed to staff the CIC position all night. There were numerous instances when all 5 controllers were working over 2 hours on position and we had 4 sectors open, plus the CIC and no controllers on break.The fact that I was working a non-typical configuration (outside of COVID) was also a contributing factor. I was not able to have a normal range for my sector and if I was using a low altitude scope and map, I may have noticed the weather earlier and issued it quicker to the aircraft.COVID schedules, minimal staffing, working long sessions on position and controllers continuously having to staff the CIC position have created additional strain and fatigue on the controllers.
ASRS:1796399.s: An air traffic controller managing a combined sector due to COVID staffing shortages issued altitude changes to Aircraft X after the pilot reported severe turbulence. The controller descended the aircraft from 14,000 to 10,000 feet, where the ride improved and no injuries or damage were reported, though the controller cited fatigue and non-typical sector configuration as contributing factors.

ASRS:1796402.n: WSMR (White Sands Missile Range) was GPS jamming. Aircraft X was significantly off course prior to taking position. Leaving controller put Aircraft X on a vector to miss restricted airspace. Aircraft X asked to go back on course direct to DNA, assuming he could navigate direct by his request, I gave him direct his destination again. I move on in my traffic scan and come back to Aircraft X making a 90 degree left hand turn. I had cleared Aircraft X to descend previously because he was no longer in conflict with WSMR after being vectored out, but with his 90 degree left hand turn he went back into WSMR descending and I didn't catch it in time. After realizing it I told Aircraft X to stop his descent but it was too late as he was passing through FL216. I called WSMR and asked them to 'stop buzzer', the answered with 'O.K.'. Facility Manager on Duty later informed me we can't ask them to 'stop buzzer' and to just keep putting aircraft on headings. Give controllers the ability to have WSMR stop GPS jamming during high traffic periods and move their jamming operations to mid shifts.
ASRS:1796402.s: An air traffic controller vectored Aircraft X away from White Sands Missile Range GPS jamming but failed to notice the aircraft turned back into the restricted area while descending. The aircraft passed through FL216 before the controller could stop the descent, prompting a request to cease jamming that was later deemed procedurally incorrect.

ASRS:1796431.n: I was running the bags for Aircraft X I ran the first set of bags out of the front on the aircraft and D ran the rear.... when he arrived to the bag room he had a bag that actually had a boat motor in it and had gas leaking out of it the bag was ripped open and dripping gas he reported it and was told by the supervisor on call to place the bag in the oversize bin but he didn't feel comfortable to do that and I didn't feel that was the right thing to do so I made a phone call to another supervisor to get better verification on what protocol is and finally he told me to place it in a tub and have Baggage Service come pick it up with a cart and not to place it on the oversize bin cause then any bags placed after would get contaminated with the gas I felt more comfortable with this . ... but this definitely needs to get investigated on how this bag made it on the plane and actually went through 3 stops without getting flagged ... the lead called Maintenance to check the pit since some of the gas spilled inside the pit just wanted to notify you all on this occurrence today ... thanks in advance
ASRS:1796431.s: Baggage handlers discovered a leaking boat motor in a bag on Aircraft X, prompting a supervisor to initially order it into an oversize bin. The handler refused, contacted another supervisor for correct protocol, and secured the item in a tub to prevent contamination while Maintenance inspected the spill.

ASRS:1796437.n: Very light 757, 16.7 on the fuel, almost empty payload, operating from ZZZ to ZZZ1, daytime VMC. High winds in effect. Vref was 111, Vapp is 126. I was PF (Pilot Flying), and decided to fly faster on final since we were in a light 757, and my limited experience with this situation led to this. Missed approach procedures were reviewed multiple times as other jets had to go around several times. Runway was dry, over XX;000 feet long, plenty of distance. I decided to fly a new Vapp of 135, as the jet was having problems controlling the airspeed since the winds were about 060/22G30. Our divert was ZZZ1, and we knew that several aircraft attempting to land had to execute missed approaches. All this into account, I decided to fly around 135 KIAS, as this felt like a more stable approach. The airspeed wouldn't stabilize safely below this number, as it was all over the place and I had to fight with the autothrottles to maintain within 15 kts of the initial Vapp of 126--it just wouldn't stabilize at a speed below 135. My reasoning is that since I was light, in a 757, long runway, daytime VMC, and super gusty winds, I had plenty of room to stop safely without encountering hot brakes or running out of concrete. We landed uneventfully, although long, as I touched down past the touchdown zone--this was the only cost of flying faster, and I felt it was worth it, all things considered. We landed and were able to taxi clear on taxiway, no problem. If I was in a 767 or a heavier 757, I wouldn't have even thought of this, and we would have flown the Vapp given, for better or worse. Were we technically unstable? Yes, I believe we were. Were we safer, in my eyes, flying a more stable approach with the winds we had? Yes, I also believe this to be the case. We never had a windshear warning, and we never felt unsafe, but looking back, I was in the wrong, even though I felt more stable, which led to a safer approach. However, the AOM procedures don't allow for this, so I was technically in the wrong, even though the airplane flew better and safer, in my opinion. Next time, I will fly the Vapp given, and if we have to divert, then so be it.
ASRS:1796437.s: The Pilot Flying of a light Boeing 757 increased the approach speed to 135 KIAS due to gusty winds and autothrottle instability, resulting in a long landing past the touchdown zone. Although the landing was uneventful, the pilot acknowledged the approach was technically unstable and violated AOM procedures.

ASRS:1796447.n: Approximately at 6,000 feet, the 'L HYD Quantity' message and light illuminated. Shortly after we received the 'L HYD RES/PRESS' message and light. We requested priority handling and leveled off at 7,000 feet. While returning to the outer marker of our departure runway to hold we began performing the QRH checklist for the loss of the Left Hydraulic System. After determining we loss only the Left Hydraulic System but, the aircraft was safe to fly, we contacted Operations Control and Maintenance Control. The aircraft was overweight and required a significant fuel burn off to land below the Structural Landing Weight of the aircraft. Maintenance Control, Operations Control and the crew determined together that landing at ZZZZ was the safer course of action based on many factors. We received a release to divert to ZZZZ and continue to hold for another :45 minutes to finish the fuel burn required to land below the structure landing weight. The landing was uneventful and the runway was closed for around twenty minutes. Fire rescue gave the all clear and the aircraft was towed from the runway to the gate. Maintenance found two hydraulic leaks, one hydraulic flex line in the left gear well and the other leak was from left engine hydraulic pump.
ASRS:1796447.s: The crew experienced a Left Hydraulic System failure at 6,000 feet, triggering priority handling and a diversion to ZZZZ. After burning fuel to meet landing weight limits, they landed safely; maintenance later identified leaks in the left gear well flex line and left engine pump.

ASRS:1796448.n: While on visual approach to Runway XX and configuring, we had configured normally through gear down. The Captain called 'flaps 30' and I reached for the handle while looking at the speed. The trend indicator was well below 185 and I was too focused on the trend rather than the actual speed. I was too quick to move the flap handle. We were actually about 187 knots. We got the flap overspeed warning for about one to two seconds as our speed continued to dissipate. It was my first flight from furlough and recurrent training. I was allowing myself to rush, even though there was no need to rush at the time. I made an error of referencing the trend before the actual speed. I also need to refresh my habit of not touching the flap handle until I have stated 'speed checks.'
ASRS:1796448.s: The First Officer triggered a flap overspeed warning during visual approach while configuring flaps 30 at 187 knots. The error occurred because the pilot referenced the speed trend indicator instead of the actual airspeed and rushed the configuration after returning from furlough.

ASRS:1796483.n: Since COVID, these particular international schedules have been in a lot of flux. Most sequences, up until now, have been 'rockets' where we only get to rest a relatively short amount of time during the day after an all-night flight, and then fly back all night. I have written about this before, and this is to reiterate: these sequences are sub-optimal in terms of safety due to the limited rest. The threat on these sequences is NOT a virus, it's the cumulative fatigue after being up for two straight nights. There is no reason not to make ALL these flights have a longer sleep opportunity with a 30 plus hour layover. Three times in the last 2 months we lined up for the wrong runway in ZZZ after the double all-nighter. Fortunately, someone caught the error before it was critical, but it is reflective of the fact that the three of us are sleep-deprived. In this aircraft category, you have an older pilot group to begin with. Give us the opportunity to get enough rest.Upon arrival in ZZZ, I was extremely tired, and felt my ability to monitor was degraded.Schedule all these international trips as longer layovers. It's a safety issue, pure and simple.
