ASRS:1796483.s: Pilots reported degraded monitoring ability and three runway lineup errors at ZZZ following consecutive all-night international flights. The reporter attributes these safety incidents to cumulative fatigue caused by short layovers and requests longer rest periods.

ASRS:1796489.n: Flight Attendant reported that faint musty dirty sock odor had grown stronger. No medical attention requested[Captain stated] odor related to contamination of air conditioning pack and suggested proper maintenance.
ASRS:1796489.s: A flight attendant reported a strengthening musty odor during the flight. The captain attributed the smell to air conditioning pack contamination and recommended proper maintenance, with no medical attention required.

ASRS:1796510.n: On SID's, when assigned climb via clearances, and when the top altitude is higher than the flies altitude, it is expected to climb to the restriction, top of SID. This particular SID says in the top altitude box, FL230 is the top. Upon further reading, it should say FL230 or filed altitude, whichever is lower, as the SID says in the textual description. Perhaps this is an issue with Jeppesen charts. Once past the 10,000 foot hold down at MUGBE, the Captain set FL230 as the expected clearance. Just before passing FL200, Captain queried ATC to confirm FL230, but received a response approaching FL220. A clearance was given to descend FL200, and we complied. It was then that we reviewed the textual part of the chart and noticed our error. The expectation that other SID's do not include this exception is biggest cause. Also, not detailed re-reading lengthy textual descriptions on SID's every single use, contributes. ATC clearances can include 'climb via, except maintain...'. This clearance would easily eliminate this oversight and airports like DEN, should have knowledge of the departures to aid in this. Also, Jeppesen charts should include these little nuances in the top altitude box on the SID, since this isn't true of all SID's.
ASRS:1796510.s: The crew climbed to FL230 on a SID due to misinterpreting the chart's top altitude box, ignoring a textual restriction to file altitude. After ATC queried and issued a descent clearance to FL200, the crew realized the error, attributing it to chart design and failure to read detailed text.

ASRS:1796542.n: Arriving from ZZZ, myself and the Captain were preparing for an ILS to Runway 12 based on available weather at hand. Once handed off to Approach Control, we were instructed to expect the RNP 30. Given our close proximity to the airport, I scrambled quickly to load the FMS and review the changes. I failed to notice the available IAFs available and was instead hastily looking for one of the IFs in the FMS. Given our plan to conduct a visual approach and use the RNP for guidance, I elected to select 'no approach VIAs' and to add the additional fixes requested by ATC. As we progressed on the approach, we got multiple GPWS alerts while in VMC, including 'pull up.' The Captain discontinued the approach and elected for a go-around followed by the published hold to troubleshoot. We later completed an ILS to Runway 12, circle 30 without event. Thoroughly review approach plate and recognize the appropriate approach VIA option. If needing additional time, request delay vectors.
ASRS:1796542.s: The pilot and Captain experienced multiple GPWS alerts, including "pull up," during a visual approach using an RNP 30 procedure due to incorrect FMS setup. The Captain executed a go-around and hold to troubleshoot before successfully completing an ILS approach to Runway 12.

ASRS:1796611.n: On approach to landing at ORD Runway 9C at approximately 200 feet we received a GPWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) alert 'TOO LOW, TERRAIN.' The alert repeated itself several times until touchdown. It was day VMC, some light rain falling. We were on glide slope and in a safe position to land so we continued the approach and considered the alert erroneous. It's possible that since the runway is fairly new at ORD, that the GPWS database had not been updated. Perhaps a message to pilots operating into ORD should be made aware of possible erroneous GPWS alert associated with Runway 9C.
ASRS:1796611.s: Pilots flying into ORD Runway 9C received repeated erroneous "TOO LOW, TERRAIN" GPWS alerts at 200 feet during a VMC approach in light rain. The crew continued the safe landing, suspecting the alert resulted from an outdated GPWS database for the new runway.

ASRS:1796613.n: Normal departure and flight enroute to ZZZ with thunderstorm approaching ZZZ airport on arrival from the west. Radar vectors for ILS XXL for approach, multiple speed adjustments from ATC on approach and no reports of wind gusts on initial arrival from ATC with winds 180/6 from ATIS. Storm had moved over field when on approach. On short final there was an RVR (Runway Visual Range) update from recall of greater than 5,000 RVR and moderate to heavy rain but no winds passed from recall. VMC around 1,100 feet and could see right and center runway but then went into torrential rain downpour around 400-500 feet on short final where Captain made an EFIS lights call and then I shortly after picked up runway lights and landing environment just prior to minimums and was a little high but was adjusting in close. Around 30-40 feet we had an instantaneous airspeed loss of around 10kts and at that time I had decided to go-around but with the airspeed loss and instantaneous loss of lift we touched down as go-around decision was made. We had a semi-hard landing and bounced and go-around selected all simultaneously. We were slow to put the speed brake back in after touching down but did eventually secure it and maintained attitude as we executed go around. Go-around procedures were completed airborne. Vectored back around by ATC for uneventful approach, landing and taxi in. The Captain and I both did a walk around of the aircraft post flight to ensure integrity of aircraft and check tail skid as a precaution but didn't notice the skid was ground down as we later were informed from the Director of Operations and Maintenance. We debriefed the event. Windshear/airspeed loss at low altitude while simultaneously executing go-around and didn't maintain proper go-around pitch once touching down as indicated from tail skid damage. Quicker reaction from crew with go-around with instantaneous airspeed loss and loss of lift and maintain proper attitude of aircraft on touchdown when executing go-around. Follow rules to live by, do not make large control inputs when in flare/go-around close to ground.
ASRS:1796613.s: The flight crew experienced an instantaneous 10-knot airspeed loss and lift loss at 30-40 feet during a thunderstorm approach, resulting in a semi-hard landing and tail skid damage while executing a go-around. The crew attributed the incident to windshear and improper pitch maintenance during the low-altitude go-around decision.

ASRS:1796618.n: ZZZ ramp informed me that position 11R on the main deck contains class 9 lithium ion batteries 129.2 kg. This is not on DG Manifest. The duty officer and flight crew were advised.
ASRS:1796618.s: Ramp personnel informed the flight crew that 129.2 kg of Class 9 lithium-ion batteries were found in position 11R on the main deck, which was not listed on the DG Manifest. The duty officer and flight crew were advised of the discrepancy.

ASRS:1796637.n: While on approach to ZZZ we were cleared to descend to 3,000 feet at which time we had the runway in sight. Upon reaching 3,000 feet the controller gave us a low altitude alert and wanted to verify we were level at 3,600. The PNF (Pilot Not Flying) responded that we were level at 3,000 and had the airport in sight. The controller advised he had only cleared us to descend to 3,600 not 3,000. We then called the airport in sight and he cleared us for the visual approach and we initiated a successful landing. After landing the Tower Manager contacted the flight crew via telephone at the FBO and advised there was a possible pilot deviation. We were in contact with ZZZ Approach. We were to expect radar vectors for the ILS XX. During the descent there were thunderstorms in the area. The approach controller instructed to descend to 3,000. As we leveled at 3,000 the controller ask to confirm our altitude. I informed the controller we were level at 3,000. He informed us we should have been at 3,600. We informed him we thought he had said 3,000. By this time we were clear of clouds and has the airport in sight. We climbed to 3,600 and received radar vectors as we were cleared for the approach.
ASRS:1796637.s: The flight crew descended to 3,000 feet on approach to ZZZ, believing they were cleared, while the controller intended 3,600 feet. The crew climbed to 3,600 feet after the discrepancy was identified, then received a visual approach clearance and landed successfully.

ASRS:1796638.n: Climbing through 16,000 feet to FL 200 we experienced a high whistle sound from the front of the airplane. I felt pressure on my ears, nose, and head and had the air pushed out of my lungs. We identified a cabin depressurization and I reached for my O2 mask. I took a long inhale from the oxygen and then proceeded with additional memory items. The Captain began an priority descent. I reached for the Pax oxygen switch with my right hand and the PA button with my left hand. I communicated with the Captain that I was going off comms to tell Pax to put on oxygen masks. The Captain stated 'Wait. They are going to be fine here in 2-3 seconds and I don't want to replace the masks.' This occurred around 13,500 feet. So I did not complete memory items per the Captain's instruction. I contacted ATC and advised we were on an priority descent because of depressurization. We received a new assigned altitude of 10,000 feet. The Cabin started to repressurize around 11,000. ATC asked if we wished to declare priority handling and the Captain declined. We were able to continue to ZZZ without incident.There were several deviations from our normal operating procedures that concern me. First the disregard from memory items on the checklist. Second, the captain did not have his O2 mask plugged in. He believed he could plug it in fast enough if needed and that he doesn't plug it in because he forgets to unplug it after a flight. This caused a delay in performing a memory item. The Captain was able to plug his oxygen mask in but never donned it during controlled handling decent. Also, we did not formally ask for priority handling with ATC. We could not diagnose the problem for the rapid depressurization so we were unaware of what triggered it. I suggested declaring priority handling to cover our bases if anything else occurred. This flight had already been abnormal with the priority descent. The Captain disagreed saying the problem is over. Lastly, I do not believe the cockpit acceptance was completed for this flight. It is typical that the FO (First Officer) does the walk around and security check while the Captain is completing the acceptance. While doing the walk around it is very apparent that the shaker pusher test is being tested from outside the airplane. You can hear the shaking on the horizontal stabilizer. I did not hear it that morning. Also upon startup, the Captain found a popped circuit breaker on his side for De-Ice. I'm not sure when the circuit breaker popped but no de-icing equipment was on so I assume it was before startup. This is another missed item on the acceptance checklist. Now, these deviations did not cause the priority handling to occur but they could have added on to make the event worse.
ASRS:1796638.s: During a climb to FL200, the crew experienced rapid depressurization and initiated a priority descent to 10,000 feet. The First Officer reported deviations including the Captain's failure to don an oxygen mask, disregard for memory items, and missed pre-flight checks, though the cause of depressurization remained undiagnosed.

ASRS:1796652.n: We were at FL350 in cruise between ZZZ and ZZZ1. ATC had given us left and right deviations and ZZZ1 when able. The radar was not painting much at the time but we were trying to deviate around what we saw on the radar. At the time everything was obscured and we were in the clouds. We did pop out just a little before the front and could make our way around a couple of the darker areas but it was not possible to get around all of it. As we crossed the front we started to get some shear in the winds that caused the airspeed to start to go up and down quite a bit. The autopilot then kicked off so my FO (First Officer) took manual control and the airspeed and altitude varied a lot as he flew the aircraft. The turbulence only got to a moderate level at most of the time but the downdrafts and updrafts made it difficult to keep any specific altitude or airspeed. Soon we hit a downdraft that was much worse than the rest and we were unable to maintain altitude even in climb power. I took control of the aircraft and told him to tell ATC we were descending because we were unable to maintain altitude at the time. We ended up descending about 1,000 feet and were able to level off at FL340 once we were through it. At the time I was just worried about keeping airspeed and not stalling the aircraft. Once we were clear ATC cleared us down to FL330 and we continued on to ZZZ2. At the time of the initial shear we were talking and did not detect the variations in airspeed that were the telling signs of the shear coming. At the time I did not declare an emergency but looking back at it I would now because we were unable to maintain altitude at the time. While enroute we were navigating around some weather that was obscured. We were communicating with ATC about the best route to take around the weather. We were not painting much if any precipitation at all angles on the radar. We were on left and right deviations and ZZZ when able. Just after passing the ZZZ1 VOR at FL350. We started to experience some light turbulence which continued to worsen. I turned on continuous ignition and continued to maneuver around the weather the best we could. The VSI (Vertical Speed Indicator) started a small trend of 120 FPM down. Our altitude quickly started to dip 300-400 feet as we encountered an unexpected large downdraft that kicked the autopilot off. The VSI showed 2,000 FPM descent. I continued to hand fly the aircraft but we were unable to maintain airspeed and altitude and began a descent down to FL340. We advised ATC that we were unable to maintain altitude because of the downdraft and that we would be leveling at FL340. ATC then gave us a descent to FL330. We continued down to FL 330 and leveled there. We exited the obscured weather and continued to ZZZ2. Limited visual and pictorial view of the weather as we deviated around it. Access to current weather information through the iPad such as tops reports.
ASRS:1796652.s: The flight crew encountered severe wind shear and downdrafts while navigating obscured weather at FL350, causing the autopilot to disengage and preventing altitude maintenance. They manually descended to FL340 and then FL330 after advising ATC, noting they would have declared an emergency in hindsight.

ASRS:1796663.n: On vectors 6 SM northwest of TRI airport at 4500, ATC was vectoring us around weather for the approach. We were level, given a left turn from 270 to 090. On about a 180 heading, we got the GPWS 'caution terrain' followed by 'terrain terrain woop woop pull up' one time. I leveled the wings and executed the terrain escape maneuver. We climbed up to 5,300 feet from 4,500 feet. As soon as I started the escape maneuver, the indications went away. We notified ATC and flew the approach without disruption. This seemed like an erroneous activation as we were above what ATC said was the MVA. But, it was night, so not 100% sure.Either a false warning or a terrain clearance issue. It seemed that we were too high to get this in a level turn. ATC indicated we were 100 feet above their MVA. Responded and leveled the wings and executed the escape maneuver. Suggest to fly at or above MSA rather than the minimum vectoring altitude.
ASRS:1796663.s: The pilot reported a GPWS terrain warning while being vectored by ATC at 4,500 feet northwest of TRI airport at night. The crew executed a terrain escape maneuver to 5,300 feet, suspecting a false warning despite ATC confirming they were 100 feet above the minimum vectoring altitude.

ASRS:1796669.n: I completed a thorough walk around and told the Captain there was a lot of ice on the aircraft and we were going to need to deice. I also recommended we take off with full Anti-ice on and the Captain agreed after a minute. We did a full deice type 1 and 4 everything went as planned. I ran the cold weather cold soaked check list to prepare for deicing. Once Deicing was completed I received all the pertinent information from iceman and wrote it down on a TOLD card. I then completed the deicing check list and we called ground for taxi. I made sure all the deice check list was completed and we taxied out for departure. Myself and the Captain talked about leaving the flaps and slats up or down while taxiing and due to having such a long hold over time we chose to lower flaps to proper flap setting for takeoff knowing that our hold over time would be reduced by 50%. As we pulled onto the runway and did our final configuration check we had a no take off and the Captain adjusted the FMS info for takeoff and the neck check was good to go. We were cleared for takeoff and I did all my flows and the before takeoff check list. Power was set and we began to roll and immediately the Captain was going left and right on the runway due to the winds being so strong and at this point I put my feet on the pedals getting ready to help the Captain. We reached V1 and I called out V1 then rotate. As soon as we rotated next thing I know is we are going left of the runway due to the winds being so strong at this point I don't remember if I called out positive rate and this allowing the Captain to call gear up. The next thing I remember is calling out acceleration and the Captain calling out flight level change and auto pilot on. At this point we are getting bumped all around due to the severe weather. The Captain then says flaps and I raise them watching the airspeed as we are bumped around. I call out speed since we are getting close to the speed warning and the Captain does not have time to get the nose up higher to stop this warning from happening then we notice all of a sudden we have a packs off message and the Captain says the packs are off and I state they are on. He resets them but to no avail. They continue to show off. At this time the Captain says the gear is down and raises it while we are being thrown all around. I ask ATC if we can level off at 11,000 and they clear us to level off at 11,000. We are still getting pounded and unable to maintain 11,000. I reach for the QRH as the Captain calls for the QRH between 11,000 and 13,000 the packs off warning message goes away and due to already being at 13,000, ATC asks if we would like to continue to climb and I state yes after looking over at the Captain and he nodded his head to say yes. I then ask about the weather and they state the weather will calm down above 20,000. We are then cleared to climb to 23,000 and I say to the Captain when we are above 20,000 I'm sorry I don't recall if I called out positive rate allowing the Captain to call for gear up and the Captain responds that he did call for gear up and he always does. But I don't recall any call out for gear up. I would really like to hear the recording just to see what all was said while we were being battered around. Everything ended up normal from this point on. Once we landed our flight attendant stated the passengers were not happy with the take off and were screaming.Unfortunately, there is not much we could have done on this take off that we did not already do. We had already talked to ground to see if other aircraft had taken off and they said everything was fine with the first 3 departures. We checked the winds with ACARS including gusts and ACARS showed the take off to all be within tolerances. I wish I remembered if I had called out positive rate and had heard gear up but I did not and don't remember.
ASRS:1796669.s: The First Officer and Captain experienced severe turbulence and a packs-off warning during takeoff in strong winds after deicing. They climbed to 23,000 feet where the warning cleared and weather improved, though passengers were distressed by the rough departure.

ASRS:1796671.n: We made a UNICOM frequency call, then taxied out to Runway X, called ZZZ Center to get clearance to takeoff, then on takeoff roll, a private aircraft calls and says that they are landing on Runway YY, resulting in a sidestep and go-around by the private aircraft. While monitoring UNICOM frequency and ZZZ center, both me and the First Officer missed calls made on the UNICOM frequency about potential traffic in the area due to a short taxi, high workload calling and obtaining departure clearance, running checklists, and making UNICOM frequency calls.In order to prevent this in the future, I could have made a 'traffic report' call on the UNICOM frequency, asking if there was any traffic in the area and what runway they were using. I could have also taxied slower to allow more time to monitor the UNICOM frequency in-between checklists. In the future I will be more diligent and alert to any potential communications on a UNICOM frequency in all phases of flight at an untowered airport.
ASRS:1796671.s: The pilot and First Officer missed UNICOM traffic calls during taxi and takeoff roll at an untowered airport due to high workload, causing a private aircraft to execute a sidestep and go-around. The reporter attributes the incident to insufficient monitoring of the UNICOM frequency while managing checklists and clearance communications.

ASRS:1796675.n: On descent into ZZZ, I selected the gear down. The right main gear light illuminated however my nose and left main gear lights remained extinguished, the nose unlocked light was on and the HYD PRESS light was on. I recycled the gear and when I selected 'up' there was no sound or movement to indicate the gear had gone up and none of the lights changed or extinguished. I put the gear back down and the HYD PRESS light extinguished and both HYD FLOW L/R illuminated. I chose to break off to the left and returned to approach frequency so I could resume flight following while running the checklist. I engaged the autopilot while I ran through the checklist. I decided to disengage the autopilot while I dropped the gear however the autopilot did not disengage. I turned the autopilot off with the switch but it remained engaged. I then tried to pull the circuit breaker however neither myself nor my passenger in the copilot seat could pull it. I turned the autopilot switch back on, reengaged the autopilot, and then disengaged it for the second time which finally released the flight controls. I decided to return to ZZZ1, advised ATC, and finished my gear checklist. I did have to blow the gear down and requested emergency vehicles. On the ground, Maintenance inspected the aircraft and there was hydraulic fluid all over the ground and the hydraulic reservoir was completely empty. The aircraft parked with no further incident.
ASRS:1796675.s: During descent into ZZZ, the pilot encountered landing gear and autopilot malfunctions caused by a hydraulic system failure. The crew executed an emergency gear extension, landed safely, and maintenance found the hydraulic reservoir empty with fluid spilled on the ground.

ASRS:1796684.n: We were approaching BZN, planning RNAV RNP 30 Approach. When we checked in with Big Sky Approach they assigned us the RNAV A Approach and cleared us direct SURPE. I typed it in manually and we proceeded direct. In my search in the FMS for that approach, it was not in the database. We had it in the Jeppessen FD Pro, but not in the database. Prior to reaching SURPE we became VFR, called the field and completed a visual approach. Having it in the Jeppessen charts and not in the database in the FMS is not cool. Leads one down a path to red. ATIS is not digital so our awareness of what approach is being used was late, late, late in the flight. Brought us into the red. Into the red at an incredibly critical phase of flight is also not cool. Set up a liaison to make the airports like this aware of our fleet capabilities. Example: we have charts in the Jeppessen, but not in the FMS database so don't assign said approach. We were inbound to BZN VOR expecting vectors to the final portion of RNAV (RNP) Runway 30. We were planning to request direct JAPER intersection for the balance of the approach. The airport was reporting VFR conditions but we were still IMC in the descent. We were handed off to Big Sky Approach about 20 DME from the airport. Without given a chance to request JAPER we were directed to proceed to SURPE intersection on the RNAV (GPS)-A. That's when our situational awareness went red. We accepted the approach as it was listed in our FD Pro. I manually put SURPE in the legs page and descended to 10,000 feet as directed. The First Officer tried to pull up the RNAV (GPS) - A in the FMC but it was not there. Luckily we broke out into VMC approaching SURPE and completed a visual approach.I can think of three. First, the controllers need to be aware of which approaches they can and cannot assign. Secondly, if an approach is published in FD Pro but not available in the FMC that discrepancy should be clearly spelled out. Finally, I made an assumption that if a procedure is in the FD Pro it would also be in the FMC.Big Sky needs to know which of their approaches are not in our FMC's. This would help them immensely to plan for our arrivals. We also need to complete an internal audit of all airports we serve to either remove or annotate in the pages which FD Pro approaches are not found in the FMC. I will now compare each approach in FD Pro to the FMC when arriving at a unfamiliar airport as I never want to be trapped in this situation again.
ASRS:1796684.s: The crew received a clearance for the RNAV (GPS)-A approach at BZN, but the procedure was missing from their FMS database despite being in their Jeppesen charts. They manually entered the SURPE waypoint and completed a visual approach after breaking out of IMC, attributing the error to controller unawareness of aircraft database limitations.

ASRS:1796705.n: In Governor's Harbor [airport], there is an over 8,000 foot strip. There is no taxiway, no tower, and a major hill in the middle of the runway where neither side can see the opposite end. When operating there, each pilot must trust that the others are making calls both to taxi out but also for landing. Aircraft there also repeatedly take off with a tail wind so it is difficult to know which side is being used at any time. In our case, we were departing off of Runway 15 and we made three radio calls, one to back taxi, one to position for takeoff, and one for takeoff. While cresting the hill on the takeoff roll we discovered that a multi engine piston aircraft was pointed right at us. We were past V1 and we continued to rotate and takeoff as the other aircraft did a 180 and attempted to head back to the ramp at the end of the runway. I do not know if they were taking off with a tailwind or taxing to 15 but they made no radio call and obviously were not listening to UNICOM. The FBO also made a call to the aircraft telling them that the runway was active and they needed to clear. Our crew followed every procedure to make this a safe takeoff, unfortunately we cannot prevent others from disregarding the rules of safe operations.This was a pretty close call, especially if the aircraft was trying to takeoff with a tailwind. If we had been 20 seconds later it could have been catastrophic. The fact that it is uncontrolled, has no taxiway, and you cannot see either side from either end makes this a very dangerous airport to operate in especially when the locals do not follow proper communication procedures. We as our crew did absolutely nothing wrong, we had no reason to believe that an aircraft would be reckless enough to not communicate and taxi without concern for themselves or anyone else, we made proper radio calls and did everything we could.
ASRS:1796705.s: The pilot reported a near-miss at Governor's Harbor while departing Runway 15 after cresting a hill that blocked visibility. A multi-engine piston aircraft entered the runway without radio communication, forcing the crew to continue takeoff past V1 while the other aircraft performed a 180-degree turn.

ASRS:1796734.n: During boarding there were 2 JS riders, plus nonrevs with seats, plus working crew in the aft galley which I attempted to work around to complete duties. There was some impediment. During MX (Maintenance) delay a NONREV from Cabin C came to aft galley and argued with me about why it was not OK for her to charge her cell phone with the vacuum outlet in the galley. I advised her of the safety policy regarding that. After demo I was in aft galley when I smelled strong oil and oil exhaust smell that extended a few rows into the cabin past Row 31, including lav. It seemed to dissipate after several minutes with forward movement of plane which is common so did not report then. During cruise a pax (passenger) from Row 33 came aft to complain of nausea and headache asking for water and pain med and denied having symptoms prior to flight and complained of fumes bothering him. I smelled oil in the aft galley area intermittently throughout flight, and was experiencing some mild symptoms myself but still did not write report on paper prior to calling CA (Captain) to keep him informed. All 3 MC crew were in galley when pax complained. FA (Flight Attendant) 4 provided water and med to pax. FA3 and FA4 both went forward for pilot breaks and cabin surveillance AFTER I called the FD about this issue so I assumed FA1 would be informed by someone else including the CA, but he was not. My mistake which I apologized to him for. During cruise we were experiencing turbulence in the aft so I waited several minutes before calling the FD to notify we were experiencing turbulence in the aft and to request SB (seat belt) sign on if they felt it was appropriate. During cruise I went forward to provide CDW about aft lav to FA1 but he was in the lav for an extended period of time and I had MC duties to attend to so I slipped the form under the FD door and called the FD to tell them same. At gate arrival a stronger smell of oil entered the aft galley area and cabin and lav so I called the FD, for a 4th time, with out calling FA1 first, to confirm AFT doors showed unarmed, asking to vent aft galley and report the very strong fumes of oil. He asked me to fill out the info on paper and to see him to debrief together and asked who all was involved. I tried to do an ALLCALL from the aft but was unsuccessful in reaching the entire crew with one call so tried to do individual calls. I was only able to reach FA3 and FA1 who began to yell at me about my poor CRM and said he only found out when the FD door opened and the CA said something about it. Both the CA and FA1 said I did not follow CRM procedures and said only the FA1 is to call the FD on cabin issues. I was unaware that was the case even for safety situations, including turbulence in the aft, that I was primarily aware of and apologized. FA1 accused me of intentionally creating conflict and of having a pattern of same. Each of the last 3 times I have flown with him he asks me what I want to be when I grow- up in front of passengers, another time we flew together he yelled at me for making a PA about the seatbelt sign prior to XA:00 as FA2 because he thought the IFM said XB:00 not XC:00 and people were sleeping, and only the FA1 makes announcements. I suppose this factored into why I was directly calling the FD and not using the loud interphone to call FA1 as well. And why I did not opt to make the turbulence without seat belt sign on announcement instead. I can't speak to why no one else told him about fumes and pax complaint. There was an opportunity during the crew briefing to establish cabin to FD flow that I think was missed. With multiple employee pre-boards and a full flight we were all highly tasked during the pre-boarding and boarding processes I have experienced both FD wanting only to speak with FA1 and stating such and also being invited to call with any safety concerns regardless of position in cabin. In my main concern and focus for safety of flight I unintentionally possibly violated CRM flowon this flight.
ASRS:1796734.s: A flight attendant reported oil fumes and passenger symptoms during cruise, directly contacting the flight deck multiple times due to high tasking and prior conflicts with the lead flight attendant. The lead flight attendant and captain criticized this communication as a CRM violation, accusing the reporter of bypassing established cabin-to-flight-deck protocols.

ASRS:1796749.n: Aircraft X in ZZZ reported possible low pressure of crew Oxygen. I have prepared a crew oxygen cylinder as a Fly Away Kit to load on rescue aircraft without following the Dangerous Goods shipping procedure. I have totally forgot that oxygen cylinder was a Dangerous Good. Aircraft departed [date/time] for ZZZ.
ASRS:1796749.s: A ground handler prepared a crew oxygen cylinder as a Fly Away Kit for Aircraft X departing for ZZZ after a reported low pressure issue. The handler admitted forgetting that the cylinder is a Dangerous Good and failed to follow required shipping procedures.

ASRS:1796769.n: While on a IFR flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1, I suffered a rapid / full cabin decompression at 27,000 feet approximately 20 miles SW from ZZZ2. The event happened about an hour into a routine flight in clear weather conditions in level flight on a direct course to ZZZ3. The complete decompression happened in a matter of a few seconds with a large pressure change inside the cabin (5.5 psi) and a simultaneous pitch noise change in the cabin. The 10,000 ft cabin altitude warning on the warning panel illuminated including the simultaneous high pitch warning from the portable 'Alt Alert' unit. The oxygen mask was deployed within seconds of concluding total cabin pressure loss by cross checking the cabin pressure control gauge. ATC was informed of the failure with a request for an immediate descent to 12,000 feet due to loss of cabin pressure. Due to the immediate request notified ATC whilst I was descending. The autopilot was set for a rapid descent to 12,000 feet. Whilst in the descent I checked if any circuit breakers had tripped but none were noted including the cabin pressure dump valve circuit breaker. Given the yearly recurrent training and surmising that the failure could be caused by a faulty squat switch for the emergency dump valve the circuit breaker was pulled for the switch and the cabin altitude was set to 1,000 feet to see if the cabin would re-pressurize. However due to the descent and low power setting the cabin would not re-pressurize until power was added back on leveling out at 12,000 feet. After leveling at 12,000 ft and analysis of the situation under the controlled descent, it was concluded that it was safe to continue flight under the present circumstances of a non pressurized cabin until further analysis of the situation could be made. With cruising power set for 12,000 feet the cabin started re-pressurizing due to the added power still with the squat switch circuit breaker pulled. At this point ATC was informed that the flight will continue to the filed destination. After the cabin reached full differential for the 12,000 foot altitude. The flight continued and the STAR into ZZZ1 was initiated and followed. Once reaching 10,000 feet the circuit breaker was re-engaged for the cabin dump squat switch with no impact and the cabin remained pressurized at full differential for the cruising altitude and the remaining flight. Suspecting that the squat switch had failed intermittently at high altitude causing the emergency dump of the cabin at flight it was decided to replace the switch and a test flight is still pending to assure that full cabin pressure can be maintained.
ASRS:1796769.s: The pilot experienced a rapid cabin decompression at 27,000 feet on an IFR flight, likely caused by a faulty emergency dump valve squat switch. After descending to 12,000 feet and pulling the switch's circuit breaker, the cabin re-pressurized, allowing the flight to continue to the destination.

ASRS:1796771.n: I was vaccinated for COVID-19. I was unaware of the 48 hour no-fly rule after being vaccinated. I was the authorized instructor on board during two training flights that occurred a day later. No further issues to report.
ASRS:1796771.s: The authorized instructor flew two training flights one day after receiving a COVID-19 vaccination, unaware of the 48-hour no-fly rule. The reporter stated there were no further issues.

ASRS:1796779.n: I was in the pattern practicing take-offs and landings. After my fourth landing, the aircraft suddenly started to veer toward the left. The aircraft left the runway and entered the grass to the left of the runway. After an unknown distance, the aircraft came to a stop. There was no apparent damage to the aircraft.
ASRS:1796779.s: During pattern practice, the aircraft veered left after the fourth landing, exiting the runway into the grass before stopping. The pilot reported no apparent damage to the aircraft.

ASRS:1796832.n: While executing a recovery from a power on stall during a training flight, I made visual contact with a high wing Cessna 172 or 182 approximately 100 feet to our left and at the same altitude. I immediately maneuvered to the right and initiated a climb in order to provide more spacing with the other aircraft. I do not believe the other aircraft ever had me in sight because it continued on the same heading and altitude after the event occurred.During the entire flight, I was communicating with ZZZ Approach Control with radar contact and a squawk code. Prior to initiating the power on stall maneuver, my student and I made 2 clearing turns to the right and left, with no traffic noted above, below, or at the same altitude. I believe the other aircraft involved was directly or nearly directly below us during the turns, which caused us not to see it. After the stall recovery, I noticed the aircraft climbing up to, and leveling off at our same altitude within approximately 100 feet traveling south to north.I attempted to make contact with the approach controller, but was only able to get a response after 3 attempts and approximately 5 minutes. I initially told the controller that it was within 300 feet, but after consideration, I believe that distance was significantly less. I was not given a traffic alert or altitude restriction during this particular phase of flight.
ASRS:1796832.s: A pilot and student conducting a power-on stall training maneuver encountered a Cessna 172 or 182 at the same altitude approximately 100 feet away. The pilot attributed the near-miss to the other aircraft being below during clearing turns and noted a lack of traffic alerts from Approach Control.

ASRS:1796851.n: I was conducting a training flight and was headed to N40. Approximately 4 miles south of the airport, I made a radio call on UNICOM announcing I was 4 miles south at 2,000 feet descending to pattern with intentions to join the left downwind Runway 25 using a standard 45 degree entry. As I continued to approach the airport, I was scanning in front, to the left, and to the right of me while listening to the radio for relevant traffic. When I was about to make my entry to join a left downwind, I made a radio call announcing that I was joining the downwind leg of Runway 25. Prior to turning, I made a quick scan to the left, center, and right. I did not see any traffic. As I started my turn, I scanned left again and saw a Piper on downwind approximately 200 feet horizontally to the left of my aircraft and 60 feet vertically beneath me. Simultaneously, I heard the Piper make a radio call announcing they were breaking off the downwind and saw the Piper turn away from my aircraft. I judged that the situation was under control so I continued my turn to join downwind and made a radio call to the Piper stating that I had him in sight and apologized for cutting him off in the pattern. The rest of the flight was uneventful. Contributing factors include: 1, Either a lack of an initial radio call from the Piper, or myself missing the radio call from the Piper. 2, I had made a radio call that I was making a 45 degree entry to join the left downwind, but mispositioned my aircraft and made a turn closer to 90 degrees instead. This positioning error may have led the Piper to scan the wrong area. 3, Too fast a scan to detect an aircraft against the backdrop of the ground 4, Busy UNICOM frequency with a lot of radio calls from multiple airports. Regarding human performance considerations, I made a poor judgment to continue to approach the airport directly from the south rather than change course to put the aircraft into a better position for a 45 degree entry to downwind. Additionally, as I was not aware of any radio calls for an aircraft in the pattern at N40, I should have conducted a more thorough scan to look for unexpected aircraft. While I was scanning in all directions, I moved from one sector to another relatively quickly which likely caused me to miss the Piper and reinforce my perception that there were no other aircraft in the pattern. To prevent a recurrence of the situation, I will start thinking about my initial approach direction to an airport further out than I currently do. This should help ensure proper positioning for entry into the pattern and help other traffic locate me. I will also improve my scan and spend more time on each sector. This should greatly improve my ability to spot any unexpected aircraft.
ASRS:1796851.s: During a training flight approaching N40, the pilot nearly collided with a Piper on downwind while executing a 45-degree entry to Runway 25. The pilot attributed the incident to a positioning error, a rapid visual scan, and missed radio communications on a busy UNICOM frequency.

ASRS:1796860.n: I missed a small silver quad copter UAS by approximately 100 feet. My altitude at this point was about 2,000 AGL. I reported the near-miss to Leesburg Tower, they collected the same information presented in this report. As I understand it, UAS may not be operated above 400 AGL without a waiver, therefore the person operating that UAS was likely doing so illegally. The area where this occurred is just outside the Leesburg Maneuvering Area of the DC SFRA and therefore is quite busy with traffic going to and from JYO. I strongly support any efforts to compel all UAS operators to equip with ADS-B Out so that other aircraft can have situational awareness.
ASRS:1796860.s: A pilot reported a near-miss with a small silver quadcopter UAS at approximately 2,000 feet AGL near Leesburg. The pilot believes the UAS was operating illegally above the 400-foot limit and supports requiring ADS-B Out for better situational awareness.

ASRS:1796869.n: We had been flying on an IFR flight plan with a destination of ZZZ, a non-towered airport just north of ZZZ1. As usual, we canceled IFR once we got close to the airport, and began our VFR approach to Runway 24. Upon approach into ZZZ, got a 'Fuel Imbalance' CAS (Crew Alerting System) message with 5 'segments' of difference, without noticing any prior indication of an issue. While dealing with this issue, we also had to deal with other nearby aircraft targets as well (in the practice area right near the traffic pattern for ZZZ, no doubt). Per the appropriate checklist, we took the action of turning on the fuel pump on the fuller side. In spite of taking this action, the indication of the problem got markedly worse (increased to 6 and then to 7 segments) within only 2-3 minutes, yet we still had no controllability issues. We then ended up getting a 'Fuel Balance Fault' CAS message as well. In sum, we were close to the ground, in the vicinity of Class B, near a practice area, trying to deal with this issue. We elected to focus primarily on doing the most important things: aviate, navigate, and communicate. We flew the airplane and began a diversion towards ZZZ1, which we could clearly see. It has a longer and wider runway, which would be important in landing a bit faster than normal to avoid potential controllability issues, and it also has emergency equipment available as well. Notified ATC since the issue had happened so quickly, and the fuel monitoring device depicted that the problem had gotten markedly worse so quickly as well -- felt it best to get on the ground quickly before a controllability issue developed. Landed without incident. If we hadn't been so close to landing (instead being enroute at altitude in the middle of nowhere), we could have obviously spent more time analyzing and dealing with the issue in flight. After landing and thinking about it a bit, we believed it was an indication problem, and not an actual fuel imbalance after all. Upon further reflection overnight of our actions during the flight, we concluded that we wouldn't do anything different than we did. In general, we were pleased with what we did. It was a particularly busy time with the nearby traffic, and we quickly focused on the most important things of aviate, navigate, and communicate. The notifying ATC might be questioned, but only with hindsight, I believe -- I am comfortable with this judgment call.
ASRS:1796869.s: Pilots on an IFR flight diverting to ZZZ1 encountered a worsening Fuel Imbalance and Fuel Balance Fault CAS message during a VFR approach to non-towered ZZZ. They prioritized aviating, navigating, and communicating, diverted to ZZZ1 for a safe landing, and later concluded the issue was likely an indication fault rather than an actual imbalance.

ASRS:1796907.n: A pilot reported in proper shut down on the aircraft. Mechanics removed and replaced the carburetor on DATE. The job was approximately finished around XA:00 that day. Mechanic signed the paperwork for the carburetor. A cotter pin on the throttle cable was missed causing a loss in power resulting in an emergency landing on the road way.
ASRS:1796907.s: After mechanics replaced the carburetor and signed off, a pilot experienced power loss during flight due to a missed cotter pin on the throttle cable. This mechanical oversight caused an emergency landing on a roadway.

ASRS:1796910.n: On the PANGG 3 Arrival in to MDW, we were cleared for the RNAV (GPS) Z 13 C Approach. I, as the Pilot Flying, entered the RNAV approach into the FMC and started to verify the points. The points in our up-to-date FMC did not match the points on our up-do-date chart. We asked ATC for the RNAV (RNP) Y 13C Approach, and were issued that.
ASRS:1796910.s: The Pilot Flying on a PANGG 3 arrival into MDW found FMC waypoints for the RNAV (GPS) Z 13C approach did not match the chart. The crew requested and received a clearance for the RNAV (RNP) Y 13C approach instead.

ASRS:1796912.n: We were flying the PANGG Arrival with the Runway 13C transition. The ATIS for MDW was advertising the 'RNP' Approach to 13C. We had programmed the RNAV Y 13C. Upon check-in with Approach, we were told to expect the RNAV Z 13C. I looked at chart and noticed that was a straight-in GPS approach, which I found odd that we would be issued since the ILS was operational. I questioned ATC if they meant the 'Y' or the 'Z' approach, and they confirmed the 'Z.' The Pilot Flying loaded the approach in the FMC and began to brief the points, to which we realized none of them matched the chart. We both looked in the list of available charts and the list in the FMC database to make sure we were looking at the correct approaches, and it appeared we were. I checked both Jeppesen apps and they both had the same approach plate, dated 2018. I looked to see if there was a NOTAM I had missed or a message in the airport page and there wasn't one. My assumption was this was a new approach, since the FMC database was for (date-two days ago), and for whatever reason, we did not have the approach plate available. I notified ATC that we did not have the proper plate, and would be unable to do the approach. We were then issued the RNAV Y for 13C, and I confirmed with ATC the points on the approach to make sure we had the correct procedure. Both the First Officer and I had current Jeppesen databases. I checked after arrival if there was an update available, and there was not. My currency said there was 13 days until the next update. I called Dispatch to let them know what happened, and he thought it was due to the fact that we have tailored charts, but he would forward the information. I did mention putting a note on the weather packet. Prior to filling out this report, I checked the backup documents on the company website, and they also have the old chart dated 2018 in that database. However, government sources (NOS) have a chart dated (date-two days ago) that have the new approach with points that match our FMC database. My guess is that the Jeppesen app either did not update properly, or they have omitted the chart from this cycle.
ASRS:1796912.s: Pilots flying a PANGG arrival to MDW were issued an RNAV Z 13C approach that matched their FMC database but not their Jeppesen charts. They declined the approach due to this discrepancy, received the RNAV Y 13C instead, and attributed the issue to a potential Jeppesen update failure.

ASRS:1796914.n: Cruise FL 380 above a high undercast, seatbelt sign on, passengers and flight attendants seated. The ride had been smooth when we suddenly encountered light to moderate turbulence. I checked the weather radar, which was tilted down 1 degree and there were no returns ahead. Concerned there may be embedded precipitation below, I adjusted the tilt further down. This showed green returns ahead embedded in the undercast. These returns turned yellow as we approached. Concerned about overflying the embedded returns, the First Officer and I discussed deviation options. During the discussion, we encountered rapidly intensifying airspeed and altitude fluctuations. The aircraft began an un-commanded climb and rapid acceleration. The First Officer immediately notified Air Traffic Control of severe turbulence and requested a higher altitude commensurate with the climb. ATC granted the higher altitude. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottles but was unable to prevent an overspeed condition. In retrospect, the event may better be described as severe wave action. There was a feel of a slight and smooth aircraft loading, but not the significant jarring action typically associated with turbulence. The airspeed and altitude variations continued and we requested a block altitude which ATC immediately granted. With the rapid increase and loss of airspeed, aircraft control became my first priority. We were visually above the undercast and any possible embedded weather, so I elected not to increase aircraft loading by turning or banking the aircraft. I continued straight and may have inadvertently flown over convective activity embedded below. Discussions with the Flight Attendants after the encounter indicated they did not feel the ride was too bad and they had not received any complaints or comments from the passengers. There were no injuries, damage or passenger complaints. When the ride settled down we notified Company via ACARS of the event and continued to our destination. Appropriate logbook writeups were made and an aircraft inspection performed by Maintenance. While operating with manual radar in areas of possible convective activity embedded below, more aggressive use of the radar tilt and occasional look downs may allow more time for deviation planning. While in cruise at FL 380, we were having a mostly smooth ride. As we began to encounter some light chop to light turbulence we seated the flight attendants and passengers and asked ATC for more ride reports ahead. The last report from ATC said they had nothing more than light chop ahead so far. We had elected to stay at FL 380 due to the ride and being bit too heavy earlier in the flight for FL 400. We were above a continuous cloud deck far below us with multiple cloud layers ahead of us, but all below us. Approaching SPI VORTAC we discussed the clouds ahead and their height relative to us and whether or not we should proceed along our route or take a turn to the north to avoid possible turbulence associated with them. We could not see any specific build ups, but turned the radar on and began scanning ahead for possible convective activity or embedded thunderstorms in the clouds. Before we could make a turn and before reaching the clouds ahead, we experienced a rapid increase in airspeed. The Captain immediately tried to reduce power before we started to overspeed. Once we began to overspeed it was apparent we had encountered a very heavy mountain wave or turbulence, and due to the loss of airspeed control I immediately told Center we had encountered severe turbulence. As the Captain worked to control our speed, our altitude began to fluctuate above our cruise altitude about 300 feet. I asked the Captain if he wanted to climb with the wave and asked Center for FL 390. Center cleared us to FL 390. As we climbed to FL 390 it became apparent we were not out of the wave, so I asked Center for a block altitude to give us room to work with speed and altitude. Center gave us a block from FL 390-FL 400. We then slowly climbed to FL 400 as the wave activity and airspeed fluctuations seemed less as we climbed. We leveled at FL 400 and the turbulence was mostly gone. We held the block attitude for while until we were sure we were clear of the turbulence. The entire event took place in VMC conditions. The turbulence was not severe in itself, but the mountain wave and rapid uncontrolled airspeed increase was great enough that I felt we needed to call it severe. By the time the event was over, the wind and weather was behind us. I also felt this would let ATC know we may not be able to hold RVSM altitude separation. ATC was very helpful and we were not in the vicinity of other aircraft during this event. After the event we checked on the flight attendants and verified the passengers were OK and not appearing alarmed. The flight attendants assured us they were OK and the passengers were not commenting and did not seem alarmed. This event was much more noticeable to us on the flight deck, due to primarily being airspeed related, more than turbulence. After landing, the Captain and I fully debriefed and also debriefed with the flight attendants so they would have a better understanding of what had transpired. This is a glaring reminder for constant vigilance for turbulence and weather. Early warning is key for the safety of the passengers and aircraft. When we began to discuss the look of clouds ahead and to the left of our course, we should have made a precautionary turn, even when we felt we had enough room above and felt they did not produce a hazard by the look of them. A small turn north may have made all the difference. Also, we did not have any tops reports, which would have helped us, but is also a reminder to not only keep asking for them, but to give them out whenever possible for the safety of other aircraft and crews as well.
ASRS:1796914.s: The flight crew encountered severe mountain wave turbulence at FL 380, causing uncommanded climbs and overspeeds despite no radar returns initially. They requested and received a block altitude to FL 400 to regain control, resulting in no injuries or damage.

ASRS:1796917.n: After we pushed off gate XX, our pushback crew stopped the aircraft at a slight angle toward gate XY, while we were facing the service road between the ramp and the gate XX Safety Zone. The nose of the aircraft was approximately 30 feet from the service road. I cleared my left side, my FO (First Officer) cleared the right side, and we began our right turn to taxi to Runway XXR. Since we were very close to the service road, our nose and left wing needed to cross the service road during the right turn. As I was looking into my turn to the right, I noticed motion from the left side of the aircraft using my peripheral vision. When I turned my head to the left, I saw a fast moving (Company) tug towing baggage carts approaching from my left traveling east to west on the service road. The vehicle did not stop and continued on the road traveling between my left wing and nose. As the driver was passing by, it appeared that he did not see us. I immediately applied the brakes to prevent the tug from colliding with our aircraft. We came to a stop just short of the road as the vehicle passed by. The driver swerved left off the service road and pulled alongside another (Company) vehicle and began talking to the driver of the other vehicle. I set the parking brake, called (Company) Operations on the radio to report the near-miss incident with tug. The tug remained stopped momentarily while the two drivers spoke to each other. The second driver seemed to be telling the offending driver that he was blocking our aircraft and needed to move away. Tug did a looping turn and departed the area. If we had not stopped, we would have had a collision with the fast moving tug and baggage carts.
ASRS:1796917.s: During pushback and initial taxi, a company tug towing baggage carts crossed the service road between the aircraft's nose and left wing without stopping. The pilot applied brakes to avoid a collision, stopping just short of the road while the tug driver appeared unaware of the aircraft's position.

ASRS:1796919.n: At ZZZ, Human Remains were added in cargo but not included in Manifest. The flight crew did not have any knowledge of this until after shutdown in ZZZ1.
ASRS:1796919.s: Human remains were loaded into the cargo hold at ZZZ but omitted from the manifest. The flight crew remained unaware of this discrepancy until after the aircraft shutdown at ZZZ1.

ASRS:1796921.n: Filed to climb via DOTSS except maintain 5,000 feet. Tower cleared us for takeoff on a 210 heading up to 5,000 feet. I switched over to departure and checked on passing 1,500 feet with heading and assigned altitude of 5,000 feet. Departure cleared us direct PEVEE and climb 17,000 feet. I believed he just told me direct ENNEY and 17,000 feet, which I read back. We put it in the box and executed it. Then verified 17,000 feet in altitude window. The Captain said he was surprised we are heading back to ENNEY. I immediately called departure to clarify fix. They had a controller swap during that short time. The new controller advised us to fly 180 heading to PEVEE.Change the name of fix. Depending on how I read and pronounce and hear ENNEY and PEVEE sound the same if you don't hear the P with PEVEE. Which was the case with us. I also read back ENNEY, which the Controller didn't catch me saying incorrectly. We were cleared on the DOTSS2.CNERY. We were cleared for takeoff on Runway 24L at LAX and assigned heading 210 after departure. We had VNAV selected and deselected LNAV once we received the revised clearance. After takeoff we contacted SoCal and were given a clearance to a fix on the departure. We believed the clearance was to ENNEY intersection. I began the turn to ENNEY and questioned the turn because it didn't make sense to turn that far right to join the departure. The F/O then asked for clarification on the clearance. There appeared to have been a Controller change while we were turning. The new Controller then cleared us to turn to a 180 heading. The Controller clarified the clearance and cleared us direct PEVEE. The remainder of the flight was normal. The SoCal frequency had some static on the frequency which made it a little hard to hear the clearance. There was also some confusion on which fix we were cleared to due the the frequency static and due to misunderstanding of the annunciation of the ENNEY fix.In hind sight I don't think we clearly heard the fix we were cleared to. We started to ENNEY and the large turn is what made me question the clearance but I don't think we heard the clearance well enough and should have questioned the clearance earlier. The F/O read back ENNEY but I think it might have fell through the cracks due to the Controller change at the same time.
ASRS:1796921.s: Pilots at LAX misheard a departure clearance for fix PEVEE as ENNEY due to radio static and a controller change, causing an incorrect turn. The crew corrected the error after questioning the large turn, and the new controller reissued the correct heading to PEVEE.

ASRS:1796975.n: On pushback from gate. After tow-bar removal and headset disconnect, we were starting engines. I observed the marshaller standing in front of our aircraft giving the all clear signal with arms at 45 degrees, waiting for me to flash the taxi light. However, the tug was still directly in front of our aircraft! We could barely see the tug if we leaned forward in our seats, it was that close to our aircraft. I tried to point and gesture at the tug in my window, trying to let the ramper know that the tug was not clear of our aircraft. The ramper did not figure it out, and gave me a salute, and walked to the tug. I never flashed my taxi light at him. If we had taxied forward with the position of the tug, our aircraft would have struck the tug for sure. Before we taxied, I called Ramp Control on the radio, and informed them of this unsafe practice by our push crew. Non-SOP procedures. Unsafe practice. Poor training. Frequent occurrence.
ASRS:1796975.s: During pushback, the pilot observed a marshaller signal for clearance while the tug remained dangerously close to the aircraft. The pilot refused to flash the taxi light, alerted Ramp Control, and attributed the near collision to non-SOP procedures and poor training by the ramp crew.

ASRS:1797018.n: Airline supertug 1 was repositioning a B787 from the ZZZ Hardstand (Terminal X) to Ramp Exit XX. As the supertug was backing onto the ramp area, Aircraft X was observed entering the XX Alleyway and taxiing around the aircraft under tow (which was still in motion) to Gate XXB in what seemed to be an unsafe maneuver, for which the supertug Operator had to stop abruptly to avoid contact with Aircraft X. While it is true that the XX Alleyway is uncontrolled, the Aircraft X Flight Crew should have stopped and contacted FAA Ground as the primary overseer of all ground movement.
ASRS:1797018.s: A supertug towing a B787 from ZZZ Hardstand to Ramp Exit XX stopped abruptly to avoid Aircraft X, which taxied unsafely around the moving tow in the uncontrolled XX Alleyway. The reporter states the Aircraft X crew should have stopped and contacted FAA Ground instead of proceeding.

ASRS:1797026.n: 20 minute span out time with no communication from crew to ATC, ATC Coordinator or Dispatch. Took 12 ACARS from myself and the ATC Coordinator to finally get into contact with the crew. However none of the ATC Coordinator messages appeared to go through to the crew. Position reports updated but no response until after the 12th ACARS. Crew said they were experiencing 'weird ACARS/GPS/WIFI for while maybe military jamming or something'.
ASRS:1797026.s: The crew experienced a 20-minute communication blackout during flight, requiring 12 ACARS messages from ATC and the Coordinator to establish contact. The crew attributed the loss of ACARS, GPS, and WiFi to potential military jamming.

ASRS:1797028.n: 30 flights today. Hoping for a perfect day, no swaps, no 2nd releases. Too many flights. Yesterday, another Dispatcher with 30+ flights had a Part 91 flight. The Part 91 flight was not a typical one concerning flight planning and approaches with runway closed. The result was that the Dispatcher and Chief spent so much time on this flight to make sure it was legal and safe, that the Dispatcher was unable to leave the desk to grab their lunch out of the fridge to eat. The Dispatcher did not eat lunch due to the operational pressure to release the remaining flights on the desk before shift end. So sad that Dispatchers are forgoing lunch and bathroom breaks due to the increase in workload. What a shame to what this has become.
ASRS:1797028.s: A Dispatcher handling 30 flights missed lunch and bathroom breaks due to excessive workload caused by a complex Part 91 flight with a closed runway. The operational pressure to release remaining flights before shift end prevented the Dispatcher from taking necessary breaks.

ASRS:1797029.n: Due to extremely high workloads on [Continent] desks on [Date], I did not have the opportunity to look at METAR/ATIS information. If the crew did not have pertinent weather information, the crew would have sent me a message or called. These 3 flights that were under my supervision, were released by one of the 4 desks I took over at XA:00. The following flights affected Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1, Aircraft Y ZZZ-ZZZ2, and Aircraft Z ZZZ-ZZZ2.
ASRS:1797029.s: Due to high workloads, the dispatcher could not review METAR/ATIS data for three flights (Aircraft X, Y, and Z) released by another desk. The reporter noted that crews would have requested weather information if they lacked it.

ASRS:1797031.n: This report is to provide information into the ongoing workload issues we are seeing. I was working day shift Desk XX this day and the amount of flights on this desk if they were not following each other AND I did not have good support around me would of been un-manageable. I am on the workload committee I/WE followed all procedures but this day the Duty Officer and Chief did not want to move any flights off my desk. Thank goodness for my fellow dispatchers they convinced the Duty Officer to move the ZZZ to ZZZ1 flight from this desk there would of been no way I could of released it at sometime around XA:30 LCL time. The flights worksheets were not balanced on MIDs for the dayshift so that is why we requested the ZZZ to ZZZ1 flight be moved right away at XB:10. I just looked at my worksheet and knew I would have issues with that flight given the fact I had 4 other long hauls to release, one of them being the ZZZ2-ZZZ3 flight and due to the amount of flights I had airborne all shift.Please see the attached screen shot from DV (Dispatch View). I am also attaching the afternoon's worksheet. My fellow co-workers and myself requested to have a couple flights moved from afternoon worksheet with no luck. I have no idea what happened after I left. If you look at Desk XY that day you will notice the workload very different. They had some flight yes, but I knew if anything happened I had backup. There was lots of turbulence all the way across the North-Pacific this morning. One of my ETOPS ALT was marginal, ZZZ4, with I was updating my flights about. One thing that was good and I want to point out is that ZZZ5-ZZZ6 flight were all following each other. That provided help and was the only way this desk could be manageable. We recommend that on the committee. Same city pairs on a desks. What would of helped if the ZZZ7-ZZZ6 flight was released on another desk and or the ZZZ3-ZZZ8 flight also moved. That would of made this desk way more manageable
ASRS:1797031.s: A dispatcher reported unmanageable workload on Desk XX during day shift due to an unbalanced worksheet and refusal by management to move flights. Colleagues successfully convinced the Duty Officer to reassign one flight, preventing a release failure despite turbulence and marginal ETOPS conditions.

ASRS:1797204.n: During cruise, 3 hours in the flight, I heard a loud noise that sounded like a stall/chug. I was near L1 door. I asked the A FA (Flight Attendant), he heard it but he didn't. Later on, I went to the back of the plane. Aft galley & told the C FA what I felt and she told me she felt something 'unusual' on the floor of the aft galley, probably about the same time I was in the fwd galley. We decided to call the pilots (called them twice) but they didn't pick up. We would try again a few minutes later, figured they were busy with the sound but just then, they called for a lavatory break. We ended up forgetting to notify them. During decent, wheels down, the C FA & I felt the aft of the aircraft chug a few times and make the strange popping sounds. We both looked at each other and decided to talk about it upon landing. When we landed, we both agreed it was 'abnormal' so we called the pilots when we were disarmed and at the gate. After calling the pilots and explaining to them, the Captain told us to go to the flight deck and close the flight deck door. He ended up explaining to us that they did feel the abnormal chugs and thought it was a bird strike and didn't know until we were on the ground that the engine had failed (showed us on the monitor a red icon on the engine) but didn't really explain other wise. Myself and the rest of the crew didn't feel that great about the debrief. The A & C were able to go but the D and I had to continue on to ZZZ. That night, going to bed, I realized how serious the situation was and made me feel uneasy. On date, after landing in ZZZ1, a different Captain was talking about the incident because earlier in the day, there was an emergency landing by another airline and the [type aircraft]. Anyhow, when he realized I was on the ETOPS flight, he mentioned that we were lucky to be alive. He did an amazing job explaining that our situation was a 'compressor failure' and many things can cause that but the biggest concern was that after leaving ZZZ2 , the engine was sending pings to maintenance notifying of the engine overheating...the pilots decided to continue on to ZZZ3. Knowing that bit of information, and then to experience the compressor failure and no good CRM, I am frustrated, annoyed and somewhat uneasy flying to ZZZ2 now after hearing unfamiliar sounds about three hours into flight (the C FA heard these sounds as well), I called the pilots at about 3 hours into flight but didn't get a hold of them. I then forgot until the next set of sounds were heard at gear down. Upon parking at the gate, I called the pilots and I was instructed to talk to them with the door shut when I go to the front. After all guests were off the plane, I explained to the pilots again what sounds we heard and the Captain told me (then the rest of the crew) that the sounds heard were those in line of what is heard of a 'bird strike'. He then mention something to the fact that the engine went off line (he said this because I pointed out that the engine symbol on the instrument panel had a red square on it) about two times and we all were then confused and he said we shouldn't worry about it. Better CRM and think about the whole ready, safe, go action plan. There should have been a way better debrief by the pilots. After an event like this, I shouldn't be the one pushing for answers when I felt uneasy.
ASRS:1797204.s: Cabin crew heard abnormal engine noises during cruise and descent but failed to notify pilots until after landing. The captain later revealed an engine compressor failure occurred, which he initially misidentified as a bird strike, resulting in poor crew resource management and an inadequate debrief.

ASRS:1797205.n: Passenger in 31A had a single wheel balancing board under 160[Wh] lithium battery. One section in our manual states it's good to go under 160[Wh], however under the Dangerous Good section it states single wheel balancing device (eg, hoverboards) are prohibited. The Gate Agent, their Supervisor, and whomever answered the phone for [company] said it was allowed. We took the passenger and board. Good idea to have approved sticker!!! During boarding a passenger came on with a one wheel pint (similar to hoverboard). We were not sure if this was prohibited. The passenger said they had called ahead and was told since the non removable lithium battery was less than 160 [Wh] it was allowed as a carry on. They also had already flown from ZZZ1 to ZZZ with it. They also told me their brother had flown earlier this year with one, no problem. In our flight attendant manual section 6.500 page 7 it does seem to be allowable if stowed overhead, which we did. After take off and upon further review of the manual we discovered in section 6.500 page 4 self-balancing devices (e.g. hoverboards) are prohibited. We continued on to ZZZ1 landing safely without incident. It would be nice to have this clarified. The customer suggested a certificate of approval. Clarification and certificates of approval for questionable devices.
ASRS:1797205.s: Flight attendants boarded two passengers with single-wheel balancing devices after ground staff and the airline confirmed they were permitted due to battery ratings under 160Wh. Although the crew later found these devices prohibited in the manual, the flight landed safely without incident, highlighting a need for clearer approval documentation.

ASRS:1797222.n: Aircraft X was ready to depart ZZZ. Mechanic called maintenance for a Class 2 Air Bleed message on ECAM, the CA (Captain) just wrote up. I issued MEL 36 XXX left wing loop B fault without checking history. I thought the aircraft was on a thru flight since it was way late in the afternoon. After the aircraft departed, a ZZZ Crew Chief called maintenance and informed maintenance that the aircraft was in ZZZ all night with a Drop Dead MEL 36XXX C/N XXXXXX L/PXXXXXXX. This aircraft did not make one flight without new fault. NO NEW MEL should have been issued.I did not look at history. I thought the aircraft was on a Thru FLT. Maintenance did not say anything about history, which is was just sign-off. I was in a hurry to dispatch the aircraft. I did not take a Class 2 maintenance message as a serious fault. Wing Loops do fault very often.Always review history and do not get in a hurry. Ask the Mechanic to also review the log book.
ASRS:1797222.s: A maintenance controller issued an incorrect MEL for a Class 2 Air Bleed fault on Aircraft X at ZZZ without checking the logbook history. The error occurred because the controller assumed a through-flight and rushed dispatch, ignoring a known overnight fault that required a Drop Dead MEL.

ASRS:1797231.n: While taxiing out departing ZZZ, ATC advised that a Lear Jet had just reported moderate turbulence along our route. We acknowledged and briefly discussed the topic and after looking at radar, decided we were safe to depart since our returns showed only moderate rain. After take off and while climbing through 2,000 ft to level at 3,000 ft., we encountered severe turbulence. The aircraft was at 230 knots and began to shake rapidly and violently. Items in the cabin that were not secured moved about freely and our passengers voiced concern. I reduced power to idle to attempt to slow to maneuvering speed as the airplane violently became marginally controllable. We were assigned a level off at 3,000 ft., however, this seemed an unlikely event as I had tried to level from our turn and pushed forward on the elevator, but the plane continued to climb at idle power with the elevator forward. When we recovered, we were at 3,900 ft and immediately began our descent back to 3,000 ft as we advised center. The radar only painted green returns and although yellow returns were also adjacent to us, we were at least 10 miles from any of those yellow returns. We were given climb instructions as we leveled at 3,000 and given a controller change. As we climbed and began to top some of the clouds 9,000 feet we encountered a similar event in essentially clear air just at the tops of the clouds in level flight. Again, I reduced power to idle and tried to maintain wings level and altitude, but the aircraft was only marginally controllable and violently being pitched and rolled. Both events lasted approximately 10-20 seconds and we then reported both events to ATC center as severe turbulence. Again, radar showed nothing significant on our second encounter. Once on the ground, the aircraft was inspected for damage and none was found.
ASRS:1797231.s: The flight crew encountered severe turbulence twice while climbing from 2,000 to 9,000 feet after departing ZZZ, despite radar showing only moderate rain. The aircraft became marginally controllable with violent shaking and uncommanded climbs, though no damage was found after landing.

ASRS:1797243.n: I was in cruise flight at 6,500 ft. in VFR conditions when my airplane engine started getting rough. I applied full carburetor heat for a few minutes and expected it to clear the issue. However, after several minutes the roughness became worse and despite having full carburetor heat and full throttle (per aircraft POH (Pilots Operating Handbook)) the engine turned off. I was circling about 5 miles south of ZZZ and immediately headed towards it while still at around 5,000 ft. MSL. I spoke to Approach and advised them of my issue and that I was heading to the airport for [an] engine out landing. I kept trying to turn the engine back on during this time while also flying a left traffic for Runway XX. While making the short final approach and descending the engine came on at about 300 ft. AGL and I was able to make a fairly normal landing.
ASRS:1797243.s: The pilot experienced engine roughness and subsequent shutdown at 6,500 ft while in cruise, despite applying full carburetor heat and throttle. The engine restarted at 300 ft AGL during the approach to ZZZ, allowing for a normal landing after an engine-out declaration.

ASRS:1797245.n: I departed ZZZ for ZZZ1. My flight plan showed that I should arrive at ZZZ1 with 1,453 pounds of fuel. From the start of my taxi to take off on [Runway] XR was twelve minutes. After a couple of vectors and a brief level off at 10,000 feet, we were cleared to climb to FL370 and given direct ZZZZZ intersection. However, the flight plan called for FL390 for our initial altitude. At ZZZZZ, I was three minutes behind the flight plan and 248 pounds behind on fuel. I was later cleared to climb to FL390 about 1:10 into the flight. I reached FL390. At this time my fuel was falling further behind. When I crossed ZZZZZ1, my fuel gauge showed that I was nearly 600 pounds behind the flight plan. Shortly after, I requested and received permission to climb to FL410. At my next waypoint, ZZZZZ2, the flight plan calculated 4,098 lbs. Thirty-six minutes from ZZZZZ2, the fuel gauge was showing 4,100 lbs. The Point of Safe Return was 2:12 into the flight. A little less than two hours into the flight my co-pilot and I decided to return to ZZZ. I requested a turn from HF Radio. I informed the radio operator that if I did not get an amended clearance as soon as possible that I would have to notify ATC. The operator was unable to receive the amended ATC clearance as quickly as I had hoped. Therefore, I notified ATC and instructed my co-pilot to make a left turn towards R464. Shortly after we completed the turn, we received a new clearance to proceed via to ZZZ2. I canceled the emergency once we were heading toward the ZZZZZ3 intersection. (We chose to return to ZZZ2 because it was nine minutes closer than ZZZ.) The accuracy of the fuel gauge came into question on our return leg to ZZZ2. The fuel numbers on the flight plan began to agree with the quantity on the gauge once we were below 4,000 lbs. The actual fuel flow numbers were close to flight plan fuel flow numbers.
