When we landed at ZZZ2, we indicated 1,500 lbs. Total flight time was 4:44.
ASRS:1797245.s: The pilot and co-pilot of a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 encountered significant fuel discrepancies during climb to FL410, prompting a return to ZZZ2. The crew declared an emergency due to delayed ATC clearances and suspected fuel gauge inaccuracy, landing with 1,500 pounds of fuel.

ASRS:1797255.n: I was taxiing from the parking area to the active runway via the Taxiway at 39N [Princeton Airport]. Active was Runway 28. I noticed a car parked on the grass along the runway behind the PAPI lights. As I taxied down I noticed a person runway along the runway with orange cones on the runway. As I taxied down I noticed a white sports like 'race car' approaching me on the taxiway. They veered into the grass as I taxied down and I have to veer steer my aircraft to the right of the taxiway to avoid them passing underneath my wing. As I approached the run up area I noticed two cars, various tripods with equipment and one of the cars was behind the threshold in grass of the active runway with two people outside the car. I stopped at the runway hold short lines, and had to shut down as they weren't moving. I got out of plane and had to explain to them that they have cars, equipment and cones on an active runway. The person said he worked there and had permission from his boss to be there. I had to state repeatedly that I cannot take the runway safely with people, cars, and equipment on the active runway, which they didn't seem to understand. I reviewed showed them the runway hold short lines and reviewed that anything on the runway side of these lines has to be moved. I asked what they would do about an approaching aircraft, he indicated he had a radio- but this airport doesn't technically require radio use to land there. I reviewed what they are doing is dangerous. After they cleared their cars, equipment, cones, and people I was able to start back up and obtain my departure clearance and depart uneventfully. The field was NOT NOTAM'ed closed for race car activity in my briefings. Monitoring CTAF during my previous landing, parking, then later restarting and taxiing did not indicate any of this activity.I should have notified NY Approach Controllers after establishing contact with them but I didn't. The Controller was very busy but it was my mistake not to notify them in hindsight.
ASRS:1797255.s: A pilot taxiing at Princeton Airport encountered unauthorized race cars, equipment, and personnel on the active runway and taxiway, forcing a shutdown and manual intervention to clear the area. The incident occurred because the activity was not NOTAM'd or broadcast on CTAF, and the pilot failed to notify Approach Control.

ASRS:1797262.n: I was descending to land in a targeted landing field east of high-value homes when a drone operator sent his equipment into my balloon. The drone tore through a low panel of fabric, fell into the pilot compartment, hit me on the head, and flopped around on the floor like a fish in a boat. It distracted me and so I overburned and aborted my approach to landing. I then landed at an alternate landing site, [Name] High School - where 2 other balloons had landed.
ASRS:1797262.s: A balloon pilot descending for landing was struck by a drone that tore through the envelope and entered the basket, hitting the pilot on the head. The distraction caused an overburn and approach abort, resulting in a landing at an alternate site.

ASRS:1797291.n: I was seated on the jumpseat on flight deck and the First Officer demanded I wear a face mask after pushback per policy, while they both (Pilot Crew Members) did not, which is inconsistent with Safety and general communication requirements requested of a Jumpseat Crew Member. Here is why:To ride on the jumpseat we must be a current licensed pilot, with current medical license and fit to perform duties.1. We are consistently asked to be a second set of eyes. Because I wear glasses where I wear my face mask my glasses fog up. I'm unable to see instruments and other traffic.2.The face masks impedes verbal communication with the other Crew Members if needing to intervene because the Crew is wearing headsets, jet noise and unable to effectively hear or read lips. This is well documented in studies.3. The time to useful consciousness is limited. Having glasses and face mask impedes putting on O2 mask on in the event of a Rapid Decompression. The flight deck door is locked, we have NO rubber jungle that falls and I'm solely responsible for my own Safety to get my mask on. This is an impediment to Safety as a Jumpseater. I am not treated the same as the operating Crew Members, even though I'm asked to be a Safety Observer.
ASRS:1797291.s: A jumpseat pilot reported that the First Officer required them to wear a face mask during pushback while the operating crew did not. The reporter stated this policy created safety hazards by fogging glasses, impeding communication, and delaying oxygen mask donning during potential rapid decompression.

ASRS:1797299.n: At FL380, in smooth air, we encountered a sudden non-mountainous wave. We encountered fluctuations in speed up to plus and minus 25 knots (roughly M88 to M78) and altitude deviations of up to 300-400 feet. Rates of climb and descent reached 1800 feet per minute. Event lasted for about a minute before we descended with clearance to FL360. The aircraft over speed was probably by a few knots, but not over 5 knots.
ASRS:1797299.s: The flight crew encountered sudden non-mountainous wave turbulence at FL380, causing speed fluctuations of ±25 knots and altitude deviations up to 400 feet. The event lasted one minute before the crew descended to FL360 with clearance, resulting in a minor overspeed of less than 5 knots.

ASRS:1797324.n: GPS and radio signals very intermittent when approaching and flying through this area. We could hear ATC when we received ACARS requesting frequency 133.45 but obviously missed them handing us off to next sector.
ASRS:1797324.s: The crew experienced intermittent GPS and radio signals while approaching and flying through the area. They missed the ATC handoff to the next sector because they only heard the controller after receiving an ACARS request for frequency 133.45.

ASRS:1797333.n: We were conducting a visual approach on Runway 16L which it was backed up with RNAV X RWY 16L. We were on MYBAD RNAV approach and we decided to call the field in sight in VMC conditions and we were cleared for the visual approach. We sequence the flight plan and verified runway, once we intercepted NAV we disconnected the autopilot and started our descent to cross SEKAW at 7,800 ft. During final configuration we descended below the profile momentarily and we got the EGPWS [Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning Systems] 'Caution terrain' and immediately we corrected the profile and continue with the approach.
ASRS:1797333.s: Pilots conducting a visual approach on Runway 16L descended below the profile during final configuration, triggering an EGPWS 'Caution terrain' warning. They immediately corrected the descent to rejoin the profile and continued the approach.

ASRS:1797338.n: Before turning left base for RWY 36L at 4,000 feet, we noticed we were following a larger aircraft. I noticed on my range scale the preceding aircraft was more than 5 miles ahead. We were heading south on the arrival. Approach turned us left heading 090. We were still slightly more than 5 miles in trail. Approximately half way through the left turn the aircraft rolled further left to approximately 50 degrees, resulting in the AP disconnecting and the 'Bank Angle Aural'. I assumed manual control and initially leveled the wings, maintained our altitude and resumed the turn manually. Once level on the 090 heading i asked for the AP to be turned back on and we let ATC know we just encountered wake turbulence. They let us know we were 5 miles in trail of an A321. The rest of the flight continued with no further event.
ASRS:1797338.s: During the arrival for RWY 36L at 4,000 feet, the crew encountered wake turbulence from a preceding A321 while turning left. The turbulence caused a 50-degree bank, disconnecting the autopilot and triggering a bank angle aural warning, requiring manual control to recover.

ASRS:1797357.n: Out of an abundance of caution and to the best of my memory I can recall that shortly after the initial climb and in a clean configuration the Captain alerted me that he had some difficulty with the electric trim on his control yoke. I observed that it was indeed intermittent. After I completed the Climb Checklist we tried some trouble-shooting with both autopilots and my trim switch. With no caution lights, I referred to the QRH to help diagnose the issue with the proper checklist. During this time the Captain was contacting Dispatch and Maintenance for assistance while I talked to ATC. At some point in this process we were able to notice that my autopilot would engage and I became the Pilot Flying. We stopped the climb and slowed the aircraft. The Captain proceeded with the Stabilizer Trim Inoperative Checklist which calls to cutout both stab trim cutout switches and manually trim the aircraft. As I flew manually we elected to advise ATC and return to ZZZ. The Captain informed the Company, ATC, flight attendants and passengers and offered his assistance to me. I vaguely recall that during the descent a Speed Trim Fail light illuminated as a result from the cutout switches being selected to cutout. There was some discussion that we may or may not be over the max landing weight upon arrival and therefore an AML entry was entered after landing along with a Speed Trim Fail, Stabilizer Trim Failure, and inoperative autopilots entries. I performed a safe Flaps 15 landing [and] all passengers and crew deplaned safely with no injuries. I can attest that the training I have received was very beneficial to the successful outcome from this event. I believe as a crew we worked the problem out very well with the strategy and am thankful for the Captain's knowledge, professional conduct, and reassurance to everyone for a safe outcome. The mechanic did state that perhaps the event may have been caused by a software issue. During climbout and after cleanup, I noticed that the electric stabilizer trim was intermittent. Then it became unresponsive. At this point the Speed Trim system appeared to actuate for about half a second and never actuated again. We attempted to engage the A autopilot. It wouldn't engage. The B autopilot did engage and I passed control of the aircraft to the FO (First Officer). We conducted the 'Stabilizer Trim Inoperative' checklist. Within about 5 minutes of engaging the B, it disengaged itself and the FO hand flew the aircraft for the remainder of the flight. We advised ATC and returned to ZZZ. We selected Runway XX and requested a 15 mile final to get fully configured and trimmed as well as possible. The FO was able to manually trim the aircraft without difficulty. During the descent, at about 12,000-15,000 feet, the 'Speed Trim Fail' light illuminated. We conducted a Flaps 15 landing and taxied back to the gate. I made an AML entry for the Stab Trim, Speed Trim Fail light and for possible overweight landing.I think the focus of the MAX simulator session was helpful in dealing with this situation.
ASRS:1797357.s: During climb, the crew experienced intermittent electric stabilizer trim that became unresponsive, causing autopilot disengagement and a Speed Trim Fail light. They manually trimmed the aircraft, returned to ZZZ, and performed a safe Flaps 15 landing with no injuries, suspecting a software issue.

ASRS:1797386.n: During decent in ZZZ, [we] received [a] lightning strike. Approximately 5 minutes later, [we] lost [the] Captain's air data and airspeed was INOP. [We] received many related and unrelated EICAS messages to air data failure [and] also received many other EICAS messages, such as EEC for both engines, ground proximity, rudder ratio, etc. [There were] so many messages I lost track. We ran QRH procedures for unreliable airspeed [and requested priority handling] with ATC. Captain landed safely. [We] notified [the Dispatcher], Duty Officer, and Maintenance. [The] event [was] documented in [the] aircraft maintenance logbook. I do not know for sure but suspect a lightning strike [was the cause].
ASRS:1797386.s: During descent in ZZZ, the crew received a lightning strike followed by a loss of the Captain's air data and multiple EICAS messages. The pilots executed unreliable airspeed procedures and landed safely, suspecting the lightning strike caused the failure.

ASRS:1797396.n: Significant wake turbulence associated with takeoff behind A321. Departing Runway 25R at PHX, [we were] lined up and cleared for takeoff behind a departing A321 as it rotated downfield. Our takeoff sequence started normally with flex numbers and a standard rotation at Vr. Between 100-200 feet AGL, we experienced an abrupt roll to the left of approximately 20-30 degrees. Aircraft control was immediately regained as we cleared the wake of the preceding aircraft. This is the second encounter I've had departing behind a presumably 'heavy' A321 and encountering such significant wake turbulence, however this is the first time it has occurred so low the ground. Tower cleared our takeoff just as the [preceding] aircraft wheels left the pavement in which we then began our takeoff roll. It may be considered advisable to further follow similar events with regional aircraft taking off behind A321. An immediate departure behind this aircraft type should possibly be delayed to avoid wake turbulence at low altitudes.
ASRS:1797396.s: A pilot reported significant wake turbulence while departing Runway 25R at PHX behind an A321. Between 100 and 200 feet AGL, the aircraft rolled 20-30 degrees left immediately after the preceding aircraft rotated, requiring control recovery.

ASRS:1797406.n: VNAV (vertical navigation) would not arm before takeoff. Because I was flying the Max for the first time I considered this may be something different or weird about the new airplane. After writing this up on the ground the mechanics did a reboot of the airplane and these problems seemed to go away but now we experienced the failure of the Captain's FMC multiple times. Upon arrival at the airplane that morning I found the FMC switch in the 'R' position instead of the normal 'BOTH.' During preflight, with the FMC programmed, I engaged LNAV (lateral navigation) and VNAV with the Master on my (First Officer) side. A few minutes later I noticed VNAV disengaged. I reengaged it. A few minutes later I noticed it disengaged again. This time I told the Captain and he said he noticed it as well. This was my first flight in the Max so I chalked it up as a Max-ism. I thought it would 'fix itself' airborne. The Captain and I discussed it and decided to just proceed and attempt to engage it airborne after multiple attempts on the ground to keep it engaged. This was the only discrepancy I noticed on the ground. Once airborne we did attempt to engage VNAV but it would disengage within a couple seconds. I climbed out in LVL CHG (level change mode) all the way to FLXXX when ALT HLD (altitude hold) engaged. After a few minutes at cruise the Captain decided we should try switching everything to his side so we switched to CMD A and engaged VNAV. After this we had no further issues with VNAV. We agreed I would continue to be pilot flying utilizing the A autopilot and the master on his side. During cruise shortly after engaging VNAV as previously discussed I began noticing weird things on my ND (navigation display) and PFD. On the PFD on my speed tape the minimum and maximum maneuvering amber bars would simultaneously shoot out. The minimum would jump up about 8 knots while the maximum would simultaneously shoot down about 2 knots and then immediately retract. Also the ND would ratchet instead of making smooth movements. This was especially noticeable in turns. Lastly we noticed ANP (actual navigation performance) going as high as 1.3. By the end of the flight I would say it was back in the normal range, less than 0.1. I flew the STAR in LNAV/VNAV to the bottom and performed a visual [approach] with no other issues. We wrote this up on the ground doing our best to explain this to Maintenance. The Captain and I decided if we set up the box and selected the master on my side and engaged VNAV and it stayed engaged we would be satisfied and then switch everything to his side. After boarding was complete and we were just about to shut the door both FMC's blanked with a MAP and VTK (vertical track) on Captain's PFD. We called Maintenance back out for another 'reset'. We then closed the door and pushed back. As I began to start the engine we had the same failure again on the FMC. Captain called Maintenance and they told us to return to gate. By this point the Captain and I agreed we would not be taking this airplane. With its previous history that we learned about in previous log pages, along with the multiple issues we experienced, combined with the complicated process involving an MEL for both FMCs and an early wake up we agreed it would not be the safest course of action. Hindsight is 20/20 and looking back armed with the information I have now I would have never left the gate in ZZZ. During my preflight I noticed the FO (First Officer) engaging VNAV and it disengaging a few minutes later. He tried a couple of times and it would not stay engaged. He told me he found the FMC switch in the Both on R and switched it back to normal. We discussed waiting for final numbers and trying again. It continued not to engage after final numbers and I decided to push back and start and try again on taxi. A couple times during taxi we tried to engage it and would only last seconds. We discussed departing old school bug up N1 flaps 1 and try again airborne knowing the jet can fly without VNAV. We both were comfortable with that decision. It was his leg and the F/D (flight director) was on his side. There were no other discrepancies. As we rolled out on the runway and were cleared for take off I engage VNAV and it stayed on until 500 feet and disconnected. I am guessing it held on with TOGA (takeoff/go-around). We tried engaging VNAV a couple times in climb and after level off at FLXXX with no success. We were on autopilot CMD B (command B). At that point I selected CMD A and then engaged VNAV and it stayed on. We decided to leave it on CMD A. The remainder of the flight VNAV remained engaged. It was the FO's first time in the Max and my second leg so he remained the pilot flying using CMD A. About the same time we were switching sides we noticed on his speed tape the minimum and maximum amber bars would jump up from the bottom about 5 knots and down from the top about 2-3 knots. Also the ND (navigation display) would glitch from left to right 5-7 degrees. Both of those continued the entire flight, the ND would glitch more in a turn. All 3 airspeeds were matched the entire flight and Captain's side had no issues of glitching and we received no cautions about airspeed. A little while later we received a scratch pad message that I don't remember exact wording but was about FMC position when I looked at all latitude and longitudes FMC, IRSL (left inertial reference system), IRSR, GPSL (GPS left), GPSR were normal within a couple of decimal points looking normal to me. I then noticed the ANP was 1.3 and bouncing between 1.2 and 1.3. I monitored that and it started to decrease back to normal around .03, .02 but it took 20 to 30 minutes and would move between .02 and .11. Towards the end of the flight it seemed to be more steady around .03, .02. No other scratch pad messages and the flight had no other issues. We landed [and] I wrote up the problems and we both talked to the 3 maintenance technicians to relay as much info as we could. I know that they powered down the aircraft and did operation tests that all passed and signed off the aircraft. We boarded the passengers for [our next] flight. We discussed that we would check both sides for VNAV engagement, also monitor all speed tapes and ND's for any glitching before takeoff. As we were about to close the door both FMC's blanked out and Map flag, VTK flag, and no runway flag on my side only appeared. No FMC prompt on either FMC screens only ACARS, ACMS (aircraft condition monitoring system), SAT (satellite). I called Maintenance and they came out and talked about that they had Captain's FMC history. I asked about it and we looked it up in the previous logbook, first I had heard about that. I was thinking new airplane I did not realize that there was an entire logbook already used below the current logbook. They then switched the FMC switch to both on R and the flags on my side went away and FMC prompts returned. I told them I cannot takeoff like that. They called Maintenance Control I believe and they did a circuit breaker reset which fixed the flags and returned the FMC prompts and the FMC switch back to normal. We closed the door and started the pushback. As the FO was about to start engine 2 the same flags returned on my side and no FMC prompts on both sides. Maintenance Control told us to return to the gate because he could not MEL it. We returned to the gate and Maintenance again did the circuit breaker reset that only lasted a few minutes before the flags returned. They decided to MEL the FMC with my approval. The FO and I did not want to continue with this aircraft because of our history with it and that it had only been powered down and 2 circuit breaker resets. We now would be manually setting bugs and thrust for the entire flight in an aircraft we both had very little time in and had an early morning show to start the day and it was now late afternoon.
ASRS:1797406.s: First Officers and Captains experienced repeated VNAV disengagements, FMC blanking, and display glitches on a Boeing 737 Max during preflight, taxi, and cruise. The crew ultimately refused to fly the aircraft after maintenance resets failed to resolve the persistent FMC failures and navigation anomalies.

ASRS:1797411.n: As we arrived in ZZZ, the First Officer and myself had planned on the ILS to RWY (Runway) XX as the winds had favored that runway. The winds had shifted and favored RWY XY as we were handed off to approach control. As I was the flying pilot, the FO (First Officer) hastily entered the RNP to Runway XY. This was also our first time into ZZZ. As the aircraft captured Final App... it looked as if we were on profile... and we were also visual. I soon realized that the altitude constraints had not been loaded due to the fact that the approach via had not been entered. I arrested the descent, however, we did get the 'pull up warning ....a go around was performed followed by the published hold. We then performed the ILS to RWY XX, circle to [Runway] XY to a normal landing."
ASRS:1797411.s: The crew missed altitude constraints during an RNP approach to Runway XY at ZZZ because the approach via was not entered, triggering a pull-up warning. They executed a go-around, held, and subsequently landed normally via an ILS to Runway XX followed by a circle to Runway XY.

ASRS:1797439.n: I was thanking passengers as they disembarked onto the jet-bridge in ZZZ, and I was trying to call rows to deplane on the PA. The cleaning crew were at the front door (1Left) trying to get on the plane while the passengers were leaving, and the pilots were also trying to gather their bags and leave. This made the situation very chaotic. I was not aware of it being a 'quick-turn', as I am always happy to try and help out with the quick-turn cleaning.The cleaners slipped on a few at a time, in between passengers leaving. I saw the two aft crewmembers with their luggage, and moving forward through the cabin, towards me. The cleaners were already onboard, cleaning throughout the plane. I said, 'last but not least!' to the final passenger, thanked her and gathered my belongings. I looked back and only saw the cleaners, and my crew who were almost to me. I didn't see any more passengers and thought we were done. I double-checked my doors and the forward lavatory and stepped off the plane. When the aft crew stepped off, there was a male passenger with them who had been mixed in with the cleaners. He did not have his boarding pass with him. He said he wouldn't leave without it, and that his seat was XX6. He wanted to go look for it himself, but crew went to look. His boarding card was found under his seat.A contributing factor is having so many people onboard/in jetbridge and the cleaning crew coming onboard (sometimes in just sweatshirts, hoodies, jackets, hats, masks, etc.) and mixing in with disembarking passengers, and vice versa. Flights are more full now, and anyone can be mistaken for a cleaner.Other factors: double-checking the passengers haven't lowered or removed their masks, as they often do now, as they are coming down the aisle towards me and the boarding door. The passengers are trying to look down the aisle and gauge how far we've gotten with the row announcements to deplane. Also, 2-3 pilots using the lavatory, gathering bags and leaving, while passengers are disembarking causes more confusion. All of this, and the extra amount of ground-staff/cleaners onboard and in the jet-bridge in civilian clothing, causes more confusion, multitasking/load at the boarding/deplaning door.I assumed the last passenger I saw, and said goodbye to, was our final passenger onboard.I would not have stepped off the plane had I known there was still one passenger onboard.I will also alert corporate security to this incident, and the added potential for this confusion during disembarkation.
ASRS:1797439.s: A cabin crew member disembarked prematurely during deplaning at ZZZ, mistakenly believing the aircraft was empty due to chaotic mixing of passengers, pilots, and cleaning staff in civilian clothing. One passenger remained onboard with his boarding pass under his seat, an incident attributed to high passenger loads and ground staff blending in with disembarking travelers.

ASRS:1797471.n: [Passenger] had two 425g containers of pesticide in his checked baggage.Containers were found by the TSA during the security screening of baggage.Items removed by the TSA.PAX notified. Passenger is a [frequent flier member]. Nothing more to add.
ASRS:1797471.s: A frequent flier passenger attempted to check two 425g pesticide containers, which were discovered and removed by TSA during baggage screening. The passenger was notified of the removal, and no further action was required.

ASRS:1797486.n: While supervising the duties of PIC flight for a new student, the student was performing a short approach power off 180. The student turned in on a base leg, less than a mile from the runway and we lost sight of the runway due to a hill and trees (common for Runway XX at this airport). Upon realizing we were low, I told the student to climb twice, to which he did not respond. Finally he added power and began to climb. Tower inquired as to whether we could see the runway, to which I replied we were unable. They stated that the trees looked pretty high and I said 'the plane felt kind of low'. I did not perceive that we were in danger of CFIT.
ASRS:1797486.s: A flight instructor supervising a student pilot during a short approach power-off 180 lost sight of the runway due to terrain. The student failed to respond to initial climb commands, eventually adding power after the instructor repeated the instruction, though the instructor did not perceive a CFIT danger.

ASRS:1797490.n: Was flying to ZZZ from ZZZ1 for aerial sightseeing trip in newly built (72 hrs) RV-10. Have always wanted to fly over the Canyon. Approximately 75% of the way there, conditions began to slowly deteriorate. Reported ceilings at destination were fine, and from nearest weather reporting airport (ZZZ2). But no weather reported in between on my route. Clouds kept getting lower and terrain kept rising. About 40 miles from ZZZ, I should have turned back to ZZZ2 and landed. But, I was under the clouds and could see the ground just fine. Conditions kept getting worse, then better, then worse then better. I pressed on. At one point, I found myself getting too close to ground (about 1,000 ft AGL) when the clouds 'engulfed me'. I was now in IMC. I should have turned around, but decided that I could see some sunlight peeking through and decided to climb up to get on top of clouds and out of possible rising terrain. At 10,300 [ft.] I still was in IMC conditions. Decided then to get an air-born clearance for IFR into ZZZ. I contacted ZZZ3 Center, and proceeded to get clearance for RNAV [Runway] XX into ZZZ. I was being vectored for entry into approach when auto pilot suddenly disengaged, I lost airspeed indication and my AOA stall warning buzzer was going off! When I informed controller of the situation that just erupted, he [provided assistance] to help get me down. It was VERY unsettling! It took a good 4 minutes to realize that these things were happening due to a frozen pitot tube! I live in [the] south and NEVER have to worry about freezing temps. In the current situation, I didn't' realize outside temps had fallen to 27 degrees. When I finally realized what happened, I turned on pitot heat, and airspeed indication was restored within 10 seconds. I was then vectored for a visual approach and landed safely at ZZZ.What led to situation? Bad decision making. I should have turned around before getting into full bore IMC. I think my instrument rating gave me TOO MUCH confidence. Entering IMC unexpectedly, put me behind the airplane and my situational awareness deteriorated to near zero! I also found myself overwhelmed when alarms went off and auto pilot kicked off and in trying to figure out why, I failed to 'aviate' the airplane. At one point I realized I was in a steep left turn (about 45 degrees) which could have led to more problems. Once I saw this, I did correct, but it could have ended in a loss of control quickly!Another lesson is to WATCH the temps! A frozen pitot might not have become my only problem. I realize now I was also at risk for ice on wings. Another dangerous situation. Many lessons learned, but main one is to not push limits in unfamiliar terrain. I should have turned around and avoided the layering of consequences that followed from that one bad decision.
ASRS:1797490.s: A pilot flying a new RV-10 into IMC during a sightseeing trip encountered a frozen pitot tube at 10,300 ft, causing lost airspeed and autopilot disengagement. The pilot attributed the incident to poor decision-making in deteriorating weather and unfamiliar terrain, but recovered after activating pitot heat and landing safely.

ASRS:1797511.n: The aircraft lost power soon after reaching cruise altitude of FL250. There was an undercast that was lighter and more broken towards the south. I executed a glide towards ZZZ where it looked like I could divert without needing to fly an instrument approach. I notified ATC and determined that the ceiling in ZZZ was 8,000 ft. I maintained best glide until I was in the immediate vicinity of ZZZ and could start seeing landmarks through the undercast. I descended in VMC conditions and executed a visual approach into ZZZ without incident.A local repair station determined that an induction hose has wiggled loose of the connection at the left intercooler which would result in loss of turbocharging and erratic induction air pressures that would lead to a loss of power at altitude. They reconnected the hose and ground tested the aircraft before returning it to service. I retrieved the aircraft after an extended runup test and flew it back to base uneventfully. The induction hose is located in an area of the engine compartment that would not be visible in the preflight.
ASRS:1797511.s: The pilot experienced a power loss at FL250 due to a loose induction hose on the left intercooler, causing a loss of turbocharging. The aircraft was safely diverted to ZZZ for a visual approach, and the repair station reconnected the hose before returning the aircraft to service.

ASRS:1797539.n: While training on final radar Aircraft X was being vectored for sequence to the runway. The aircraft was descended below the normal downwind altitude to avoid traffic in an adjacent sector airspace. Due to traffic volume and complexity, the aircraft was vectored into a 6,000 foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA). Upon realization of the error, he was immediately climbed and turned away from the higher MVA area.
ASRS:1797539.s: During final radar training, an air traffic controller vectored Aircraft X below normal downwind altitude into a 6,000-foot Minimum Vectoring Altitude area due to traffic complexity. The controller immediately climbed and turned the aircraft away from the higher MVA area upon realizing the error.

ASRS:1797551.n: I wanted to share an experience on the new RNAV Visual Approach Runway 17L in MCO. There are two fixes that initiate this approach, CELOT and FELUK. On paper they look different, but in the heat of the moment over the radio they sound similar. During a recent approach we requested this procedure. Approaching from the northwest we were given direct FELUK, cross it at or above 3,000 ft. and cleared for the RNAV visual. Expectation bias led me to hear CELOT (the closer of the two fixes and the logical transition from our position) and I initially loaded that into the FMC, but fortunately the First Officer had heard FELUK and after a quick clarification with ATC we loaded and flew that transition. Definitely weird since we passed CELOT to fly to FELUK, which also required what I would call an inefficient turn to final. Not sure why the Controller did this. Perhaps for separation, or perhaps in the heat of the moment he thought that was the closest and most logical fix for us. I'd like to see one of the fixes renamed so they sound distinctly different, perhaps change one of the names such that both are not two syllables in length. Perhaps also add an alert that vectoring to the opposite side (further away) fix is possible.
ASRS:1797551.s: A flight crew approaching MCO for an RNAV visual approach to Runway 17L initially misheard the ATC clearance for fix FELUK as CELOT due to similar-sounding names. The First Officer corrected the error before the crew loaded the wrong fix into the FMC, preventing a deviation from the intended inefficient turn to final.

ASRS:1797563.n: We were flying the VALLY2 SID out of MIA. The SID note states, 'SPEED RESTRICTION...Turbojet aircraft accelerate to 250 knots, if unable, advise ATC.' I was the PF (Pilot Flying) and at 10,000 feet, I asked the Captain for Economy Climb. We accelerated to ECON CLB. Shortly after reaching this speed, ATC instructed us to fly 250 knots and stated something like...Aircraft X, maintain 250 knots, Center will give you a higher speed, you've already accelerated. (Not verbatim, I cannot remember the exact phraseology). It gave us the impression that we missed a published speed restriction. After rereading the SID note, we are both confident that this is not a speed restriction. We are also confident that we did not miss an ATC assigned speed restriction. If however our interpretation of this SID note is incorrect, it is not written as it should be. The Jeppesen Chart Legends publication has a section written about speed restrictions. It clearly states that 'speed restrictions vary widely within individual procedures.' If we unintentionally violated a speed restriction in this case, perhaps this 'wide variation' in depicted speed restrictions needs to be better address from a human factors perspective, since the VALLY2 SID does not clearly depict a 250 knot speed restriction with terminology such as 'maintain 250 until advised by ATC' or 'do not exceed 250 knots etc.
ASRS:1797563.s: The Pilot Flying and Captain accelerated to Economy Climb above 10,000 feet on the VALLY2 SID from MIA. ATC instructed them to maintain 250 knots, implying a missed restriction, though the crew concluded the SID note was ambiguous and not a mandatory speed limit.

ASRS:1797710.n: When checking in with MCO final Approach Control we were given speed reduction 190 to mkr (Marker Radio Beacon), Drones reported near ORL Executive, all traffic now arriving Runway 17L and R. Cleared visual Runway 17L maintain GS on approach slow to 170. Caution traffic on right to Runway 17R, contact Tower on freq. We received our landing clearance for Runway 17L. Second birds on path siting. We were on ref and GS. About 1,100 ft. I realized we weren't fully configured. Called for gear/F3 then F Full/Landing checklist. Landing checklist completed by 800 ft. We were still at ref and on GS fully stable, we landed normally and taxied off at Taxiway F. We received no alerts during approach.I believe we were distracted more than usual as well as feeling a little tired that afternoon. I will most assuredly use this experience as a learning example of avoiding potential complacency by carefully applying our procedures to prevent any re occurrence going forward.
ASRS:1797710.s: The flight crew approached Orlando International Runway 17L while managing drone reports and traffic, realizing at 1,100 feet they were not fully configured. They completed the landing checklist by 800 feet and landed normally, attributing the configuration delay to distraction and fatigue.

ASRS:1797712.n: Student Pilot flying. On the 45 to enter downwind on [Runway] 16, at approximately 1,100 ft. MSL (TPA 1,000 ft.), a turn in the opposite direction caused potential collision with traffic on crosswind turning to downwind. Situation was realized simultaneously by Tower and myself (CFI) at which point I took [control of] the airplane, as I saw other planes in the base for [Runway] 16. 'Traffic to follow' was mis-identified. To avoid collision the turn was continued to the left, away from downwind, at which point Tower instructions to climb to 1,500 ft. MSL and proceed east to a known reporting point were followed. Situation was stabilized, instructions from the Tower to re-enter the pattern for 16 were followed and successfully completed.What contributed to this situation:1) Student and CFI not adequately briefing the approach based on ATIS. 2) Not correctly identifying 'traffic to follow'. 3) Student Pilot did not realize she could ask for clarification or question my thinking. 4) I did not have the correct runway (16) approach visualized, I was distracted with coaching the Student Pilot.How to avoid in the future: Slow down the process to adequately brief the approach and ask for questions to understand that my student and I are thinking the same procedure with the given information. Properly identifying the 'traffic to follow' and verifying with Tower.
ASRS:1797712.s: A student pilot and CFI flying a traffic pattern for Runway 16 misidentified "traffic to follow," causing a potential collision at 1,100 ft. The CFI took control to avoid the conflict, attributing the incident to inadequate briefing, poor traffic identification, and distraction.

ASRS:1797718.n: I was holding short of [the] runway. I thought that the Tower had instructed me to taxi to [the parallel runway] for take off. I began to move the aircraft. At the same time I looked to the left and observed another aircraft on a half mile final. I applied brakes and at the same time the Tower radioed 'stop, stop'. By that time the nose of the aircraft had passed the limit line and I had committed a runway incursion. Since I was in a tail dragger I was able to lock my right wheel, spin around, and return to the correct side of the limit line. The landing aircraft did a go-around.There were two primary factors that caused the runway incursion. First, I should have waited for a response from the Tower before moving the aircraft. That would have given the Tower time to tell me to remain where I was. Secondly, I should have visually cleared the final approach area before movement. I would have seen the aircraft and not gone past the limit line. Another factor was that, since I was in an open cockpit aircraft there was wind noise from the prop wash as well as engine noise that resulted in me mishearing the instructions from the Tower.In the future I plan to 1. before moving the aircraft, give the Tower time to correct any misinterpretation of instructions, 2. check for traffic before moving the aircraft, and 3. allowing a few more feet distance from the limit line as an added safety margin to prevent movement past the limit line.
ASRS:1797718.s: The pilot of a taildragger aircraft committed a runway incursion while holding short by misinterpreting Tower instructions due to cockpit noise and failing to visually clear the final approach area. The pilot stopped after the nose crossed the limit line, spun the aircraft back, and the landing aircraft executed a go-around.

ASRS:1797754.n: The HOU ATIS states Runway 17/35 is closed, along with Taxiway G2 and G3. The Jepp 10-9 Page does not identify any of these surfaces. Ground Control gave us a clearance to taxi on H and hold short of Runway 35. So, does the runway exist or not? The Jepp 10-9 should reflect the proper surfaces that ATC is using in their communications. I think this can create confusion. Fix the Jepp or have ATC stop issuing instructions including surfaces that no longer exist.
ASRS:1797754.s: The pilot reported a conflict between HOU ATIS and Jepp 10-9 charts regarding the closure of Runway 17/35 and Taxiways G2/G3. Ground Control issued a taxi clearance referencing the closed runway, causing confusion due to the chart not reflecting current surface status.

ASRS:1797758.n: On a visual approach to Runway 16L to the RNO airport we received a EGPWS Pull Up Warning. The warning came as I was telling the First Officer who was the Pilot Flying that he looked low. The First Officer disengaged the autopilot and began an aggressive climb. We rejoined the glidepath and landed. I believe I had expectation bias that he would recognize that we were getting low. The truth is we were momentarily in the red and thanks to the aircraft warning we made a recovery. During descent into RNO landing [Runway] 16L on downwind, the Controller cleared us for the visual to after another aircraft that was on final. Slightly past abeam that aircraft and at 9,000 ft. MSL, I squared the turn to base and began a descent and then angled the turn to final and select LNAV. We intercepted final and as we rolled out still descending and I noticed, as did the PM, that we were low. As I was arresting the descent and rolling out, an EGPWS took place. We initiated an escape maneuver with an aggressive climb and corrected and climbed up onto the approach path.
ASRS:1797758.s: During a visual approach to Runway 16L at RNO, the crew received an EGPWS Pull Up warning at 9,000 ft MSL after descending below the glidepath. The Pilot Flying disengaged the autopilot and executed an aggressive climb to recover the approach, attributing the deviation to expectation bias regarding altitude awareness.

ASRS:1797767.n: The information for GRR discusses the clearance from light poles east of Gates B7 and B8, as well as north of the B Concourse. To have the stated clearance from the light poles, you need to be on the yellow taxi line. The problem is that the yellow taxi line has been removed from the ramp. The line needs to be repainted so we can navigate to Gate 2, in all lighting/weather conditions, without the threat of hitting light poles. Repaint the taxi line to ensure taxi safety around the B Concourse. No taxi lines on ramp.
ASRS:1797767.s: A pilot reported that missing yellow taxi lines on the ramp near Gates B7, B8, and the B Concourse prevent maintaining required clearance from light poles. The reporter requested repainting the lines to ensure safe navigation to Gate 2 in all conditions and avoid striking the poles.

ASRS:1797796.n: [Company Material] was rejected. This shipment of two arcraft engines (possible Helicopter engines) was booked from ZZZ to ZZZZ via ZZZ1 . Upon inspection of the shipment, we noticed that this had some oil like substance on the bottom of the shipping crate and missing the purge certificate from the submitted documents. Should have had a purge certification for each engine and maybe have been classified as Class 9 DG.
ASRS:1797796.s: Ground personnel rejected a shipment of two aircraft engines booked from ZZZ to ZZZZ via ZZZ1 due to an oil-like substance on the crate and a missing purge certificate. The reporter noted the engines likely required Class 9 Dangerous Goods classification and individual purge certifications.

ASRS:1797802.n: We were going to load Aircraft X to ZZZ while loading the mail there was a box that had a Dangerous Goods (DG) sticker on it but there was no paperwork for it. At this time it was decided to be held off and sent back to air freight. The [package] was then rebooked for Aircraft Y to ZZZ and we were told it was ok to load cause we have an agreement with the [US] Post Office. We then notified the Supervisor on Duty in which notified the Manger about the concern they made a phone call and emailed the Regional Freight Manger and was told it was ok to board. We had then notified the pilot which the contacted the DG hotline and was told to hold off aircraft because without paperwork he would not have any ability to react in case of an incident so refused boarding of mail [package]. Also we are unaware of any other DG's being shipped cause of mail items being shipped in sacks.
ASRS:1797802.s: Ground crew and a pilot refused to load a mail package with a Dangerous Goods sticker but no paperwork onto Aircraft X. The pilot contacted the DG hotline, which mandated holding the aircraft due to the lack of documentation required for emergency response.

ASRS:1797806.n: During the descent at approx 12,000 feet our ACM (additional crew member/jump seater) noticed 2 bright white sparks which came from over the galley area, quickly followed by acrid smell and smoke in the courier area ceiling area. He came up to the flight deck to report this about the same time the smell and smoke were noticed in the flight deck. The CA (Captain) left his seat briefly and upon seeing the smoke in the ceiling area, came back up and notified ATC. I noted to the CA and ACM that they should immediately pull all the galley circuit breakers, that we didn't need that equipment and likely the cause of the problem. The ACM did this immediately. As the PF (pilot flying), I continued to fly expeditiously to the airport while the CA (Pilot Monitoring) accomplished the smoke/fire/fumes checklist. My O2 mask was pulled but not donned. Shortly after the galley CB's were pulled the smoke and fumes began to dissipate. The CA notified ATC that the situation was improving but we still requested priority handling. We were already on final and visual with [runway] XXR and cleared to land. Landing was uneventful and we exited the runway, taxiing to our ramp followed by fire and rescue equipment. After shutdown, the CA went to disarm and open doors for personnel with he found that the cabin doors would not open electrically. That was when he noticed the ground service bus CB was popped. Maintenance was contacted via interphone and notified that we could not open doors electrically. Rather than blow the door open pneumatically we chose to wait for Maintenance to get the door open. (There was no evidence at this point that smoke/fire was a threat). Maintenance personnel were able to mechanically open the door. Fire personnel came up and we described the above situation. Quick action by our ACM and expeditious handling by ATC and all crew members brought this to a successful conclusion. During descend into ZZZ1 ACM [Additional Crew Member] onboard brought to our attention that sparks and smoke was coming from behind galley area. Smoke and fumes were confirmed and ATC was notified. We requested priority handling to airport. CB's to galley were pulled. Smoke and fumes subsided. No delay occurred in our handling from ATC. After block in the ground service CB was noted popped. Communication was established with MX and Manuel operation of entry door utilized due to door on that buss.
ASRS:1797806.s: During descent at 12,000 feet, an additional crew member reported sparks and smoke from the galley, prompting the pilots to pull galley circuit breakers and request priority handling. The aircraft landed safely, but the ground service bus circuit breaker had tripped, requiring maintenance to manually open the cabin doors.

ASRS:1797833.n: During cruise one of the flights attendants called me up and said they could smell something like burning paper around Row 33. No smoke was observed. As the flight attendants searched for the source of the smell, we started the smoke, fumes checklist in the QRH. The smell dissipated after 5 minutes and before any configuration changes were made in the flight deck. I decided to continue on since there were [no] indications of smoke anymore. There were no complaints or reports of any injuries to passengers or crew members. A smoke fumes report was filled and an AML entry of the event followed by a company report.No smoke was seen, only the odor of smoke smelt. The FA (Flight Attendant) said it was like burning paper. Before I completed our smoke checklist, the smell had completely dissipated.
ASRS:1797833.s: During cruise, a flight attendant reported a burning paper odor near Row 33, prompting the crew to initiate the smoke and fumes checklist. The smell dissipated within five minutes without smoke sightings or injuries, so the flight continued with no configuration changes.

ASRS:1797836.n: We were holding short of [the] runway and Tower reported they were seeing smoke coming from our engines but couldn't tell which one. Aircraft behind us immediately reported smoke from the #2 Engine. Tower asked us to taxi clear while I was pulling up the Engine page on the system display. I identified that the oil quantity on #2 Engine was falling rapidly from 8 quarts to 7.5 to 7 to 6.5. At that point, the aircraft behind us reported 'you have flames shooting out #2'. We had no flight deck indications of an engine fire during the entire event. Tower told us to stop where we were and that 'we are rolling the trucks'. I stopped the aircraft and called for the QRC. My FO determined we had a quick action item, ENG 1(2) FIRE (on ground). We ran the checklist which required the discharge of both fire bottles on #2 Engine. I notified the Cabin Crew, then made an announcement to the passengers and stated that we had to shut down the right engine and that we would wait for the emergency equipment to inspect the aircraft. Shortly thereafter, ARFF showed up to the aircraft while simultaneously, I was starting the APU. Upon visual inspection by ARFF, they determined there was still a small residual fire in the #2 Engine. ARFF requested that we shut down of both Engines (#2 was already properly shut down via the QRC). After the APU finished its starting cycle, I shut down the #1 Engine. As the ARFF started their fire suppression on Engine #2, I made another announcement to the passengers that they were doing this as a precaution. The First Officer and I discussed and agreed that if we needed to evacuate, it would be out the left side of the aircraft. When ARFF was finished with their visual inspection and suppression efforts, we were notified to wait for Maintenance to show up for their own inspection. When that was completed, we were told that we would be towed back to the gate. I then made another PA announcement updating the cabin crew and passengers as to what was happening.Everyone involved in this event played a significant part. Both the Tower and the aircraft behind us provided information needed to make necessary decisions due to the fact that we had no indications on the flight deck that a catastrophic engine failure was going to occur. Communication between ARFF and the flight deck was clear and concise, as was the communication with the cabin crew. By following the SOPs that are in place, a positive outcome was achieved. I'm not sure if this type of event can be prevented other than Airbus develop some kind of warning that the engine oil quantity is rapidly decreasing.
ASRS:1797836.s: The flight crew held short of the runway when Tower and a following aircraft reported smoke and flames from Engine #2, despite no flight deck fire warnings. The crew executed the engine fire checklist, discharged fire bottles, and shut down both engines while ARFF suppressed a residual fire, resulting in a safe tow back to the gate.

ASRS:1797877.n: I was PM (Pilot Monitoring) on our flight to ZZZ. We departed the runway and flew the ZZZZZ departure. All was well through 10,000 feet and shortly thereafter, the A/P was coupled. We were VMC and it was a normal, 270 knot climb. Approximately 8 miles before ZZZZZ, maybe climbing through 14,000 feet, the aircraft began an uncommanded, soft turn to the right of course. It then increased to a more abrupt banking turn to the right, accompanied with about 4-5 degrees of nose-down pitch attitude. The turn to the right was approximately 40-50 degrees total. The airspeed quickly increased and I saw airspeed tape up to, but not into, the barber pole. I don't recall any aural warning and the EICAS was clear. This evolution was quick. The CA (Captain) and I exchanged a few words as he detected the error, followed by an A/P disconnect and a manual recovery, which began with a pitch input and throttle adjustment. I was talking to Center as this began and was queried immediately. I replied that we experienced a perceived autopilot anomaly, but were correcting. We were instructed to rejoin the departure at ZZZZZ and continue from there. The CA and I discussed the event, and once back on profile, we re-engaged A/P and continued the flight in normal fashion.I'm still not sure what happened. The DP (Departure Procedure) was loaded directly from the FMS data base, with no modifications. We were climbing VIA, in magenta FLCH. When the aircraft began to stray, the A/P was following the flight director cue the whole time. The pitch down was concerning and both of us suspected a trim runaway at first, but as the yoke was pushing forward from the A/P, the CA quickly de-coupled the A/P and recovered back on course. Looking back, we performed normally and programmed the FMS normally. I have no explanation for this event, but I am grateful we were VMC at the time and that we recovered in a timely manner. The CA did further consulting once we landed in ZZZ. I was PF (Pilot Flying). We departed the runway and flew the ZZZZZ departure. All was well through 10,000 feet and shortly thereafter, the A/P was coupled. We were VMC and it was a normal climb. Approximately 8 miles before ZZZZZ, maybe climbing through 14,000 feet, the aircraft began an uncommanded, soft turn to the right off course. It then increased to a more abrupt banking turn to the right, the airspeed quickly increased and I saw airspeed tape up to, but not into, the barber pole. I don't recall any aural warning and the EICAS was clear. This evolution was quick. The FO (First Officer) and I exchanged a few words I disconnect the auto pilot and a manual recovery, which began with a pitch input and throttle adjustment. FO was talking to Center as this began and was queried immediately. He replied we experienced an anomaly, but were correcting. We were instructed to rejoin the departure at ZZZZZ and continue from there. Hand flew for a few minutes once back on course, we re-engaged A/P and continued the flight, which was uneventful.
ASRS:1797877.s: During a climb through 14,000 feet on the ZZZZZ departure, the aircraft executed an uncommanded right turn and nose-down pitch while in autopilot FLCH mode. The crew disconnected the autopilot and manually recovered the aircraft, suspecting a trim runaway, though no specific cause was identified.

ASRS:1797878.n: During cruise STAB OUT OF TRIM light illuminated intermittently. Complied with STAB OUT OF TRIM QRH procedure. Maintenance notified via ACARS. Descending with autopilot and autothrottle on, aircraft did not level off at the preselected 4,000 feet. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottle and began to return to 4,000 feet. I tried the electric trim and found it to be inoperative. I notified the Captain of the inoperative electric trim. The Captain tried his electric trim and also found it to be inoperative. Captain conferred with me about disconnecting the STAB TRIM CUT OUT switches. I agreed and the STAB TRIM CUT OUT switches were disconnected. Captain opened the QRH and we complied with the STAB OUT OF TRIM QRH procedure. The STAB OUT OF TRIM QRH procedure directed us to the STABILIZER TRIM INOPERATIVE procedure, which we complied with. I tried to operate the manual trim with my left hand could not move the trim wheel through a full rotation. I notified the Captain of this and he tried the manual trim. Captain seem to require both hands to operate the manual trim. Captain notified ATC and we requested delay vectors. We requested the longer Runway of XXR. We performed a flaps 15 landing on XXR. Descended below assigned altitude of 4,000 feet due to malfunctioning elevator trim. This report is being submitted to cover the altitude deviation on approach into ZZZ. The altitude deviation was a direct result of a malfunction of the stabilizer/stabilizer trim system. The other required category reports will be covered in a separate irregularity report.Approximately two hours after departure and level at FL350, the STAB OUT OF TRIM (amber) light illuminated. We ran the STABILIZER OUT OF TRIM QRH procedure. Autopilot B was engaged and remained engaged while the light was eliminated, the aircraft maintained altitude and airspeed in light mountain wave and light chop conditions. Since the auto pilot appeared to be trimming the aircraft normally and in accordance with QRH, we continued normal operation. We notified maintenance control and Dispatch via ACARS and made a maintenance logbook entry for the condition. Dispatch acknowledged receiving the message. The light remained illuminated for approximately 10 mins. During this time both the first officer and myself reviewed not only the QRH, but Stabilizer Trim Inoperative QRH procedure in the event that these stabilizers stopped trimming at some subsequent point. We also reviewed be available information in both the flight handbook as well as the systems handbook.The STAB OUT OF TRIM light continued to illuminate intermittently in durations that ranged from several minutes to just a few seconds. We also climbed to FL370 with no abnormal indications and with the B autopilot remaining engaged. I observed some movement of the trim wheel at various times.During the cruise portion of the flight, the light was extinguished most of the time, but we did have the intermittent illuminations periodically. We informed dispatch and maintenance control that the light was illuminating intermittently.On the arrival into ZZZ we were given several intermediate level offs as well as crossing altitude and airspeed restrictions all of which were met with autopilot B engaged.While being vectored around some weather, for a visual approach to Runway XXL, we were kept somewhat high on the profile and were in a fairly aggressive dissent to 4,000 feet. Autopilot B remained engaged throughout this descent. At 4,000 feet the flight directors commanded a level off but the aircraft continued to descend below 4,000 feet and did not capture the altitude, the first officer (pilot flying) immediately disengaged the auto pilot and auto throttles and began to correct The flight path, but due to the out of trim condition of the stabilizer the aircraft descended to approximately 3,500 feet before being able to level off the aircraft with considerable back pressure on the yoke.We informed ZZZ Approach that we had a stabilizer issue and were attempting to correct back to 4000 feet. They directed us to maintain 3000 feet. At about this time, the first officer informed me that 'I don't have any trim' and I saw him activate the yoke stabilizer trim switches for nose up and nose down trim with no movement of the stabilizer trim wheels. I attempted to trim the stabilizer using the yoke switches on my side with no effect as well. The first officer was holding a great deal of back pressure on the yolk and stated 'I need nose up trim' at this point with his concurrence after having verified that neither yolk could trim the stabilizer electrically, I selected both stabilizer trim cut out switches to cut out.At this point I told the first officer that he was going to continue to be the pilot flying and also have the radios while I reviewed the QRH procedures. After I verified that we had accomplished all of the steps and had been directed to the next QRH section. Well I was reviewing the QRH procedures the first officer attempted to trim the aircraft manually and stated 'I can't move the wheel'. It was at this point I believe where I [requested priority] with approach and told them that we had a stabilizer trim failure and we were attempting to trim the aircraft manually we requested and receiveda vector to do this and we reported our souls on board as well as fuel and requested ARFF assistance at the airport. At this point I attempted to trim the stabilizer nose up manually from my side but was unable to turn the stabilizer trim wheel. I directed the first officer to attempt to slow the aircraft to clean maneuver speed in an attempt to unload the stabilizer so that we could trim the aircraft manually. At some point approaching clean maneuver speed I was able to begin moving the trim wheel nose up but it was still quite difficult and required a significant two-handed effort to move the wheel at all. I managed to get several turn nose up trim and the first officer said 'that's good'. At this point, we were in a more or less in trim condition at clean maneuver and clean. We continue to execute QRH and requested the longer Runway (XXR). It was at about this point I believe that I informed the flight attendants of our situation and that we would be landing in about 5 to 10 minutes, to expect a normal landing but that there would be fire trucks standing by.We completed QRH and had a normal flaps 15 landing on Runway XXRWe rolled out normally and cleared the runway and informed ground control and the ARFF captain that we did not require any further assistance.We taxi to the gate and shut down the aircraft, debriefed the flight attendants, and spoke with maintenance on the ground about our situation.
ASRS:1797878.s: During cruise, pilots experienced intermittent STAB OUT OF TRIM lights and subsequent electric trim failure, causing an altitude deviation below 4,000 feet. After disconnecting trim cut-out switches and manually trimming the stabilizer with two hands, they executed a safe flaps 15 landing on Runway XXR.

ASRS:1798002.n: This was my first landing at ZZZ. Landed safely and as I was rolling to exit [the runway] wind gust blew my plane to the right side of the runway, into the grass where I ran into a sign. In the correction process of getting the airplane back into the wing scraped another sign. Both signs were damaged but, I believe, returned immediately to service. The airplane sustained minor damage to the wings.As I was on final, the wind direction changed from 11:00 o'clock to my 9:00 o'clock, effectively a crosswind or a wind shear that blew my plane to right, which made me lose control momentarily. I recovered and taxied safely to the FBO but not before the collision.Lesson learned... The winds and conditions at this airport are unpredictable. The wind directions can abruptly change. Next time I will pay more attention to the wind socks on the field as I takeoff or from a safe altitude above before choosing a runway to land. I will not [fail to] ask for and validate the advisories before I commit to and line up for landing.
ASRS:1798002.s: A pilot landing at ZZZ lost control due to an abrupt wind shift, causing the aircraft to blow off the runway into grass and strike two signs. The incident resulted in minor wing damage and damaged signs, which the pilot attributed to unpredictable wind conditions and a failure to validate advisories before landing.

ASRS:1798003.n: I was on a downwind for Runway XX at ZZZ and issued a visual approach clearance with restriction maintain 3,000 feet until turning base and told to contact Tower. I turned base and started the descent. Upon contacting Tower, I was instructed to immediately climb to avoid a traffic conflict below me. I then noticed the traffic alert on my ADS-B screen 400 feet below me and climbed to avoid while on base. Shortly after I was issued cleared to land on Runway XX for ZZZ.
ASRS:1798003.s: An air traffic controller issued a visual approach clearance to a pilot on downwind for Runway XX at ZZZ, restricting descent until base. The pilot was later instructed to climb to avoid a traffic conflict 400 feet below, which was confirmed on the ADS-B screen, before receiving a landing clearance.

ASRS:1798019.n: Aircraft X was rolling out after having been cleared for the option. Smoke appeared around the aircraft that's cause was initially unclear. ATC was advised and as the aircraft continued to roll it became unclear as to whether it would be able to stop on the runway due to having damaged rear tires. The newly constructed hangar was a factor as it started to obscure the aircraft as it was slowing down. Eventually it did stop on the runway but was unable to exit, and was partially blocked from view. Allow for complete visibility of the departure end of the runway.
ASRS:1798019.s: Aircraft X rolled out after an option clearance when smoke appeared and rear tires were damaged, raising concerns about stopping distance. The aircraft stopped on the runway but could not exit due to a newly constructed hangar obscuring visibility.

ASRS:1798022.n: Aircraft X checked on my frequency as a pop up IFR requesting a clearance to ALB. He requested 4,000 feet for altitude, I told him he would need to climb to 5,000 feet for a clearance to ALB. I cleared him reaching 6,000 feet cleared to ALB airport via direct. Reaching 6,000 feet he told me he was picking up icing and requested 8,000 feet. I climbed him to 8,000 feet and asked him the type and intensity of ice. He said Light Rime. I had my Supervisor put the pilot report in the computer.I then noticed Aircraft X descending instead of climbing. I verified he was in the climb. He said he was having a problem with his auto pilot. I told him he was descending and that he needs to climb. He continued descending at which point I gave him a low altitude alert and told him my minimum IFR altitude in the area is 3600 feet an he needs to climb to 6000 feet. He continued to descend so I asked him if wanted vectors to the closest airport. He said he had the airport in front of him in sight. I asked if he wanted to land there. He said yes. I cleared him for a Visual Approach. I asked if he was requesting priority handling. He said yes. I read him the NOTAMs. I asked him how many people were on board. He didn't reply. He was low and close to the airport. I told him to change to advisory frequency and report his cancellation.
ASRS:1798022.s: An ATC controller managed Aircraft X, a pop-up IFR flight to ALB, which encountered light rime ice and an autopilot failure causing an unintended descent. The controller issued low altitude alerts, cleared the aircraft for a visual approach to the nearest airport, and instructed the pilot to cancel IFR upon landing.

ASRS:1798025.n: I had just been relieved on Local [positions] combined and this occurred during my two minute overlap and the relieving Controller had the position. Departure traffic was slow and GCN [Ground Control North] 'Convenience taxiing' Runway XL arrivals at their discretion mostly south on Runway YL to hold short of Runway XC. The relieving Controller cleared Aircraft Y for takeoff from Runway XC full length. Aircraft X was taxiing south on Runway YL to hold short of Runway XC (presumably, at the time of this report as I have not heard the audio replay from that position). The relieving Controller saw Aircraft X continuing towards Runway XC at a rate of speed not consistent with holding short and keyed up and said 'Aircraft X stop stop stop', which they did. He then keyed up and said 'Aircraft Y, cancel takeoff clearance stop stop'. Aircraft Y, said something to the effect of 'Say again' and shortly thereafter rotated. The ASDE did alert sometime after the relieving Controller told Aircraft X to stop. Aircraft X appeared from my point of view to be over the hold line and extremely close to Runway XC. Aircraft Y, rotated near the point of conflict and I believe had Aircraft X continued a collision would have been difficult to avoid. Aircraft X was then given a crossing clearance. I then completed my overlap.Discontinue this operation immediately (convenience taxi down Runway YL). In my opinion this represents the culmination of drift that this facility has acquired during the lower 'COVID traffic' we have experienced in the last year (I am guilty of this too as I did this operation until I saw it not work today). There are periods of pronounced lulls in traffic (at least departure wise) where it would be poor service not to shortcut arrivals. However, to taxi on a runway to hold short of a runway I think is now demonstrably unsafe. I believe it requires the flight crews (and possibly ATC) to digest too much information quickly and perform too flawlessly for little appreciable gain. We will always have to perform up field crossings due to the layout of the airport, but I believe we should keep them on a taxiway with a good hold short read back as this is a routine occurrence in the NAS and should elicit better performance from flight crews. After landing on Runway XXL tower cleared us to join Taxiway 1 and contact ground on XYZ.YA [Frequency]. The Ground Controller issued a taxi clearance limit of taxi right hand turn onto Runway 22R -Then hold short of Taxiway 2 - Monitor Tower on XYX.XA [Frequency]. The taxi clearance was written down and verbalized after it was given. The clearance limit issued only included a hold short of [Taxiway 2]. As we approached Runway XC the flight crew acknowledged an aircraft was in position on Runway XC. As we were passing Taxiway 3 told us to stop immediately as the aircraft had been issued a takeoff clearance. We stopped immediately. The aircraft on Runway XC was issued a cancel takeoff clearance which they did not do and continued the takeoff. During our monitoring phase of the taxi we were never issued a hold short clearance just the hold short of Taxiway 2 Nor did we hear a takeoff clearance for the aircraft on Runway XC. Once clear of the conflict - Tower issued a number to contact them. As we responded the with the read back we heard the aircraft following us tell Tower that they had received the same clearance as we had received.Poor ATC communication and poor clearance limits expectations were the biggest causes of this event. Flight deck protocol was followed by utilizing sterile flight deck and writing and readying back clearances and following airport charts. An expectation from tower that wasn't issued via the taxi clearance was what the greatest factor contributing To the eventWe debriefed the event and acknowledged even though the taxi limit was followed the importance of vigilance in an high demand taxi environment like ZZZ [Airport] we must be adhered to and even questioned to clarify and avoid the type of scenario to happen as a crew again.
ASRS:1798025.s: A relieving controller and flight crews were involved in a runway incursion at ZZZ Airport where an aircraft taxiing on Runway YL nearly collided with another taking off from Runway XC. The event was caused by convenience taxiing, unclear hold-short clearances, and poor communication, resulting in a last-minute stop and canceled takeoff.

ASRS:1798031.n: I was not personally involved but heard and observed some of the event as it was taking place. There was training on the Radar Assist and Radar at the sector. A departure was in conflict with an arrival to the same airport. The instructor told the departure to turn to the north below the Minimum IFR Altitude. I would not normally have been aware of the situation except the instructor was having a discussion with student about the safest remedy to the situation which caught my attention. There was also a Supervisor monitoring that sector, but I'm not sure if they actually saw what happened or even know that an error occurred.About 30 minutes later I heard another discussion taking place about another aircraft below the Minimum IFR Altitude (MIA). When I looked at the sector there was a slow aircraft departing Approach's airspace to the north. The aircraft was at 8,000 feet in a 9, 500 MIA. I don't know any more details about that aircraft.
ASRS:1798031.s: An air traffic control instructor directed a departing aircraft to turn north below the Minimum IFR Altitude during a conflict with an arrival. Later, a second departing aircraft was observed at 8,000 feet in a sector with a 9,500-foot Minimum IFR Altitude.

ASRS:1798037.n: ILS Maintenance and company, 2 vehicles, proceeded from the terminal to the approach end of Runway 6 to change a light near the threshold. ILS Maintenance correctly read back all instructions but due to the line of sight obstruction, the new academy hangar, was not visible for 6 minutes. While there was no conflicting traffic, had there been, we would have been unable to ensure that the vehicle was clear of the runway edge line. Perform the necessary structural adjustments/changes to the academy hangar to allow for full visibility of the entire approach end of Runway 6.
ASRS:1798037.s: ILS Maintenance personnel in two vehicles entered Runway 6 to replace a threshold light but were obscured by the new academy hangar for six minutes. This visibility blockage prevented controllers from verifying the vehicles remained clear of the runway edge line, prompting a request for structural changes to the hangar.

ASRS:1798043.n: Around XA:00 pm local I was working Area D mids at sector X when the nightly COVID cleaning crew came through and cleaned half of our area. After they left I asked the other Controller in the area to go set up to bring the sector over to Sector Y, so when the cleaning crew comes back they could clean where I was sitting. Controller went over, opened the position, and took control of the airspace. I then went over to take the position back from at Sector Y so I could sit down and continue working, and at this time we realized that the VCSC [Voice Communication Switch] was not properly configured for the mids position. There were only 5 or 6 frequencies on the panel out of the 16 or so for Area D, and very few random landlines were available for ZZZ, ZZZ1, and ZZZ2 [Airport] towers. We had to scramble to tell other sectors to use only the frequencies that we had up, as the standard frequencies were not available. To make things worse, there was a massive push of ZZZ3 [Airport] departure traffic at this time coming out over ZZZ4 [Airport] and we didn't have the frequency they use OR the landline to ZZZ3 to tell them to use a frequency we had up. The other Controller then went over to sector A which wasn't being used but had all the correct landlines and used it to call the sectors around me including ZZZ3 and tell them to put aircraft on a different frequency. It was a pretty bad situation considering if any of those departures had an issue and had to return to ZZZ3 I would have had no way to communicate or coordinate with the ZZZ3 approach controllers. I had to work like that for 15 minutes or so until the crew came back to clean the rest of the area and we moved the position back to Sector X.This is the third or fourth time I've reported this by now, we need a massive overhaul at this point of the Area D VCSC system to get everything where it needs to be, and have management properly trained on how to format it and be able to quickly fix it when there is something missing.
ASRS:1798043.s: An Area D air traffic controller reported that a VCSC configuration error during a cleaning break left only 5 of 16 frequencies available, preventing communication with ZZZ3 departures. The controller used an alternate sector to coordinate frequency changes for 15 minutes, citing a need for a system overhaul and better management training.

ASRS:1798045.n: Aircraft X departed ZZZ Runway X on runway heading the Tower switched the aircraft to me on departure I believed this small faster climbing aircraft with the winds the way they were could turn and climb before getting into the MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude). I told the aircraft to climb to 060 and turn to a 290 heading as to turn tighter than the MVA. They climbed slower than I have seen [aircraft type] climb and took a much wider turn than anticipated. They just clipped the very edge of the ring for the MVA and allowed to Low Altitude alert to go off. I made them do a tighter turn to a 280 to get them facing away from the obstruction.This is a Controller mistake thinking an aircraft could do something in which it is capable of but a pilot may not.
ASRS:1798045.s: An air traffic controller issued a climb and turn clearance to Aircraft X during departure, assuming it could avoid Minimum Vectoring Altitude (MVA) terrain. The aircraft climbed slowly and turned widely, triggering a Low Altitude alert, which the controller attributed to their own error in overestimating the pilot's ability to execute the maneuver.

ASRS:1798148.n: During a visual approach into BHM, on downwind for Runway 6. Clear day, we were cleared for the visual at 5000 feet. I descended the aircraft to the final approach altitude of 2,200 feet. The Tower Controller asked if we had towers to the right in sight. We did, towers were at 2,049 feet, and were the highest obstacle listed on the ILS Runway 6, At that same moment the aircraft GPWS [announced] 'terrain terrain pull up.' I quickly disconnected the autopilot and climbed to 2,600 feet. We had terrain (the towers) in sight the entire time. The flight continued uneventful and we landed normally.I descended below the MSA for the approach. Though I had the obstacle in sight. I should have held altitude longer until passing the towers, being cleared for the visual approach may have prompted me to set up early and descend when I shouldn't have.
ASRS:1798148.s: The pilot descended below the 2,200-foot minimum sector altitude during a visual approach to Runway 6 at BHM, triggering a GPWS warning despite having the 2,049-foot towers in sight. The pilot attributed the premature descent to the visual clearance and climbed to 2,600 feet before landing normally.

ASRS:1798178.n: While on approach to Runway 24 at ROA we received an EGPWS caution for terrain appeared. An EGPWS caution for terrain appeared along with an audible terrain. ROA Approach assigned an altitude of 4,000 ft. prior to clearing us for the visual approach 24. Setup to intercept final approach course south of HIBAN intersection and north of WUDAG. While on base leg with gear retracted a ground proximity warning caution appeared and disappeared immediately. A climb was initiated to comply with caution and message disappeared we presumed it was erroneous. The descent rate was arrested right as the message disappeared.
