Visual approach separation from all terrain was constantly maintained. Request full RNAV approach day or night to Runway 24 and ensure Roanoke Approach provides an adequate vectoring altitude.
ASRS:1798178.s: The flight crew received an erroneous EGPWS terrain caution while on a visual approach to Runway 24 at ROA with gear retracted. They initiated a climb to comply, arresting the descent rate as the warning disappeared, and requested a full RNAV approach with adequate vectoring altitudes.

ASRS:1798179.n: I was Pilot Monitoring on Aircraft X. The departure and cruise phases of flight were normal. The Pilot Flying briefed all of the appropriate items for the approach into ROA prior to our descent. We had discussed the mountainous terrain in the area and how we were going to request vectors to final for Runway 24. ATC had no issues with our request for vectors so they gave us turns for a base leg and a descent to 4,000 feet. I cannot remember exactly how far our base leg was from the runway but I believe it was in between HIBAN and PROSE. In anticipation of our base to final turn we had flaps 9 and gear down. At that point we had not left 4,000 feet and had not called the field in sight. As we were crossing over the mountains, the aircraft gave us a 'terrain terrain.' Since it was daytime and all of the terrain in the area was in sight and not a factor, we continued the approach. We then called the field in sight and landed safely. I believe we had over 1,000 feet clearance at the time of the incident.Aural alert of terrain.The aircraft thinking we were too close to terrain.Continued the approach visually without incident.A possible solution could be to provide flight crews a suggested path to follow when arriving into ROA during day VMC. We could have requested vectors for the full RNAV approach but that may have caused us to be placed too far out on the approach unnecessarily. We planned on receiving vectors and delaying our descent from 4,000 feet until we passed the terrain intentionally to avoid an aural alert from the aircraft. Another possible solution would be to cross over that terrain a little higher and either descend faster to reestablish or overshoot final slightly where there is no terrain in order to reestablish on final on glide path.
ASRS:1798179.s: The Pilot Monitoring on Aircraft X received a terrain alert while crossing mountains during a visual approach to Runway 24 at ROA. The crew continued the approach visually, maintaining over 1,000 feet clearance, and landed safely despite the aircraft incorrectly indicating proximity to terrain.

ASRS:1798191.n: Briefed the RNDRZ1 approach...and company messages. After BERBN, aircraft started initial turn to left. Flight crew corrected and turned heading to 079 ...however, at same time, ATC gave us a heading of 080. Vectors to follow traffic on final. Called both traffic and field in sight, turned final behind [another airline] traffic, normal approach and landing. Advised on taxi to gate, to call LAS approach. Had nice conversation with Controller...who advised...that over 300 airplanes have had identical situation occur. (Fairly new procedure in effect). Situation notified, and no aircraft deviations had occurred.Our confusion, per the Jeppesen page…says…Expect a heading of 079...Absent any addition ATC instructions... FMC is programmed to turn left, and join the transition to the runway. Interesting note...if over 300 aircraft have done same...why not have Approach Controller…confirm a heading after BERBN Intersection...as this is a new set up in the approaches to LAS? Validated the Arrival/CA briefed approach. The company messages regarding LAS were discussed. After BERBN on the RNDRZ 1 arrival, the aircraft FMS initiated a left turn towards the northeast. We caught this at which time a correction was applied, but before correction was commenced ATC initiated a turn to a 080 heading. When the vector was instructed, traffic was called for the other aircraft on straight in final, and at that time visual contact was established and reported to ATC. We were advised to maintain visual separation and cleared the visual approach. A normal approach to landing was made with no traffic advisories (TA) or resolution advisories (RA).We specifically discussed what to expect if cleared for the visual vs an instrument approach after BERBN, yet the automation management threat was not trapped. The LAS STAR is confusing as to what to expect when waiting for an approach clearance. We never received any additional ATC instructions on what to expect after BERBN and when the aircraft began to turn this created a confusing environment.This procedure at LAS should be simplified and more awareness needs to be presented. It would be beneficial if ATC could provide (for example) 'Fly 080 heading after BERBN this is radar vectors expect the visual approach' OR 'Anticipate BERBN for the instrument approach clearance'. Also, would help if ATC would be willing to give a heads up in the NOTAMs. Also, include a message on the release when flying into this airport.
ASRS:1798191.s: Flight crew flying the RNDRZ1 arrival into LAS corrected an FMS-initiated left turn after BERBN while ATC simultaneously vectored them heading 080 for a visual approach. The crew attributed the confusion to the new procedure's ambiguity regarding expected headings and automation behavior, though no deviations occurred.

ASRS:1798193.n: During passenger boarding there was confusion regarding the carriage of batteries in overhead compartment in passenger cabin. Initially batteries were thought not to be allowed. CSM (Customer Service Manager) was very concerned that the passenger required them for a mobility device. He stated that we carry them all the time in cabin and he was certain that they are permitted. After discussing situation with gate agent, supervisor, Dispatch, and CSM a reference was found in manual leading me to believe that batteries were allowed in cabin. Flight eventually departed late and was otherwise uneventful. Having time the following morning I looked deeper into FOM. The table in FOM which led me to agree with all involved that batteries were permissible has a hyperlink. The link leads to more information stating that the batteries were not allowed. Both gate agent supervisor and CSM stated that [Company] allows these batteries in the passenger cabin and that we carry them all the time. The passenger carried these on a prior flight the same day from ZZZ1. [Captain suggests] FOM could be written more clearly without having to jump around reference to reference to obtain the proper information. Agents should be made aware these items are not allowed to be carried in passenger cabin.
ASRS:1798193.s: During boarding, crew and ground staff incorrectly permitted a passenger to carry mobility device batteries in the cabin based on a misleading FOM hyperlink. The flight departed late, and the Captain later discovered the batteries were actually prohibited, recommending clearer manuals and staff training.

ASRS:1798204.n: Received a climb RA while flying the [Runway] XXL RNAV X. We climbed at 1500-2000 FPM, a small civilian aircraft flew under our aircraft and missed us by 400 feet. We heard approach control give traffic advisory to the other aircraft for a '737'. We received no traffic advisories. I consider this event a near miss.No traffic advisories received from approach or vectoring to either aircraft to avoid the conflict.The Approach Controller needs to do their job. Not vector another aircraft into our aircraft. The pilot of the other aircraft should not take climbing vectors into a 737. (Day VFR Weather, 10 miles plus visibility) Cleared RNAV (RNP) X [Runway] XXL at ZZZ and subsequently received a TCAS RA approaching ZZZZZ. A light civil aircraft called us in sight and approach told them to maintain visual separation. Light civil aircraft was being vectored by approach control when RA commanded a climb to which the Captain (Pilot Flying) executed. We never saw the aircraft but the TCAS display showed them 400 feet below us. When resolved we were cleared a visual approach and landing without further incident.
ASRS:1798204.s: While flying an RNAV approach, the crew received a climb RA and executed it, avoiding a light civil aircraft vectored by Approach Control that passed 400 feet below. The pilot reported a near miss caused by Approach failing to provide traffic advisories or prevent the conflict.

ASRS:1798227.n: On a Visual Approach Tower instructed another aircraft to 'line up and wait' on an intersecting runway. On very short final I heard [callsign] 'stop' repeatedly from the Controller. I scanned the airport environment and saw what I believe was a small aircraft moving from my right down the intersecting runway toward the intersection to our runway. While in the landing flare I called for a go-around immediately before the Controller said '... go-around'. Immediately after I heard the Controller, I said 'go-around' 3 times in rapid succession as the pilot flying was simultaneously executing the go-around. Once climbing I responded to that controller that we were going around. From my perspective we would climb over the other aircraft. Once we began to climb, I lost sight of the aircraft as it was moving to my left. We coordinated with the tower to make right traffic and remain with him. We made an uneventful visual pattern and landed.There was nothing we could have done to prevent as we were non-offending aircraft. The FAA has repeatedly made incursions a priority for safety information. I don't know how else to ensure people remain vigilant when receiving this type of ATC instruction. As we were beginning to flare for landing after being cleared to land, we heard the Tower Controller yell repeatedly on the frequency for another aircraft to stop. It was then that we saw a high wing single engine aircraft rolling for takeoff on the intersecting runway and rapidly approaching the intersection. I began pitching up and adding power at the same time the First Officer called for a go-around and simultaneously we heard the Tower Controller calling '...Go-Around.' As we climbed out, we crossed above and over the high wing aircraft who appeared to be beginning his rotation for takeoff. We then proceeded with a normal go-around and told the Tower we could enter a visual traffic pattern for a return to landing.Prevention would have been out of the control of our crew or ATC. Prevention would rest with the crew of the offending aircraft by being more alert and assuring a proper takeoff clearance prior to departing.
ASRS:1798227.s: The flight crew executed a go-around during the landing flare after a single-engine aircraft entered an intersecting runway without clearance. The crew climbed over the intruding aircraft, which was beginning its takeoff roll, and completed an uneventful landing after the incident.

ASRS:1798250.n: This flight was the first leg of a four day for the Captain and I. The Captain said he would be the pilot flying, that I would be pilot monitoring and he briefed everything up, including threats. We made each other aware of our lack of recent flying experience and lack of proficiency. I informed him that I only have a little over 700 hours on type, that most of that time was trans-cons prior to the pandemic and that I haven't flown much in the past twelve months. I also informed him to the best of my knowledge this would be my first time flying into ZZZZ [Airport]. We agreed that we would take things slow and that we were doing everything correctly. Our taxi out, take off, departure and cruise were routine and uneventful. Approximately twenty minutes prior to the Top of Descent the Captain briefed our descent and approach into ZZZZ and we ran the descent checklist. Center gave us a descent, followed by descend via the X Arrival. We were handed off to approach and told to expect the VOR [Runway] X, after ZZZZZ [Intersection] to fly present heading for a vector to the VOR approach. Prior to ZZZZZ the Captain called for flaps 1, After ZZZZZ he called flaps 5, slowed to 190 knots and approach gave us the vector and cleared us for the VOR X approach. We were at or near the final approach fix when the Captain called gear down, flaps fifteen followed by flaps 30 landing checklist. I set final approach altitude, we were VOR/LOC and VNAV descending per the approach and slowing to our vref of 156 knots. At 1000 feet we were fully configured, and I believe we were at 165 knots. I called 1000 feet, the Captain was task saturated so I said 1,000 feet, set missed approach altitude and said cleared to land. I noticed VNAV had kicked off, I verbalized it and re-selected VNAV, I thought it went to VNAV PTH, but in our debrief I learned it went to VNAV SPD. Between 1,000 and 500 feet the fastest speed I saw was 170 knots. At 500 feet I called 500 feet and saw 171 knots and almost called a go-around. I called 15 knots fast, the Captain said correcting and I saw the speed slowly begin to decrease. I was focused on airspeed as we were at the limit for a stabilized approach and I was looking at the runway as I was concerned, we were going to be high. We continued our approach and I was beginning to become uncomfortable, at approximately 200 feet I noticed we were at 170 knots (it may have been a couple knots faster) but 170 is what I recall. At approximately 200 feet I called that we were high and fast, the Captain said correcting and I saw the speed slowly begin to decrease and he pitched down to correct. At approximately 100 feet I wanted to call for a go-around as we were fast, 170 knots or faster, however I was unable to verbalize it. We touched down hard and flat, we may have had a small bounce, but I don't believe that we did. The Captain deployed the reverser's and we made a normal exit onto taxiway and proceeded to parking. Upon parking, we debriefed this event, we both conducted thorough post flight inspections of the exterior. To the best of our knowledge the aircraft was nott damaged. The Captain contacted Maintenance and they wrote up the hard landing. The Captain also called the Duty Manager.Factors that led to this event were both of our lack of recent flying experience, unfamiliar airport, night operation, Runway X PAPI out of service, the change from VNAV PTH to VNAV SPD and I did not call for a go-around.I have learned from this event and will call for a go-around if I become uncomfortable or we become unstable in the future. We were flying into ZZZZ [Airport] on the VOR [Runway] X approach at night. I had not flown for a year. Currency was a factor. While on approach I configured on time and landing checklist was called for and completed. At 500 feet we were 15 knots fast (171 knots) and the FO said we are fast. I said correcting. At 200 feet I was 17 knots (173 knots) fast the FO said we are fast, I tried to correct. Also, at 200 feet the FO called out high. I over corrected and landed abruptly from 50 feet to touch down. I do not believe this was a bounced landing but may have been. Our pitch was flat, and we landed main gear first. Our descent rate from 50 feet to 0 feet was extreme. The failure of myself or as a crew to not call a Go Around was the primary mitigating factor. Also executing an off center VOR approach with a PAPI OTS at night was a factor. I felt I was not high but in reality, it was due to lack of visible surroundings. Furthermore, the VOR approach only gave guidance to 1,054 feet MSL. To further complicate issues the VNAV disconnected. So, in essence we were left minimal visual guidance. Winds were 20 knots reported and was another factor. My FO stated he was about to call for go-around at 500 feet and 200 feet, but neither of us did. After landing we taxied in normally. We both did several post flight inspections. I also notified Maintenance and the Duty Pilot of the events. This was the first leg of a 4 day with an FO I've never flown with. All briefings were completed. The FO and I discussed before departure how infrequently we have flown due to the pandemic. He had never been to ZZZ [Airport]. I had not been in 2 years. All approach briefings were concluded in a timely manner. The STAR in use was the X arrival. After ZZZZZ [Intersection] we were instructed to fly present heading for radar vectors to join the VOR X LOC. The VOR approach X is a very tricky approach. It is offset with limited visual guidance. Flaps 1 was initiated prior to ZZZZZ. Flaps 5 was initiated after ZZZZZ. Best to our knowledge we were configured by the FAF. The FMA was showing VOR/LOC and VNAV path commencement to approach, at some point we lost VNAV path and went to VNAV speed. I accomplished a LAVS check but did not add 2 and 4 mile rings. I may have gotten very close to exceeding flaps 30 speed. I also believe my flare was minimal at best. Having a PAPI would have been beneficial.
ASRS:1798250.s: A Captain and First Officer with limited recent experience flew a night VOR approach into ZZZZ Airport, resulting in a hard landing due to excessive speed and altitude. Contributing factors included VNAV mode changes, an out-of-service PAPI, high winds, and the crew's failure to execute a go-around despite being unstable.

ASRS:1798253.n: We were flying the ILS 27R to ORD. When cleared for the approach level at 4,000 ft, we twice had to disconnect the autopilot from the aircraft wake ahead of us. Spacing was the usual 3 miles and winds were straight down the path at 40 kts. Other aircraft were radioing similar issues with wake. I decided to hand fly the approach the rest of the way to better control the speed and avoid the wake. The Final Controller told us to slow to 170 kts and contact Tower. We were cleared to land by Tower and continued the approach at 170 kts. Spacing was holding at 3 miles, but as we approached the marker I noticed our spacing was closing faster than normal. At about 2.5 outside the marker I made the decision to start slowing to avoid going around. (Full disclosure, I have been in the exact situation before and had to go around twice on this approach.) What I misjudged was how fast the 737-700 slows down. We were at approach speed too early and the Tower asked our speed and instructions. We made the aircraft behind us go around from my error in speed control. While on ILS 27R into ORD, we were experiencing wake turbulence from the aircraft ahead of us and appeared to be quickly closing the distance between us. We had been assigned 170 kts until the final approach fix 'SIBLY' and began slowing 2 miles prior to the fix to stop the closure. The Tower Controller queried our speed, and emphasized we were to hold 170 until the fix.
ASRS:1798253.s: Pilots flying a Boeing 737-700 on the ILS 27R approach to ORD encountered wake turbulence and misjudged deceleration rates while slowing early. This speed error caused the aircraft behind to execute a go-around after Tower controllers queried the deviation from the assigned 170 kts.

ASRS:1798292.n: We had returned to the gate 2 times for passenger related issues. We then taxied out to the hold short line. We sat there awaiting the final closeout for ten minutes or so. When the close out came, there was no performance uplink, so I went to change ZFW and CG to match the latest closeout. I then verified that the V-speeds matched the takeoff performance page and we departed. The flight plan had us filed for FL380, but the VNAV page capped us at FL370. We then leveled off at FL360. After some discussion given our light weight and nearly standard day temperatures, we began looking for the reason for the low Maximum Altitude. We found that I had entered the ZFW incorrectly from the final closeout.Causal factors could include feeling a little rushed to get going after the half hour delay. Another factor could have been the lack of an uplink that led me to manually enter data. Additionally, while I have been to training recently and am fully current, there is no smoothness or rhythm to my flying due to a lack of consistent time in the aircraft. Hopefully having a regular line in Month will improve my proficiency. After returning to the gate for a passenger issue, we were running slightly behind schedule. Original closeout deleted and after starting the second pushback, we had a new closeout (Rev 01) with good numbers which were accepted by the FMS. During the second pushback, we were directed to tow back to the gate for a baggage issue. Finally pushed back a third time and during taxi for departure, we received an ACARS message that closeout had been deleted and to wait for new numbers. Received revision 02 (one pax less) of the closeout. Did not get the prompt to accept new numbers. Got another message of a deleted closeout and to wait for new numbers. As we were getting more behind schedule, we ran through the numbers with the latest closeout (Rev 02) and confirmed the numbers as OK for a Flaps 10 degree, 10 knot tailwind TPS, with a plan to then cover the changes (if any) in the next closeout revision. Waited approximately 20 more minutes at the end of the runway, number one for departure and finally got Revision 03 of the closeout, which was unchanged from Revision 02. No prompt to accept the new numbers, so we manually updated them. After I had checked the PERF page TOW numbers with the latest closeout numbers, the First Officer noticed that the ZFW was slightly off and updated it, but entered XYZ.X instead of correct number XAZ.X. (Unnoticed at the time) Original number had been XAB.C. V-speeds did not delete from the FMS, and with a slightly lighter TOW than the plan, I figured we were good to go. V-speeds did not need to be changed, so we didn't. We then completed all items of the Before Takeoff checklist and took off normally. During the climbout, VNAV showed a max altitude of only FL360 instead of the planned FL380. I found this odd, as we were lighter than the original planned weight and the temp at altitude was normal. When we leveled off at FL360, I looked again at the closeout and compared it to the FMS perf page and then discovered the ZFW entry error. Corrected it then and the VNAV max altitude fixed itself. Remainder of flight uneventful.Because we were late and at the end of the runway, I may have rushed the FO to enter the ZFW data too quickly, which resulted in wrong data in the FMS. I did not specifically verify the entered ZFW number because I had previously seen that the revised TOW was below the planned TOW and we didn't need to calculate new TPS numbers. Even though the entered ZFW was incorrect, it was not used in calculating new QRH V-speeds, so the error went undetected as we went with the planned TPS.In the future, if a closeout does not uplink, I will call up the perf page on my FMS (as opposed to looking at the FO's perf page) and confirm each entry with the closeout.
ASRS:1798292.s: The pilot and First Officer manually entered an incorrect Zero Fuel Weight into the FMS during taxi due to a lack of uplink and schedule pressure. This error caused the VNAV to cap the climb at FL360 instead of the planned FL380, which was corrected after level-off.

ASRS:1798303.n: A fellow colleague advised that COVID vaccines were not loaded on the aircraft and they needed to be. Aircraft had already pushed, so they returned to blocks to get the vaccine loaded.
ASRS:1798303.s: A colleague advised that COVID vaccines were missing, causing the aircraft to return to blocks after pushback. The crew then loaded the vaccines before proceeding.

ASRS:1798314.n: I was pilot monitoring for this leg ZZZ to ZZZ1, we taxied out to Runway XX we were given position and hold initially, once we were in position and lined up, I transferred control to the First Officer. We were then given takeoff clearance, I read back the clearance '[Flight ABCB] Cleared for takeoff' the FO advanced the thrust levers, and 'said Runway XX set thrust' I called thrust set heading Checks. Soon after that while I was waiting to make the 80 knots call the FO said 'I don't think Aircraft Y is going to Stop' I immediately looked to see what he was talking about. And I see Aircraft Y, approaching the runway at [taxiway] it had not yet to appeared cross the hold short line, it took a split second to see it was not going to stop, the nose was just to the runway edge, I called abort I have the aircraft. Applying maximum breaking and full thrust reverser, we stopped 200-300 feet short of the [aircraft] as its nose was reaching the edge of the runway, as we reached a full stop the tower asked us if we could accept an intersection takeoff, we declined and exited the runway ran the aborted takeoff checklist and called Operations, they directed us to return to the gate.I am not sure why Aircraft Y flight crossed the runway we never heard them on the radio. We were cleared for takeoff on Runway XX and proceeded our takeoff roll. I noticed Aircraft Y approaching from my right at a rate of speed that concerned me. I quickly brought it to the attention of the Pilot monitoring and Captain. I wanted him helping to make decisions in this situation. We immediately came to the same conclusion as I called to abort the takeoff. We immediately went to idle then full reverse with max braking and were able to stop before impact. Aircraft Y wasn't on our frequency and proceeded across the runway. I notified Tower of the abort and they asked if we could continue from there and we declined. We decided it was safe to exit the runway. We cleared the runway and preformed the appropriate checklist. Then returned to the gate as directed by Operations.ATC apparently cleared us on separate frequencies.
ASRS:1798314.s: The Pilot Monitoring aborted takeoff on Runway XX after observing Aircraft Y crossing the hold short line without radio contact. The crew stopped 200–300 feet short of the runway edge using maximum braking and reverse thrust, then returned to the gate after ATC cleared both aircraft on separate frequencies.

ASRS:1798317.n: After landing in Myrtle Beach on Runway 36 we were asked to exit left on B5, turn left on B, left on B3, short of 36. We were then cleared to cross 36 and taxi to the ramp via A4. However the A4 on the airport does not match our charts. Our charts list A4 as taxiway Z. We stopped the aircraft and inquired with Tower, who said that proceeding straight would put us on A4 and that our charts are incorrect. The chart should be updated to reflect the changes on the ground as soon as possible. [Caused by] incorrect taxi diagram almost lead to an incorrect turn on an active runway. Suggest chart needs to be updated to reflect actual taxiways at the airport.
ASRS:1798317.s: The flight crew landed at Myrtle Beach and stopped after discovering charted taxiway A4 did not match the airport layout. Tower confirmed the charts were incorrect, noting the discrepancy almost caused an incorrect turn onto active Runway 36.

ASRS:1798323.n: The curtain that divides first class and coach between row X and row Y on aircraft left is blocking from a visual standpoint an emergency light that's mounted on the wall. In every other B737 fleet the curtain is installed with a restraining strap on the wall on the aircraft right side of the plane to avoid this situation on the 737-900. This problem seems to be a problem on the MAX 9 planes. I brought this attention to the pilots who brought the attention to Maintenance. The mechanic was mad saying I was going to delay the flight that was already delayed because he noticed the problem as well when he came out to inspect it. He then said it would be good to go because the emergency light is only one light. They just said it came out of the factory like that and it wasn't a problem. I find this a serious safety concern and not in compliance with FAA safety standards. If the emergency lighting system isn't important it wouldn't have been installed.
ASRS:1798323.s: A cabin crew member reported that a curtain on a Boeing 737 MAX 9 blocked an emergency light, a design issue not present on other 737s. Although the crew notified pilots and maintenance, a mechanic dismissed the concern as factory-standard and cleared the aircraft for departure despite the obstruction.

ASRS:1798389.n: I was enroute on an IFR flight plan. Sometime after passing ZZZZZ intersection on my assigned route and altitude I realized I had not spoken to ATC in a longer period of time than expected. About 18 miles south of ZZZ [VOR], I received a traffic alert on my ADS-B display of traffic 1,000 feet below, 2 miles. This prompted me to then call to ATC on my assigned frequency. Since I reached no one, and it had been longer than expected I figured they forgot about me and I searched for a frequency to reestablish contact. (I have had ATC miss handoffs occasionally before). I believe it was ZZZ Center I contacted, who then told me to contact ZZZ Approach. I was initially told they were 'too busy for flight following'. I advised them I was on an IFR flight plan. After another attempt or two to have them accept this, my communication with them was established. Several minutes later I was given a telephone number to call after landing, and upon querying why, they just said it was ZZZ Center. I do not know for sure what problem was supposed to be. But I suspect since I received the ADS-B traffic alert, it was a possible loss of separation. When I was somewhere in the vicinity of ZZZZZ intersection, a Controller told all aircraft 'don't call in, I'll call you'. I never received a call from this Controller, and it was only after I did not feel comfortable waiting longer for a call that I then called back to establish contact. I do not believe I missed a call or checking in on a frequency change. ATC was somewhat overwhelmed in spots in this area. I had noticed in my home area flying that some of the frequencies were not staffed during the COVID pandemic, and I think some of the facilities may have needed to re staff more quickly as traffic began to grow again.
ASRS:1798389.s: A pilot on an IFR enroute flight lost contact with ZZZ Center after a controller instructed aircraft not to call in. The pilot reestablished communication via ADS-B traffic alerts and subsequent calls, suspecting a potential loss of separation caused by understaffed facilities and overwhelmed controllers.

ASRS:1798401.n: I am reporting this in the interest of flight safety and for the furtherance of drone operations in the NAS (National Airspace System). For experience in the hours to clarify I went to flight school and earned a PPL (Private Pilot License) and have roughly X00 hours flight in helicopters combined with instrument and commercial type training, along with XX hours of fixed wing flight experience. 10 hours in drones however that is measured in flight logs stored within the aircraft flight logs and is subject to some error like all things are. The issue was that I was hired to film [an event] that was not permitted (something I did not know). The other issue was that the area I was operating in [an area] on the San Francisco sectional chart as no flight below 1,000 ft. AGL. I was aware of this area and knew approximately where it was but at the time believed it to be much farther north. The issue with drone operations vs. commercial manned aircraft operations is that the infrastructure is built around manned flight and to precisely pinpoint a physical address on a sectional is quite cumbersome. For the most part a sectional is helpful for areas in general but you could literally find yourself operating inside a hole within several boundaries. This is where applications such as Airmap, B4uFly, and UASidekick can be a huge help in checking and re-checking an area. I do understand the responsibility falls onto the PIC in this case and that I should have been more diligent and this is a lesson learned. But I cannot imagine that professional operators would be pulling out plotters for every address they fly at to pinpoint the coordinates. My concern lies with the applications accuracy not that the developers do not try but 4 of the top applications did not alert me to an airspace issue, this along with my presumed thought that the restriction was much farther north let me to believe I had the all clear. As drone operators the only official source we have is one that is geared towards manned flight and as usage continues to grow my fear is that a more serious incursion is inevitable. Helicopters operators have a chart that is most helpful to them when operating at low level, and this is very helpful as I have used these to navigate Los Angeles and San Francisco class B. Drones are an emerging business and as a responsible operator I am always concerned about flight safety. But usage is only increasing, something as simple as doing a roof inspection of a residential home reduces risk increases productivity and improves the accuracy and level of service. Drones may be small but they are making a huge impact.As drone operators the only official source we have is one that is geared towards manned flight and as usage continues to grow my fear is that a more serious incursion is inevitable. Drones may be small but they are making a huge impact.
ASRS:1798401.s: A drone operator with a PPL inadvertently flew a drone below 1,000 feet AGL in a restricted area near San Francisco while filming an unpermitted event. The incursion occurred because four airspace apps failed to alert the pilot, and the operator incorrectly believed the restriction was located farther north.

ASRS:1798411.n: We were flying and cleared on the IFR approach and had 3 flight school planes come within 500 feet. One of the planes pointed straight at us at our altitude within 100 feet at us. I read their tail number. We veered immediately. All three planes climbed straight up out of an adjacent airport. I notified ATC and they said it's a beehive there right now and he can't tell what's happened there.
ASRS:1798411.s: The pilot reported that while on an IFR approach, three flight school aircraft from an adjacent airport climbed within 500 feet, with one coming within 100 feet at the same altitude. The pilot veered to avoid a collision and notified ATC, who stated the area was a "beehive" and could not explain the incident.

ASRS:1798430.n: On VMC descent on the PIGLT6 Arrival just past JAFAR intersection at 12,000 feet, aircraft on autopilot started to bank left up to 20 degrees with associated turbulence. Shortly after aircraft stabilized level, aircraft rolled to the left again and started to go past 30 degrees in the roll without any corrective action by the autopilot. First Officer estimated our bank angle at its maximum was between 35-40 degrees. I disengaged the autopilot and went to manual control and took the sidestick to the right and the airplane responded immediately. We asked for an immediate turn off the arrival and we queried the controller about the target 7 miles in front of us (TCAS estimate) and it was a 767. We made a PIREP about the turbulence and continued to a safe landing. First Officer stated he was very close to stating 'upset recover' as part of our training. The downside to all of these satellite based RNAV arrivals is that it puts everybody on the exact same spot in the sky over a path and makes the trailing aircraft susceptible to upsets. The controller could have slowed us or spaced us out but it wasn't his fault that we are all tracking in line. This effort to get more aircraft throughput by ATC will end up in more of these incidents and could hurt somebody. We need to space out more on the arrivals and only ATC can make that happen. This isn't all their fault. It is the very design of these procedures by non-pilots that put pressure on our controllers.
ASRS:1798430.s: During a VMC descent on the PIGLT6 arrival past JAFAR at 12,000 feet, the aircraft experienced severe turbulence and uncommanded autopilot rolls up to 40 degrees. The pilot disengaged the autopilot, recovered manually, and attributed the upset to wake turbulence from a preceding 767 caused by tight RNAV arrival spacing.

ASRS:1798433.n: I was in cruise from ZZZ to ZZZ1 at 3,000 feet MSL with the autopilot engaged. Flight following with Approach was established and we were in communication. I saw an aircraft converging from the left and took evasive action to avoid a collision. The aircraft appeared slightly lower, so I chose to climb.I reported the near miss to Approach (frequency we were on). They responded claiming to have called us multiple times about the converging traffic. We did not receive any transmissions in-regards to traffic. The radios were silent.
ASRS:1798433.s: A pilot in cruise at 3,000 feet MSL with autopilot engaged took evasive climbing action to avoid a converging aircraft. The pilot reported a near miss, noting that Approach claimed to have issued traffic advisories that were never received due to silent radios.

ASRS:1798444.n: I was a CFI giving instruction to a first-time tailwheel student in a Aircraft X. The Aircraft X [vintage aircraft] primary trainer that lacks an electrical system and therefore has no radios with which to communicate with other aircraft. The only electronic equipment onboard is a 406 ELT and a battery powered intercom to allow communication between instructor and student. We had finished the airwork/aircraft familiarization portion of our flight and had returned to the traffic pattern for takeoff and landing practice. We operate out of ZZZ, [local city], just north of downtown. ZZZ is a busy GA airport with heavy flight school traffic, helicopter traffic, and [vintage aircraft] traffic in the form of [vintage military], aerobatic, and vintage aircraft. The local flight school is well aware of our [aircraft type] operation and it always extra vigilant of possible NORDO traffic because we operate regularly. Worth noting is that Runway XX [north] utilizes a left-traffic pattern while Runway XX [south] uses right-traffic. This is due to obstacles east of the airport and to keep all traffic over the river rather than over the city. The weather at the time of the incident was good VFR, nearly unlimited visibility with northeast wind of 5-10 kts. The windsock unmistakably favored Runway XX [north] all day and was consistent. I had been at the airport since late morning and everyone had been using Runway XX [north] all day. When in the pattern and scanning for traffic, I noted that we were the only aircraft in the area, but a flight school aircraft was taxiing out for departure on Runway XX [north]. On approach to our first landing, I noticed the Aircraft Y holding short and appeared to be waiting for us to land. After we crossed the threshold, the Cessna taxied into position to depart. After our touch and go and on the upwind leg, my student exclaimed 'dude what's that?' I leaned around him (I was in the rear seat) to see an airplane filling our windshield. I quickly took control and aggressively turned into the downwind. While in the turn, I observed an Aircraft Z pass behind us on final to Runway XX [south]. I estimate the horizontal separation to be 1000 feet or less and vertical separation to be less than 50 feet. Once in the downwind, I observed the Aircraft Z that had taxied into position behind us execute an emergency turn off the Runway, presumably as surprised as I was to see an airplane landing on the opposing Runway with a very obvious tailwind.From the downwind, I witnessed Aircraft Z land and clear the Runway. The Cessna was still holding short, so I executed a short approach and put the Aircraft X on the ground as quickly as possible, student and self very shaken. I taxied to parking in front of the hangar and shut down. I noticed the Aircraft Z pilot was walking toward us, presumably to apologize. Instead, he verbally accused my student and me of causing a dangerous situation by not having a radio. I reminded him of the windsock and weather conditions which clearly favor Runway XX [north] to which he replied that he got his weather report from 'Center' and they told him winds were calm. He then informed me that he made several radio calls, including 'left downwind, left base, and final for XX [south]'. I reminded him that Runway XX [south] utilizes a right traffic pattern, so nobody would be looking for him on the east side of the airport. After a short discussion with the instructor in the aircraft involved, he never heard any radio calls from the offending Aircraft Z other than his last call that he was clearing Runway XX [south]. His account of the entire incident was identical to mine, as we discussed it with the event still very fresh in our minds. He has offered to provide a written statement as well.I am 100% confident that we did nothing wrong nor did we violate any FAR's. I am submitting this report purely for the need for such a close call to be documented and hopefully learned from in the future. The negligence of an irresponsible pilot nearly caused a mid-air collision, and did cause a Runway incursion. If it were up to me, some serious remedial training would be required for the offending pilot to continue to use his privileges as a pilot. Everyone makes mistakes or misses a 'RP' [right-hand pattern] note on a sectional chart from time to time, but when that minor error almost gets people killed, something should be done. His defensive and rude 'I didn't do anything wrong, its your fault for not hearing me' attitude certainly didn't indicate to me that he realized the seriousness of his actions. I sincerely hope this report can be of use to others in the future and a harsh reminder to us all of the unforgiving nature of flying at an uncontrolled field.
ASRS:1798444.s: A CFI and student in a non-radio vintage aircraft nearly collided with an Aircraft Z during landing practice at an uncontrolled airport. The Aircraft Z pilot incorrectly entered a left traffic pattern for a right-hand runway while claiming calm winds, causing a runway incursion and a close call with less than 50 feet vertical separation.

ASRS:1798455.n: I was sitting in the right front seat of Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Aircraft X was at FL450 and just received instruction to descend at maintain Flight Level 240 over I believe ZZZZZ. As the Captain pulled the thrust levers back approximately 3/4' Aircraft X was vacating Flight Level 450 and started to descend, I watched the number two engine N1 and N2 continue to decrease while the number one engine N1 and N2 remained consistent with the selected thrust lever position. The Captain immediately noticed this at this time and I grabbed the emergency checklist book and opened it up to 'loss of engine at altitude during flight'. I read off the items listed and the Captain completed all the listed tasks. Once those were completed, I read off the items for restarting procedures. Upon reaching Flight Level 250 the engine was restarted and the flight continue to destinations, ZZZ1 and landed without incident or any other anomaly. The take away from this experience was, that in any event such as this, it is extremely important to have the cockpit organized and know where specific checklist items are in case there is a need.
ASRS:1798455.s: During descent from FL450 to FL240, the First Officer observed Engine 2 N1 and N2 decreasing while Engine 1 remained stable. The crew executed the loss of engine checklist, successfully restarted Engine 2 at FL250, and landed without further incident.

ASRS:1798463.n: I was flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1 via [airway] at [altitude]. I had just leveled out at cruise altitude when the engine began to run rough. This part of the route was most treacherous in terms of landing options being in the mountains. I chose to turn from my position direct back to the ZZZ2 airport and towards [land mark] which I thought would be a better landing spot to put it down if the engine did decide to quit. I maintained altitude to stay high while enroute back to ZZZ2 to keep our options open. The power did not fluctuate it was just running rough. I did go through the checklist to which nothing seemed to change the roughness. I held off on the magneto check because I wanted to get to a spot, I was comfortable with losing power to do the mag check (over ZZZ2) I listened to the ATIS and was going to begin my call up to the Tower from 15 miles to the north. At this point before I made the call the engine began running extremely rough. This prompted me to request priority handling with Tower. Tower gave me the landing clearance then and there for Runway XX. We communicated and I decided to stay high until over the top of the field then spiral down for the airport to stay within gliding distance. I did this because I know that historically most engine problems just seem to get worse when you make changes to the throttle and since I had to reduce power at some point to land the plane, I decided I was going to stay in a position to land safely with no power if it did happen. I spiraled down to join a left downwind for Runway XX and landed and taxied in. On the ground shortly after we performed a magneto check in which the L magneto dropped approximately 800 RPM and the engine began running extremely rough. The pre-takeoff magneto check was performed prior to the flight with no issues and magneto drops within tolerances. The airplane is in maintenance right now and I have just heard today that there was apparently a plastic piece on the magneto that should've been removed when they were installed that came loose and somehow affected the timing of the left magneto. In terms of the human factor, I had my girlfriend who is an instrument rated private pilot in the left seat, and her mother in the back. Geographically I didn't want to take any chances so we turned back towards the [landmark], airport with a long runway, and flatter terrain because I have never dealt with an engine running that rough and couldn't figure out why and expected the engine to fail. I believe my only inaction was checking the magnetos which I purposefully refrained from until we were over the airport. By the time we were over the airport and had the field made, I just decided we would focus on landing and deal with it on the ground.
ASRS:1798463.s: The pilot experienced rough engine operation during cruise and returned to ZZZ2, landing safely after requesting priority. Post-flight maintenance revealed a loose plastic piece on the left magneto installation caused timing issues, which was confirmed by an 800 RPM drop during a ground magneto check.

ASRS:1798468.n: While my student was doing a solo he veered off the runway during takeoff - no injuries. I debriefed the student, he said it went left and he lost control. I briefed him on rudder usage. Instructor action will be that he will work on takeoffs with the student and have another instructor fly with him before re-solo. After landing on centerline I put flaps up and accelerated to full throttle. The plane continued pulling to the left despite pressing on right rudder. As I veered to the left, headed towards the grass, I reduced power and ultimately going off the runway and stopping on Taxiway XX. I think [I] should have powered back sooner to prevent going off the runway.
ASRS:1798468.s: A student pilot veered left off the runway during a solo takeoff due to loss of control despite right rudder input, stopping on Taxiway XX with no injuries. The instructor attributed the incident to delayed power reduction and plans additional supervised takeoff training before re-solo.

ASRS:1798506.n: On completion of 9th landing (full stop, 3 point, 30 degrees of flaps) as aircraft rolled out (at approximately 25 mph) a gust of wind lifted the left wing and veered the aircraft to the left. Full deflection of the controls in an attempt to correct the situation had no effect. Aircraft drug the right wingtip, the right landing gear folded and the aircraft departed the pavement, nosing over and damaging the propeller. No injuries sustained by occupants.
ASRS:1798506.s: During rollout after the 9th landing, a gust lifted the left wing and veered the aircraft left despite full control deflection. The right wingtip dragged, the right gear folded, and the aircraft nosed over off the pavement, damaging the propeller with no injuries.

ASRS:1798513.n: I was flying from ZZZ1 to ZZZ just to run the plane. It was a very bumpy ride and turbulent approach on final at this uncontrolled airport. I landed a little too fast and was caught by a gust from my left side, the right wing lifted causing the plane to veer left off the runway and onto the grass where I got it slowed and re entered the runway without any damage or injury. Cause was landing before the plane had lost all lift. I was practicing a wheel landing where you flare just as the wheels touch the runway, however still flying speed which is fine in no wind conditions. Taught me a good lesson to always do stall landings in gusty windy conditions. I stopped and did a preflight before departing to make sure all was fine. I did four more touch and goes after that with no issues.
ASRS:1798513.s: The pilot experienced a runway excursion during a turbulent approach at an uncontrolled airport while practicing a wheel landing. A left gust lifted the right wing, causing the aircraft to veer onto the grass before being safely re-entered without damage or injury.

ASRS:1798524.n: I was cleared to land on 10R and planned to exit at the first available taxiway (H) which was within the landing performance data but required accurate, prompt control to do so. I successfully landed and slowed to normal exit speed, acquired what I thought was the lead-off line for H, and the taxiway edge lights on the far side of the lead-off line. What I didn't perceive was that the lead-off line had been blacked out recently as H had been moved during construction. Given the poor ambient lighting (even accounting for the excellent forward lighting from the landing lights), there was no immediate visual difference between the runway surface and the transition to the gravel surface and as the airplane departed the runway, the extra drag of the gravel and ~4' of underlying mud brought the airplane to a stop. After realizing what had happened and that I wasn't going to be able to taxi further, I coordinated with Tower, was instructed to switch to Ground and asked for a tow and passenger transport, then shut down the engine.Everything but the runway exit went as planned. I followed aircraft procedures, but departed from my usual night time post-landing technique of acquiring the lead-off line, then verifying the taxiway signage and seeing the lead-off goes between the edge lights. The erroneous lead-off line combined with the adjacent line of taxiway edge lights and the still-night-but-approaching-daylight contributed to my disregard of my usual next exit criterion that the lead-off lights guide between the taxiway lights, resulting in exiting the runway surface next to the intended taxiway exactly on the blacked out lead-off line that led to the previous location of Taxiway H.The bottom line contributors were fatigue after an earlier transport, planning an aggressive landing while fatigued, and visual cues that combined with my disregard of solid techniques in the process of achieving the required performance to meet the plan. In the future I will accept and use the available runway rather than plan for an expedited profile that approaches the limits of my current capabilities.
ASRS:1798524.s: The pilot landed on runway 10R at night and exited onto a blacked-out lead-off line for a relocated Taxiway H due to fatigue and poor visual cues. The aircraft stopped in mud and gravel, requiring a tow after the pilot failed to verify taxiway signage before exiting.

ASRS:1798540.n: Cleared to line up and wait Runway XX. When cleared for takeoff, pushed power to approximate 40% then selected TO/GA. As the thrust levers advanced, there was a very loud bang and yaw to the left. We had just started rolling. The thrust levers were brought to idle and we stopped on the runway. Initially, with the bang and yaw I thought we hit something or ran over something. As I was looking out the window, the First Officer stated we had a #1 Engine failure. Tower asked if we wanted equipment. We asked if they saw smoke or damage, and they replied 'No', along with another aircraft on the taxiway. I made a PA for everyone to remain seated. I then called the F/A's (Flight Attendants) and asked them to look at the Captain side engine for smoke or flames. They reported it looked normal. We ran the Engine Failure Checklist, and discussed running the Rejected Takeoff Checklist. Since the event happened as the aircraft had just started to roll (probably less than 10 knots) we didn't run the Rejected Takeoff Checklist, knowing that brake energy and cooling wouldn't be an issue. After we taxied to the gate, I made calls to Dispatch, Maintenance, and the Chief Pilot on call, while the First Officer went to the ramp to inspect the aircraft. He discovered bent and broken turbine blades with metal pieces loose in the engine. He came back upstairs and called ZZZ Ground to do a runway check for engine debris. I made a PA to the passengers explaining that we had an engine failure at power up, and the aircraft would be taken out of service. They would receive more flight information in the terminal. After the passengers had deplaned, the crew got together and debriefed the event. I informed the F/As of what had happened and let them ask questions.
ASRS:1798540.s: The flight crew experienced a loud bang and left yaw during takeoff power application on Runway XX, causing an immediate stop. Inspection revealed bent and broken turbine blades in Engine #1, resulting in the aircraft being taken out of service.

ASRS:1798556.n: The NIITZ 1 RNAV Departure from Runway 8L depicts FLAAR as prior to the lake. The E/O (Engine Out) Page for 8L shows it as past the lake. I realize that DP1 is an altitude (3,500 feet - 6,000 feet) but the diagram does not match up. I expressed my concerns to a Check Airman friend and he did a better job of analyzing the problem. He noted the brown arc on the E/O (MSA circle we assume) shows FLAAR to be at 25 NM. I used the FIX Page of the FMC and put the LAS/12.7 arc and it lands on top of FLAAR. So, I see two problems. The 'terrain' and the omission of 'Not to Scale' could create confusion when you are trying to build a visual model of the E/O. Also, I'm not sure we recognize the hold at FLAAR is really only 12.7 NM from LAS, not 25 where it may seem less threatening to following traffic.My friends words: I agree that if you were trying to create a mental image of what you were doing in case you lost an engine, then the engine out diagram (picture) would lead you astray. The dilemma arises from the 12.7 ring and FLAAR being almost coincident. It gets worse, because 12.7 and FLAAR have nothing to do with one another. 12.7 only matters if you are below 3,500 feet. And FLAAR only matters if you are above 3,500 feet. So we are mixing altitudes with rings with fixes with terrain features with no warning that the drawing is not to scale! The disturbing part to me is that the E/O has the standard 25 NM MSA ring (at least that's what I think it is, and it is at 25 NM), which lends credence to FLAAR being 25 NM out (not about 13). So you are totally right! The written text is fine, but the diagram is very misleading. I think we need to put 'NOT TO SCALE'. Or get rid of the terrain features. But the mixing and matching just leads to confusion (at the worst time).
ASRS:1798556.s: A pilot and a Check Airman identified misleading Engine Out diagrams for the NIITZ 1 RNAV departure from Runway 8L, where the chart incorrectly depicted the FLAAR fix distance relative to terrain. They concluded that the lack of a "Not to Scale" warning and conflicting altitude rings could confuse crews during an engine failure.

ASRS:1798564.n: We pushed off of [the] gate. My First Officer (F/O) gave a courtesy push call to Ground and we were told to expect Runway XXL. After push, F/O requested taxi. A different voice than previous Controller on same frequency gave us taxi clearance. Clearance was 'Taxi Runway XXL via Hotel and Golf.' Taxiing from the non-movement area, approaching Taxiway, I announced 'clear left' and I looked as far back as I could see over my left shoulder out of the left cockpit window. As I started a slow turn onto the taxiway, I visually cleared left again and saw a (other carrier) 757 rapidly approaching so I immediately stopped and set the parking brake. The traffic passed very close to us. This entire event was witnessed by a Company aircraft, which was holding short of the taxiway. We thought he was waiting for us so he could taxi into the ramp. My First Officer double checked our taxi clearance with Ground, about two minutes after the traffic passed. He confirmed it was 'Taxi XXL via Hotel and Golf.' After we had our clearance confirmation, the holding Company aircraft mentioned on the frequency something to the effect that the 757 passed very close to us. On taxi out to Runway XXL in ZZZ, our clearance was 'Taxi XXL via H, G'. Approaching H from the ramp area, we noticed an inbound Company aircraft that we needed to either yield to, or hear confirmation that he was going to yield to us prior to entering the ramp. The Crew of that aircraft saw us as well and were able to reach Ground Control before we could to clarify whether they should enter the ramp before us or after we had past. Ground Control advised them to hold position and issued us no further instructions so we were continuing with our previously assigned clearance to taxi via H, G to XXL. Approaching the taxiway the Captain cleared left and noted that Company aircraft was waiting, while I cleared Right. While making the turn onto the taxiway, the Captain did one more glance to the left and brought the aircraft to an abrupt stop. Just then I noticed a (other carrier) 757 taxiing down G that we had had no prior information on. The Captain was able to stop the aircraft and maintain separation. We held there for (other carrier) aircraft to pass by on G and then re-cleared both left and right and proceeded onto G as previously instructed. We confirmed our clearance with Ground Control to which they again verified we were to taxi XXL via H, G. No hold shorts or information concerning other aircraft were given other than the inbound Company aircraft being told to hold his position when he made the inquiry about entering the ramp in reference to us taxiing out. The (other carrier) 757 was never mentioned.
ASRS:1798564.s: The flight crew experienced two near-mid-air collisions with an unannounced 757 while taxiing to Runway XXL via Taxiways H and G. The Captain stopped the aircraft both times after visually spotting the approaching traffic, as Ground Control had provided no information regarding the 757's presence.

ASRS:1798576.n: After the addition of thrust for T/O (takeoff) and selection of TO/GA (takeoff go-around) and N1 attaining T/O power, the aircraft was already rolling and had achieved approximately 15 knots of forward motion. At that point we heard a very loud bang followed by a hard left yawing motion. The PF (Pilot Flying) immediately retarded the throttles to idle, and applied smooth breaking, which brought us to a complete stop. We were angled left by about 30-40 degrees in relation to the center line of Runway 4, just prior to taxiway. I immediately informed ATC that we had stopped on the runway, the PF informed the PAX (passengers) to stay seated. At that point we began to assess the situation. Initially we thought it was a blown tire or nose wheel steering issue. In that moment of assessing I noticed the #1 Engine Fail Caution illuminate in the #1 EGT Gauge. I informed the PF of the indication. It was the only indication we saw. No fire, no red lines only the engine failure alert caution. We reviewed the Rejected Takeoff Procedure, completed the QRH for Engine Failure. We then assessed the rolling and breaking capability of the aircraft and we found it to be normal. We got clearance to exit the runway and return to the gate. As we pulled in to the gate, we remembered that we had not run an After Landing Checklist and quickly completed that, followed by the Parking Checklist. Then, the jetbridge malfunctioned and we had to wait until Airport Ops came to fix it. Once the jetbridge was attached I exited the aircraft to inspect Engine #1. I found the N1 fan blades and the stators directly behind them to be in a normal appearance. When I looked into the tailpipe of the turbine section, I found metal debris from the engine and both the aft fan blades and stators in front of them to be damaged and missing pieces. I hustled back to the Flight Deck to inform Ground Control that they needed to do a FOD check of the runway as we had, had and engine failure and that they needed to check for small engine parts.
ASRS:1798576.s: During takeoff roll at approximately 15 knots, the crew rejected the takeoff after a loud bang, left yaw, and Engine #1 failure indication. Post-flight inspection revealed damaged fan blades and stators with metal debris in the tailpipe, prompting a request for a runway FOD check.

ASRS:1798577.n: Tower gave us a clearance for takeoff and gave us an advice of a traffic on the left side. We had a TA (traffic advisory) but also we had visual contact with the aircraft. By the time we changed frequencies Departure was already asking 'Aircraft X are you up?' I answered, 'Yes, Aircraft X leaving 2000 for 3000 feet.' ATC gave us, 'Turn left heading 150 and expedite your turn. You have traffic.' Simultaneously, the First Officer responded to an RA and leveled off around 2600 feet and continued to expedite the turn. The traffic was at 500 feet above us on the right side. After clear of conflict ATC gave us multiple headings and altitudes to back on course. We had the feeling that ATC did not inform us about the second traffic and there was no way to avoid an RA, since we were in between the two conflicting aircraft. From our stand point an RA was unavoidable because the proximity to both aircraft. ATC should have delayed our takeoff or assigned a heading to avoid the conflict.
ASRS:1798577.s: The flight crew received a takeoff clearance with traffic advisories but encountered an unavoidable Resolution Advisory while climbing between two conflicting aircraft. The crew leveled off at 2,600 feet to comply with the RA, attributing the conflict to ATC failing to inform them of the second traffic or delay the departure.

ASRS:1798584.n: Before we pushed off of the gate we were advised from the pushback driver to hold off on engine start, as we're were waiting for another aircraft that had already pushed back behind us. As we began the pushback, he cleared us to start engines and we did. When the pushback was complete, we did our flows and the before taxi checklist. At this point I saw an aircraft taxiing out for departure, that was also in the alleyway. We were on the left taxi line, which is the inbound line for the alleyway on our chart. I noticed that there was an aircraft taxiing into the alleyway, and they were already on the inbound line. Since no communication is necessary to taxi from the alleyway I turned on my taxi light and was adding power and asked my First Officer if it was clear right, and he said there was an aircraft just about to pass us. I was just about to pull right to clear the traffic that was coming at us. Had we not cleared right, we were both in agreement we would have hit Company who overtook us as they were taxiing rather fast. We're not sure why they decided to pass us on the right.
ASRS:1798584.s: The flight crew experienced a near collision while taxiing on the inbound line after another aircraft overtook them on the right. The pilots avoided impact by maneuvering right, attributing the event to the other aircraft's decision to pass quickly without communication.

ASRS:1798622.n: We were in visual conditions on approach to GEG, when we were cleared by GEG Approach control to descend to an altitude of 3,900 feet, while also being cleared for the visual approach Runway 21. As we began to descend, I as the pilot monitoring, looked outside and noticed some tall radio towers. I brought the towers to the Captain's attention and he immediately stopped the descent in order to prevent us from coming any closer to the towers. If I remember correctly we stopped the descent at approximately 5,300 feet. We then flew over the towers and after clearing them we continued our descent to 3,900 ft and commenced the visual approach to a successful and safe landing. We were never given any warning about the towers and did not notice the towers on the approach plate until after landing and getting to the hotel. Since this was my first time flying into GEG, and the Captain had not flown to GEG in years, we were both unfamiliar with the area and after this incident would recommend that a better warning be given on the 10-7 pages as well as on the approach plates.These warnings would not only help those who are unfamiliar with the area and specifically the radio towers, but would help remind those that are familiar with the area to possible encounters with the towers. After being cleared for a visual approach to Runway 21 in GEG, I started a descent to the SIGYOFAF altitude using FLCH with the autopilot on. During the descent the FO verbalized that he saw towers at approximately our 12:00 o'clock position. I promptly leveled off until we passed the towers and then continued the visual approach backed up with the ILS for an uneventful landing. It should be noted that there are towers on a bluff a few miles SE of the Runway 21 FAF that are higher than the FAF altitude.
ASRS:1798622.s: Pilots on a visual approach to GEG Runway 21 descended toward 3,900 feet but stopped at 5,300 feet after spotting tall radio towers higher than the FAF altitude. The crew leveled off to clear the towers, which were not warned on charts, before completing a safe landing.

ASRS:1798645.n: About an hour after flight XXXX took off out from ZZZ, Load Planning called alerting me that they had loaded extra Hazmat. According to their numbers, the aircraft was only allowed a total of 6.0 units, but 7.7 were added. I notified the crew, and the CA called me upon landing. He stated that his paperwork only showed one dangerous goods item as opposed to the three on my side. One hour into my flight, Dispatch sent ACARS message to call due to incorrect Hazmat load. Once on the ground called Dispatcher. He informed me an additional 7 lbs of Hazmat was loaded onto my aircraft. My final dangerous goods manifest had 1.1lbs. He said there was an additional add without our knowledge.
ASRS:1798645.s: Load Planning and Dispatch notified the flight crew that an extra 7 lbs of Hazmat was loaded onto the aircraft, exceeding the 6.0-unit limit. The discrepancy occurred because an additional item was added without the crew's knowledge, causing a mismatch between the manifest and the actual load.

ASRS:1798674.n: Coming into ZZZ about 30 miles out in VMC we were assigned at pilots discretion down to 4000 feet, after that we were assigned another heading and what I thought was down to 3000 feet to join the visual approach in a few miles so i descended down and a few minutes after reaching 3000 feet the controller called to let us know just that the MSA for that sector was 3700 feet to which we asked for a climb and climbed back up and let him know that we would file some paper work and told him we thought we heard 3000 feet and he said something about being VMC plus the MSA altitude and he said just to give him a call when we got on the ground and we got his number. After taking down the number he cleared us for the visual in which we were high as well as close to the final approach fix and handed us off to tower. Turning final and finishing up configuration we realized we were still a bit too high for our comfort level and standards instead of continuing we decided to execute a go around and came back around to land with no issue. Once we got to the hotel we gave the controller a call and he explained that we were in VMC conditions and he thought we might have just taken another planes altitude and that he had just noted we went below the MSA for the alert he got and there was no issues and we let him know we would file an report for our end and he said have a nice day. Misunderstanding or took another planes altitude. Asked ATC to climb to MSA and request accepted and we climbed to MSA. Nothing do exactly as we did.
ASRS:1798674.s: Pilots descending for a visual approach at ZZZ mistakenly descended below the 3700-foot MSA due to a clearance misunderstanding. They climbed back to the MSA, executed a go-around for being too high on final, and landed safely after the controller attributed the error to potential confusion with another aircraft's altitude.

ASRS:1798677.n: Our flight ELP to ZZZ. We took off on Runway 4 and were assigned the JCOXX2 Departure. In the turn towards JCOXX above 6,450 ft we got the 'terrain message' followed by the 'pull up' message. We could clearly see that we would clear the terrain with no problem. As we were continuing the climb we noticed that the terrain system failed light was illuminated. ADS-B failed light was also on for awhile, but it went out after 30 minutes or so. I wrote up the terrain system fail light in ZZZ. The ATIS in ELP was warning of heavy military jamming of GPS signals in the area. When we asked ATC if they were receiving our ADS-B signal, they said they do not use it because of the military activities. The First Officer immediately pulled up and increased the climb rate, but since we both could see that terrain was not going to be a factor we did not exceed engine limits.
ASRS:1798677.s: During the JCOXX2 departure from ELP, the crew received false terrain warnings and ADS-B failures above 6,450 ft due to military GPS jamming. The First Officer increased climb rate, but the aircraft cleared terrain safely, and the terrain system failure was reported upon arrival at ZZZ.

ASRS:1798688.n: Knowing that Runway XX would put us on a straight visual, while we were still in cruise, we thoroughly briefed the landing. There is rising terrain NE of ZZZ1 at the approach end of [Runway] XX necessitating close in maneuvering. Airport elevation is at XXXX so we decided to be fully configured with gear down and final flap selection at 7,500 feet 5NM from the Runway XX threshold to approximate a glide path. This would give us X;XXX feet buffer to get down. (Much more was briefed, this is just a highlight.) After we were switched from Center to ZZZ Approach we were told to expect vectors to Runway YY ILS. This was preferable because that would give us an instrument approach without terrain for visual backup, and it's within the 10 kt tailwind limit. However when we got switched to ZZZ Tower we were told they were not using YY and to expect vectors for a visual XX. We requested [Runway] YY again but this was refused by Tower, so we elected to get delayed vectors to allow time to set up XX again (we already had landing numbers and we had briefed it so it didn't take long). As had been briefed, we were fully configured 2,100 feet above field elevation at least 5 NM out and the FMS was used to draw an extended line from the Runway XX threshold to give better situational awareness of runway positioning during maneuvering. Green needles were used with the ILS frequency for Runway YY to give a visual indication of when we were approaching the runway centerline knowing that this would also give us reverse sensing and a false glide slope--this was briefed as well. My First Officer was flying but if it had been my leg I would've transferred controls to him anyway. I had flown with him for three days and seen him perform hand flown approaches and was supremely confident of his skills. And since we were being vectored in the NW sector for a right base to final to XX he would have the best view to make the turn to final. On final we got a visual GROUND PROX caution box on the PFD as well as aural 'glideslope' messages with an associated flashing caution some 3-6 times. Each time I canceled it and said disregard it's a false glideslope which was acknowledged by First Officer. First Officer had me cancel his flight director and he flew the visual raw data with me backing him up on descent rate, speed, and how it looked. He did a nice job and set it down without incident. [Unrelated] runways were NOTAMed closed. Runway XX PAPI was NOTAMed OTS. The reason to bring this attention is so that other crews will have notification that they may be required to land with minimal instrumentation backing them up on a visual. Other flight crews may not have the experience nor may benefit from mild weather condition. Please notify other crews that while [other] runways are closed they may be required to shoot a straight visual to XX near rising terrain, so that awareness may be raised and overall risk mitigated.
ASRS:1798688.s: The crew flew a visual approach to Runway XX near rising terrain after ATC denied a requested ILS to Runway YY. Despite false GPWS and glideslope cautions caused by using an ILS frequency for visual reference, the First Officer landed safely using raw data.

ASRS:1798694.n: Neither one of us had ever been into ZZZ. We both took the opportunity on the flight to review the company pages. Acknowledging that it is a special qualification airport and after review of company documents, we realized that controls needed to be transferred to the Captain due to my low time in the aircraft. Control of the aircraft was transferred at approximately 13,000 feet MSL. Traffic was landing XXL. We briefed and set up for the RNAV for XXL. Center handed us off to ZZZ Approach. We were asked to advise when the field was in sight. Conditions were VFR and remained so. We had the field and were cleared for the visual. We recognized immediately that we were high. We had a tailwind which made it exceptionally difficult to get configured. The Captain continued to descend and try to reduce speed. He called for gear, however, I was unable to extend the gear because we were not at the appropriate speed. We were switched to Tower. The Captain continued the descent all the while attempting to reduce speed. Best guess we were at approximately a 7 mile final. We received an EGPWS 'TERRAIN TERRAIN'. The Captain shallowed the descent. It was then followed by a 'TERRAIN TERRAIN PULL UP' and I called for the go-around. We followed the escape procedures, were vectored around the pattern, and landed without incident. Neither pilot had been into the airport. We had reviewed documents, however once cleared for the visual we did not comply with the prescribed speeds on the arrival. In retrospect, we should have continued on the RNAV arrival since we were unfamiliar with the airport. Additionally, better awareness of wind may have assisted in getting configured.
ASRS:1798694.s: Two pilots unfamiliar with ZZZ airport accepted a visual approach for XXL despite a tailwind, failing to comply with prescribed speeds. This resulted in an unstable approach, EGPWS terrain warnings, and a go-around before a safe landing.

ASRS:1798699.n: We were Filed and Cleared for 'RNDRZ1 Arrival ILS 26L' in LAS. We set and Descended to 8,000 ft. with Managed Descend Mode. Controller then gave us Descend to 6,000 ft. and pointed out traffic. When we leveled off at 6,000 feet, I queried the controller by transmitting Level 6,000 ft. just passing BERBN Fix. He said 'Roger' as we continued to look for our traffic. We were coupled with ILS 26L and the aircraft started to turn after HOGOG Fix to Heading 020. It is only then, the Controller gave us vector to 080 even as he pointed out the traffic. He then told us that we should have picked up 080 heading after BERBN. RNDRZ1 states at BERBN FIX that 'Landing RWY19L/R, 26L/R EXPECT RADAR vectors to final approach course'. Controller never gave us a vector after BERBN and since Aircraft X Connects from BERBN-BISHP-HOGOG-KODSE-HUXAR, AC started the turn to 020.The initial clearance from ATC was too close to Descend Via Cleared for the ILS 26L. Traffic watch was involved. On the Arrival (which is New) the INSET does NOT display a Track of 079 only a small print that says 079 track after BERBN. This is Aircraft X specific when we select the STAR and APPROACH. I suggest that ATC proactively assign a heading prior to or after BERBN just as they to in LAX after SLI Heading 340 on GOATZ1 Arrival. Train Crews to clear the Waypoint after BERBN so there is a Discontinuity which would Default to 079 Heading. We were filed and cleared for the RNDRZ1 arrival ILS 26L. I set 8,000 ft. in managed descent. Controller then cleared us to 6,000 feet and pointed out traffic. Leveled off at 6,000 feet and the Captain informed ATC that we were at 6,000 feet and passing BERBN and response was Roger. Continued to actively look for traffic. I was coupled to ILS 26L and just as the aircraft at HOGOG started it's turn the Controller gave us a 080 heading and was pointing out traffic at the same time. Then the controller stated that we should have flown a 080 heading out of BERBN. The RNDRZ1 states at BERBN fix that landing runway 26L expect radar vectors.From ATC initial clearance is too close to descend VIA for ILS 26L. Traffic watch was involved. Arrival the INSET does not display a track of 079 after BERBN only in the small print does it show 079. ATC should issue a heading at BERBN. The aircraft did not to link to the approach or to the arrival or remove the linked portion.
ASRS:1798699.s: Pilots flying Aircraft X on the RNDRZ1 arrival to ILS 26L at LAS turned to heading 020 after HOGOG because ATC failed to issue the expected 080 vector at BERBN. The reporter attributed the deviation to unclear chart inset data and the aircraft's flight management system linking the arrival directly to the approach.

ASRS:1798714.n: During the course of planning for my next medical certificate, I noticed the Company showed my certificate expiring two months earlier than I was aware of. Due to the COVID extension from the previous year, it appeared I did not need a new exam until the following [Month X]. I apparently did not fully understand the details of the COVID extension. Nor did [the app] alert me of the expiration of my medical. The FAA letter I received after the extension showed a [Month X] expiration in bold typeset. Further down in the letter however in normal typeset it shows an exam due six months before. The actual certificate I received in the mail from the FAA shows the following [Month X] as the expiration date.The COVID medical extension caused confusion for multiple parties, including myself, my AME, the company, and possibly even the FAA itself. The bold typeset states a [Month X] expiration which apparently does not apply to the COVID extension. The verbiage in the FAA letter is difficult to understand and lends itself to multiple interpretations.Clearer verbiage and guidance regarding the COVID medical extension would certainly have helped. Closer attention to detail by all parties involved would hopefully mitigate these types of threats during an unprecedented pandemic.
ASRS:1798714.s: A pilot discovered their company listed their medical certificate as expired two months early due to confusion over FAA COVID extension verbiage. The conflicting expiration dates on the FAA letter and certificate caused misunderstandings for the pilot, AME, and company, highlighting a need for clearer guidance.
