ASRS:1798717.n: ATC direct failure to advise hold short of RWY 9C in the initial clearance. After the switch from ground to another tower frequency no instruction was given to HOLD SHORT 9C. We were given clearance to Taxi M1, M, right onto RWY 22R HOLD SHORT OF ECHO. Aircraft Y was ahead of us given the same clearance HOLD SHORT ECHO monitor tower.Aircraft Y encroached RWY 9C as Aircraft Z was on its takeoff roll on 9C. ATC Controller YELLED AIRCRAFT Y STOP! Immediately after Aircraft Z cancel takeoff clearance STOP! The commercial jet appeared from behind the hangars with the nose wheel off the ground in a slight right bank as the controller says DO YOU SEE THAT PLANE?!Aircraft Y was given a number to contact the tower.There are no 'wig wags' installed at any intersections along this runway. There are no stop bars installed. There are multiple obstructions to visibility. Taxiing into the sun is a factor.Runway markings and signage is unacceptable for the size and scope of the runway, and it's intended use.New construction all around the airport with pilots returning to work from furlough, and layoffs or leave of absence. Trust bias that ATC Is correct in the instructions given.Attempting to move aircraft with expedience rather than a structured taxi route. No designation of any 'hot spots ' on aeronautical charts.Cease and desist using RWY 22R as a taxi way!The use of this RWY as a taxi way is the inevitable set up for a mass casualty accident!
ASRS:1798717.s: Pilots reported a runway incursion where Aircraft Y entered RWY 9C while Aircraft Z was on takeoff roll due to ATC failing to issue a hold short clearance. The reporter attributed the event to poor visibility, inadequate signage, and the unsafe use of RWY 22R as a taxiway.

ASRS:1798768.n: After the cleaners sprayed the aircraft, we were rushed to get on the plane and board. The smell of the spray was so strong, we could immediately taste and feel irritation in our throat, eyes, and taste it. Even during the demonstration my eyes were very irritated. It wasn't until after takeoff and the air was circulating that we felt a tiny bit of relief.
ASRS:1798768.s: Cabin crew reported strong chemical irritation to their eyes and throats after cleaners sprayed the aircraft before boarding. Relief was only felt after takeoff when the air circulation system began operating.

ASRS:1798799.n: On a long base to final due to multi engine aircraft in front of us. Student was turning final and I just happened to glance at my iPad connected with ADS-B sentry (aircraft only equipped with ADS-B out). I saw traffic turning at us at 200 feet above. I believe he was on a right base. I thought it might be a weird ghost reading, but checked to make sure. I reduced power angled right. While checking I saw just above and slightly above and slightly in front an aircraft in front of us. We called our final and he asked where we were that he didn't see us. We informed him that we were right behind him. Aircraft on extend downwind informed that we were about a 1/4 mile apart on final. The other aircraft broke off to the right and exited traffic pattern. I had full controls from my student at reduced power setting. We stayed on final and departed the traffic pattern on upwind without landing, just a low approach so we could breath for a second. I believe the only thing that we could have done is to amend our base call to have said ' extended base' I'm not sure why traffic was on a right base for that runway. Possibly because there was a lot of traffic and they didn't want to try to find a spot between the 4 other planes in the left traffic pattern? I believe without ADS-B in that I purchased on my own that it would have been a lot closer.
ASRS:1798799.s: A pilot and student on final approach detected a conflicting aircraft on a right base via personal ADS-B In equipment. The pilot reduced power and turned right to avoid a collision, prompting the other aircraft to break off, while the pilot attributed the safe outcome to the ADS-B In display.

ASRS:1798831.n: During a tour in ZZZ, at straight and level flight on my way to the landing zone, the helicopter seemed to be operating with reduced power when at max continuous power (MCP). Please keep in mind that during my preflight inspection of the helicopter in the morning, before conducting tours, I noticed no visible abnormalities. There was no low rotor RPM condition and no visible change in RPM throughout the tour. I noticed that with 2 passenger flights, earlier in the day, I was able to maintain MCP and 100 KIAS. Then, at the time of the occurrence, I noticed that with relatively the same weight in another 2 passenger flight that I was only able to maintain MCP and fly at 80 KIAS without decreasing in altitude. Given the 20 knot loss, I felt I should shut down prior to taking any more flights and just give the engine a once-over. Upon my inspection, I noticed oil spray over the engine on the helicopter's right side and some on the firewall. As a pilot, I felt at that point I needed to call our maintenance guy to give me his opinion on the situation. Our maintenance guy is also the Chief Pilot and Primary Manager of the company. He instructed me not to sell or take up any other flights with passengers. He then proceeded to tell me to fly the helicopter to ZZZ for him to come inspect it and make necessary repairs. Given the amount of oil I started with during pre-flight and the amount of oil in the engine after 2 hours of run time (the difference was 1.5 quarts burned, 8 quarts in the morning and 6.5 in the engine at the time of shutdown and pilot inspection) I felt I was within limits to fly the helicopter not even 5 minutes from the landing zone to Company at ZZZ. There was no oil light illumination in flight during that time or any time during tours. Both the oil temperature and oil pressure gauges were in the green. There has been a cracked cylinder on this helicopter before which resulted in reduced power as well. Given that, in my experience as a pilot, I believed this to be another cracked cylinder or maybe even a bad valve. I felt that my flight back to the airport was within limits. I topped off the oil, performed a power check and a magneto check prior to takeoff from the landing zone. I made my call to Tower, lifted off from the landing zone, flew my .03 flight over to Company, shutdown, and left back to ZZZ1 for Maintenance to handle it. This is the facts from my perspective, from what I was experiencing, to what I was told from Maintenance/Management, and how it was handled.
ASRS:1798831.s: The pilot reported reduced power and a 20-knot airspeed loss during straight-and-level flight in a helicopter, suspecting a cracked cylinder or bad valve. After discovering oil spray and a 1.5-quart oil loss, the pilot flew the aircraft back to the base for maintenance inspection.

ASRS:1798832.n: On the evening of March XXth I was piloting a Bonanza VFR from ZZZ to ZZZ1. In order to stay below the shelf of the class bravo airspace I would have to fly the x-c below 2,000 feet which I didn't want to do, both for safety and for efficiency. While on the ground at ZZZ I requested flight following at 3,000 feet, with the intent of transiting the bravo airspace enroute to ZZZ1, and was assigned a departure frequency and squawk code. The takeoff and initial climb was uneventful. We checked in with Approach, and were informed that in order to fly to my destination at 3,000 feet we would initially have to take up a westerly heading before turning south. After flying west of ZZZ2, the main cabin door opened in flight, severely inhibiting communication with ATC due to the loud wind noise captured on the front seat passenger's headset microphone. In addition to the sudden distraction, the loud wind noise picked up by the front passenger's microphone inhibited communication with ATC, requiring me to ask approach to repeat a few transmissions. I tried talking the front seat passenger through closing the door, which was unsuccessful, then I unsuccessfully attempted to close the door. Finally, I had the passenger unplug their microphone so that I could establish good communication with ATC. While still dealing with the open door and noise I heard ATC tell me to fly a heading direct to my destination of ZZZ1 and cleared into the Bravo, which I read back, and then I turned direct to ZZZ1 at 3,000 feet. After unplugging the front passenger's microphone, and reorienting myself to the aircraft's position the passenger/pilot riding in the back commented that I was inside the Class Bravo at 3,000 feet, when the floor of the Bravo was 2,000 feet at our current location. I replied that while we were attempting to close the door we were vectored on current heading of 145 and cleared into the Bravo. The pilot/passenger replied that he heard the assigned heading from ATC, but did not hear us cleared into the Bravo. Contributing factors: 1) Distraction from cabin door popping open in flight.2) Distraction/impaired communication related to wind noise.3) Distraction related to trying to close the door in order to quiet the wind noise.4) Distraction related to trying to instruct the front seat passenger on how to close the door.5) Distraction from trying to close the door myself when the front passenger was unable to do so after two attempts.Corrective Actions:1) Unplugging the passenger's microphone2) I told ATC that I wished to descend to 1,500 feet, which would keep us below the floor of the Bravo, and began my descent.My perception was that as PIC I had to 'fix' the problem myself, either through instructing a passenger, or by physically manipulating the door, when in reality, the only action that needed to be taken was simply having the passenger unplug his microphone. I exhibited poor judgment in struggling to close the door. I did so in order to reestablish good communications, but I allowed the process to distract me. The simplest, and quicker solution would have been to immodestly tell the front seat passenger to unplug his microphone. This would have saved time, confusion, and extra radio calls, as well as prevented a distraction in the cockpit. Factors affecting the quality of human performance:1) Being startled by the open door and noise.2) Failing to seek out the simplest solution.3) Possible affects of mild fatigue affecting the ability to problem solve quickly (it was the end of a long day).
ASRS:1798832.s: The pilot of a Bonanza VFR flight reported that a cabin door opening in flight caused wind noise and distraction, leading to a missed clearance into Class Bravo airspace. The pilot attributed the incident to poor judgment in attempting to close the door instead of immediately unplugging the passenger's microphone to restore communication.

ASRS:1798844.n: AIRCRAFT 1 was in the downwind. I decided I was going to turn my traffic on to base leg above my traffic to the parallel runway. AIRCRAFT 2 was downwind ahead of AIRCRAFT 1 descending to 7000 feet. I vectored them to join final, no clearance to use altitude leaving. AIRCRAFT 3 was straight in to the parallel runway. I based AIRCRAFT 1 the first time with the wrong call sign XXX , no response. AIRCRAFT 3 and AIRCRAFT 1 were head to head at same altitude with 8 miles of separation. I transmitted three additional times for AIRCRAFT 1 feet twice no response before 'say again' and finally got a read back. AIRCRAFT 1 had divergence with AIRCRAFT 3 by about 1/2 mile. I shipped AIRCRAFT 2 to turn heading 050, more panicked each time, finally got a response. Told AIRCRAFT 3 to expedite with a speed restriction, not realizing I had not cleared them for an approach. They said nothing because [of] my near miss seconds before. Local Control called and asked if they were landing, I said I thought they were cleared. AIRCRAFT 2 went around because of this mistake.This was a tight hole to get into. I pushed to get in it because without, AIRCRAFT 1 would have flown 10 more miles. If pilots would have listened, this would be a non-event, but I instead was panicked and forgot to clear AIRCRAFT 2 I feel terrible for the go around, and scared that I barely had separation, head to head, between two aircraft. I think I will be much more hesitant to attempt to get general aviation aircraft their preferred runway. Just a few minutes before this, I made another general aviation land on a different runway because I deemed it not worth the risk. It's not that I don't have cutoffs, in fact, I'm less aggressive than a lot of my coworkers. This exact situation has been completed without incident numerous times by myself and others. Plain and simple, this happened because the pilots didn't hear and then I allowed a distraction to make me forget to clear AIRCRAFT 2. That being said, at least for a while I won't be accommodating general aviation aircraft quite as much. That situation could have been much, much worse and that's going to be playing in my head for quite some time.
ASRS:1798844.s: An air traffic controller vectored three aircraft, causing a head-to-head near miss between Aircraft 1 and 3 due to radio communication failures and a missed approach clearance for Aircraft 3. The controller's distraction led to Aircraft 2 executing a go-around, with the incident attributed to pilot non-response and the controller forgetting to issue a clearance.

ASRS:1798849.n: Busy traffic, bad rides, frequency congestion, then GPS jamming. I asked the Supervisor to lower the sector traffic numbers to reflect volume and complexity. Supervisor called Traffic Management Unit and they didn't lower the sector traffic numbers. Aircraft are greatly affected by the GPS jamming and its not taken seriously by management, we've been told we can't ask to stop jamming and to just put everyone on headings. Limit the length and what time of the day that facilities can GPS jam and have it taken seriously when we call and ask them to stop.
ASRS:1798849.s: Air traffic controllers reported that GPS jamming, combined with high traffic and frequency congestion, severely affected aircraft operations. Management refused to lower sector traffic numbers or stop the jamming, instructing controllers to simply assign headings instead.

ASRS:1798850.n: Aircraft X was on heading direct to ZZZ [VOR] at 3,000 feet and cleared for a visual approach, Aircraft Y was on the [Runway] XXR Localizer for ZZZ [Airport] and descending to 3,000 feet. Conflict alert activated and I noticed Aircraft X turned east directly towards Aircraft Y. I turned Aircraft Y to a 090 heading to avoid. This incident occurred because Sector 1 and Sector 2 and Finals where combined with too much volume to safely run the amount of traffic at the time. At the time we had no one on break do to having the Special Flight Rules Area (SFRA) opened and reduced staffing levels for COVID. We should have flexibility to close SFRA and open a radar position that would alleviate sectors being overloaded.
ASRS:1798850.s: An air traffic controller managed a conflict between Aircraft X on a visual approach and Aircraft Y on the localizer at 3,000 feet by turning Aircraft Y to heading 090. The controller attributed the incident to combined sectors, high traffic volume, and reduced staffing due to an open Special Flight Rules Area and COVID-19.

ASRS:1798851.n: I was working east flow North Tower Ground/CIC. The main Tower was intermittently departing Runway XC, so I was giving aircraft shortcuts to get to their gate more quickly. I noticed that a departure Aircraft X was taxiing to XC, so I decided to give the next aircraft (Aircraft Y) a hold short at the taxiway (north) parallel taxiway prior to the runway (Taxiway 4), just as an extra precaution. However, I inadvertently said the taxiway name that was the south parallel to XC (Taxiway 5), and did not catch my error. I switched the aircraft to the XC Local Controller's frequency. They had rolled their departure (Aircraft X), and Aircraft Y continued to taxi past the hold bars of XC before they stopped. I did not clear the aircraft to cross Runway XC, nor did the other Controller. Despite my mistake in issuing the incorrect taxiway name, I do not believe anything but the phrase 'Cross Runway ##' gives them the clearance to cross a runway. I, and most other controllers are questioned frequently about runway crossings or unclear taxi instructions. The taxi instruction I gave this aircraft made no sense, because to execute it, they would have needed clearance to cross Runway XC. I made an error by using the wrong taxiway name, but there was no accompanying runway crossing given.I don't know, as I was trying to be extra safe by holding an aircraft at a point further from the runway since there was a departure, as opposed to at the runway. I suppose next time I will just have them hold short of the runway, instead of a taxiway, just so there is no confusion or possibility of mis-stating a taxiway name whatsoever. Additionally, I think that the drop in traffic due to COVID may have played a role. Pilots may have not been to ZZZ since Runway XC was under construction, and they were able to cross it at will before there were proper pavement markings. There are proper markings now, but possibly expectation bias that they were previously able to taxi in this manner played a part.
ASRS:1798851.s: A North Tower Ground controller inadvertently issued an incorrect taxiway name to Aircraft Y while holding it short of Runway XC due to a departing Aircraft X. Aircraft Y taxied past the runway hold bars before stopping, though the controller asserts no runway crossing clearance was given.

ASRS:1798864.n: Preparing for departure, the Agent informed the A-Flight Attendant (FA) there would probably be an issue with a male passenger traveling with two children over the age of two with onboard mask compliance. I contacted Dispatch who patched in the Supervisor for clarification on how to handle the situation. The passenger knew the rules well enough to know his compliance was required to get the aircraft in the air, but once we were airborne, he and his children removed their masks. The A-FA called the cockpit shortly after reaching our cruise altitude to inform me that this individual and children were not complying with the onboard mask mandate issued by the Federal Government, and that this individual had become rude and hostile when reminded that he was required to comply with the federal mandate.The A-FA also reported that children were not well behaved and were disrupting the nearby passengers. The A-FA reported that while asking this individual to wear a mask and control his children, one of the children was banging his head into the tray table of the seat back in front of the child. The FA said he touched the child's arm and said, 'You can't do that'. I notified Dispatch through ACARS of the events and set up the appropriate response team to meet the aircraft. I was kept informed of the actions of the individual for the remainder of the flight. As far as I know, the individual and children were not compliant with the mask requirement for the majority of the flight. I did talk to one of the passengers who witnessed the events. The passenger said the FA acted professionally and that the individual with his children was out of control.This situation put a significant amount of the crew's attention on this passenger and his children. I believe the event could have been prevented with better policies evolved to handle our current social environment. Prior to departure the person was identified as a problem, but the Agent was obviously reluctant to remove him from the flight. We clearly have a mandate from the Federal Government to wear masks at the airports and on flights. This person was NOT compliant at the airport waiting for the inbound aircraft. He was then boarded onto the aircraft to be handled by the flight crew.
ASRS:1798864.s: The flight crew encountered a male passenger and his two children who refused to wear masks and disrupted the cabin during cruise. The pilot notified Dispatch and arranged for a response team, noting the passenger was allowed to board despite pre-flight non-compliance.

ASRS:1798865.n: The 10-9 diagram shows a displaced threshold. The 10-9a page does not show a distance under the threshold box. This is needed for the Landing Zone calculation.
ASRS:1798865.s: A pilot reported that the 10-9 diagram displayed a displaced threshold, but the 10-9a page lacked the required distance under the threshold box. This missing data prevented the calculation of the Landing Zone.

ASRS:1798873.n: All preflight items complete INCLUDING Main Electric STAB TRIM CUTOUT switch with normal results. Student Captain was Pilot flying for this leg. Shortly after Takeoff the PF commented that his electric trim switch was not working and asked me to try mine, which also did not work. I asked him if the elevator was working and he replied that it was and felt normal. We asked ATC to level off at 12,000 ft to work on a flight control issue and was approved. We did not ask for priority handling at this time...we engaged the A Autopilot successfully but shortly after the 'STAB OUT OF TRIM' light came on. As we began to look up the appropriate Non-normal, the PF disengaged the autopilot and tried to manually trim the stabilizer. Although he was successful it looked like it was difficult to rotate so I asked to give it a shot to feel the force required to rotate. The force required to rotate was abnormally high but did provide results and we were flying a trimmed aircraft at 240 knots. By now I was considering that a Jammed Flight Control (the stabilizer in this case) was the source of our STAB OUT OF TRIM problem. So the first checklist we addressed was the Jammed or Restricted Flight Controls Non-normal and also the Jammed or Restricted Flight Controls procedure (the script/expanded explanation). Around this time we requested priority handling with ATC because checklist called for landing at nearest suitable airport. We were hoping that we might get electric trim back when moving STAB TRIM switch on pedestal to OVERRIDE. Did not happen. Called Dispatch with Maintenance Control on the line hoping for some systems expertise. Ended call with where we started. We began to discuss possible value of running STAB OUT OF TRIM checklist. We did. But before doing so we noted the hazard of running multiple checklists and capped our STAB TRIM OVERRIDE switch to normal. The Jammed Flight Control non normal resulted in moving both STAB TRIM switches to CUTOUT but also called for landing at nearest suitable with Flaps 15. About this time we got on radio again with Maintenance Control, Dispatch and also the Flight Operations. Our hope was that Flight Operations might be able to get a Hydraulics of Flight Controls Maintenance expert on with us. We discussed both checklists and Flight Operations talked about the potential effect of slower speeds. This call ended with general consensus we were on the best track and we discussed whether to land sooner or burn down to below Max landing weight. Because we felt the aircraft was stable and our condition was not likely to get worse we chose to burn fuel. I talked to PF and told him it would be prudent for me to do landing since that would be his first one from left seat in aircraft. We briefed our arrival plan which included our trim plan as we reduced airspeed and extended gear and flaps. As we descended and slowed we reminded ATC of need for priority handling equipment. Only significant thing to report was that by the time we had fully configured and slowed to final approach speed it was extremely difficult to trim manually. In fact, with one pilot exerting maximum effort, you could maybe get the manual strection about a quarter turn. All of this led us to believe that the Stabilizer was DEFINITELY jammed. Landed uneventfully, had equipment check us out then taxied to gate. Flight Attendants were given TEST brief and told there was no need to prepare for evacuation. All systems checked ok at gate, but after rotation we discovered our electric stabilizer trim was inop. The aircraft was controllable, but required moderate yoke pressure.We got vectors over the water and stopped our climb at 12,000. We engaged the autopilot momentarily, but the Stab out of Trim light led us to complete that non-normal checklist.We used the Manual Trim Procedure, but felt the force required was excessive, and the trim wheel was not rotating freely.Dispatch contacted and priority handling requested. We completed the Jammed Flight Control and the Stab Trim Inop checklists, both which call for Flaps 15 landing.After again contacting Dispatch, Maintenance Control, and Flight Operations, we planned to divert back to ZZZ.We burned down to max landing weight and landed uneventfully.
ASRS:1798873.s: The Student Captain and First Officer experienced inoperative electric stabilizer trim shortly after takeoff, leading to a "STAB OUT OF TRIM" light and excessive manual trim forces. They completed Jammed Flight Control checklists, diverted to the nearest airport, and landed safely with Flaps 15 after confirming the stabilizer was jammed.

ASRS:1798875.n: On taxi in an airline baggage truck and trolly drove right in front of us moving from our left to right, causing the Captain to brake so as not to have a ground incident. While the driver was driving quite fast, he made eye contact with us and sped through the stop line where we had expected him to stop. While impact would most likely not have occurred, it would have been uncomfortably close and did require us to brake to avoid a conflict.
ASRS:1798875.s: During taxi, an airline baggage truck and trolley drove rapidly across the aircraft's path from left to right, crossing a stop line despite eye contact. The Captain braked to avoid a close ground conflict, though no impact occurred.

ASRS:1798879.n: Landed and turned off at a high-speed taxiway. On first contact with Ground Control just clear of the runway while slowing we were instructed to '... to wait for a Follow Me car.' Just beginning the right turn from, the reserve pilot loudly called out 'car!' I quickly stopped and at that point saw a car, which, apparently, was to be our Follow Me car, speed into my view estimated speed 30 to 40 mph, from the left in front of us northbound on the centerline of the taxiway. The Follow Me car then slowed and we followed it to the pad. No further incident.
ASRS:1798879.s: After landing and turning onto a high-speed taxiway, the crew stopped when a reserve pilot spotted a Follow Me car approaching at 30–40 mph from the left. The car slowed, allowing the aircraft to follow it safely to the pad with no further incident.

ASRS:1798887.n: I was a passenger on a flight to Spokane. I was sitting in seat X. I was traveling with my spouse who was seated on the opposite side of the aircraft in seat Y. The flight enroute was uneventful. On descent, we were again in VMC conditions. A visual approach would be likely as there were no clouds between our position and the airport. The active runway was 21. As an airline pilot I have done the visual arrival into GEG Runway 21 many times from the south and am aware of the several high towers that are southeast of the airport and directly in line with the arrival into Spokane. Two of the towers are nearly 950 high, so this is a significant threat to arrival aircraft, especially if pilots are heads down and not noticing the towers. If pilots are only focused on clearing the terrain by 1,000 ft. that will clearly put the aircraft in near contact with one of these two towers since the towers themselves are nearly 1,000 ft. above ground. Having been a commuter for much of my career, I have flown over these towers as a passenger no less than 100 times. I know what the normal proximity is to those towers should be and look like from both within the cabin and flight deck on this visual approach. From my vantage point in seat 2A, our vertical proximity to the towers southeast of GEG was not normal and appeared to be dangerously close. We appeared to be much lower over the towers than I had ever seen before in nearly two decades of flying into the airport. I was definitely uncomfortable with what I was seeing and even a bit shaken by what appeared to be a 'close call'. Our arrival into Spokane was mostly normal after that event. The landing appeared to be a bit long, perhaps even out of the touchdown, but nothing of great significance. Upon arrival at the gate, my spouse and I deplaned. Once inside the terminal, my spouse asked me 'Did you see that arrival?' I said 'You mean, how close we were to those towers?' My spouse said;'YES! My God I have never seen those towers so close in my life- that wasn't right.' My spouse is also an airline pilot and commutes so he too is a valid witness to what occurred on that flight. We discussed whether or not to say something as we understand that events can happen from time to time. Because of the seriousness of what we saw, we felt it was appropriate to contact ALPA in an effort to highlight this real threat to all airlines and general aviation regarding the visual arrival into GEG. Over the years I have seen certain deviations from standard that were noteworthy but nothing that alarmed me the way this did. My hope is that additional training can be provided to all airline pilots regarding the towers in proximity to GEG. Perhaps a greater emphasis on arrival procedures. Maybe even a bigger emphasis on the Jeppesen chart itself. I also think the arrival gate coming into GEG from the south should not be allowed over the towers, either VMC or IMC. They are a threat in either scenario. Lastly, a possible change to ATC protocol would be for Approach to require visual confirmation of the towers to arriving aircraft when a visual approach is expected.
ASRS:1798887.s: Two airline pilots, seated as passengers on a flight descending for a visual approach to Spokane (GEG) Runway 21, reported the aircraft flew dangerously close to two 950-foot towers southeast of the airport. The crew observed an abnormally low vertical proximity to the towers, which they attributed to a lack of adherence to standard arrival procedures and insufficient visual confirmation.

ASRS:1798937.n: Runway 16L, the controls were transferred to me by my First Officer (FO).Oakland Center handed us off to Reno Approach, on initial contact we were advised to report the field insight for the visual approach to 16L. After calling the field in sight, I realized that we were a bit high and closer to the field than I had anticipated. Calling for gear down, my first officer called 'speed check I realized that with speed brakes extended, and all efforts to slow the airplane, with a quartering tailwind, my efforts were futile. Still descending and approaching position WORTH on the RNAV approach we were handed over to tower who cleared us for landing on Runway 16L. Being unstabilized at this time and receiving an EGPWS 'TERRAIN TERRAIN' followed by 'PULL UP" my FO and I simultaneously announced "GO AROUND.'We executed the EGPWS escape maneuver and were vectored for another visual approach, followed by an uneventful landing to Runway 16L. Never having flown into the RNO airport, having an FO just off OE (operator experience) and new to the aircraft type, gusty winds, tailwind on initial descent and approach. On landing winds were 260/variable. On arrival at the gate we were told by station personnel other aircraft had also gone around a one diverted. Suggest more emphasis on speed control throughout the descent and approach."
ASRS:1798937.s: The Captain and a new First Officer executed a go-around during a visual approach to Runway 16L at Reno due to an unstabilized descent caused by gusty quartering tailwinds and speed brake extension. After an EGPWS terrain warning, they performed an escape maneuver and landed uneventfully on a subsequent approach.

ASRS:1798953.n: There is a discrepancy in the Jeppesen's 10-9 related to DEN. While the mag variation has shifted, the airfield diagram does not reflect the new magnetic runway headings for the [runway]. The diagram indicates the mag heading as 173/353 for all north/south runways. However, if the info page is selected, the runway headings are 172/352. While the difference is not significant, it is a discrepancy that needs to be corrected to avoid potential flight safety issues. A similar issue exists for the east/west runways. RWY 8/26 is 082/262, but the 10-9 says 083/263, while 7/25 is 082/262, but the 10-9 shows 082/263. Lack of attention to detail. Develop a system at Jeppesen to identify mag variation shifts beyond simply those that require runways to be renumbered.
ASRS:1798953.s: A pilot reported discrepancies in Jeppesen's DEN 10-9 charts where airfield diagrams showed incorrect magnetic runway headings compared to the info page due to unupdated magnetic variation. The reporter attributed this to a lack of attention to detail and recommended Jeppesen develop a system to identify variation shifts beyond runway renumbering requirements.

ASRS:1798962.n: Non standard signage. Abdication by ATC to advise hold short of Runway 9C. Jet runway incursion Runway 22R at Runway 9C.Runway Signage at runway 22R and 9C only indicates Runway 9C. The standard signage should have 27C - 9C. NOTAM the lack of painted holding positions on the runway along with the lack of holding position signage. The Runway 9C sign adjacent Runway 22R is a sign designated by the Aeronautical Information Manual to be a starting position sign. That signage along with the lack of markings fails to designate the runway intersection. In pavement markings and 'WIG WAGS' could have aided in the prevention of this event.
ASRS:1798962.s: A pilot reported a jet runway incursion at Runway 22R and 9C caused by non-standard signage and ATC failure to advise holding short. The reporter attributed the event to missing holding position markings and signs that failed to designate the runway intersection.

ASRS:1798971.n: On final approach into ZZZ I was Pilot Flying. After calling for gear down we received a BRK RH FAULT advisory message. We finished configuring for landing and I called for the Quick Reference Handbook(QRH). The QRH procedure had us run the 'Landing Gear/Brake malfunction landing checklist'. At this point I called for a go around so we may accomplish the necessary items and let ATC know. After the go around I made a PA advising the passengers we had a faulty brake indication and had to go-around to run the checklist. I spoke to the Flight Attendants and told them I would update them, shortly but we should be landing in the next 5 to 10 minutes. Immediately after, I sent a free text to Dispatch advising them we had a brake fault and were executing a go around and running the procedure. I do not recall receiving a response from Dispatch.The First Officer completed the procedure as I prepared the aircraft for landing. The procedure called for a flaps full landing and longer roll out. At this point I decided it would be best to [receive priority from ATC] and have the fire equipment standing by as this was a brake issue which would cause asymmetric braking. I also requested ATC to switch our landing runway to a runway that was longer than our planned runway. After the procedure was complete I called the Flight Attendants and told them we had [an urgent situation], we will be landing in 5 minutes, expect emergency equipment and we will not be bracing. I then made another PA to let our passengers now we had an issue with one of our brakes and out of an abundance of caution I have requested the airport to deploy its safety equipment but I did expect the landing to be normal with an extended roll out. My voice remained calm and I made no mention of an emergency during the PA. At this point ATC vectored us to final and we configured and ran the appropriate landing checklist. We touched down and I used reverse thrust and very gently applied brakes.I immediately felt the right hand brake was not biting. I had to mainly use the left brake with right rudder to maintain centerline. Once the plane slowed below 60 knots I was able to slow with both brakes and used the tiller for directional control. The right brake was working but did not feel as effective. We exited the runway and were able to taxi normal, albeit at a slow speed. At this point I noticed on the STATUS page the right outboard brake temperature did not rise leading to the conclusion that it was indeed that brake which had failed. I elected to taxi with both engines to reduce asymmetric thrust. Parking at the gate was normal. I entered the discrepancy in the logbook, called Maintenance and headed to our overnight.In hindsight I do believe [advising ATC] was the right call even if the issue did not end up being serious. I was worried about asymmetric braking and was also not sure if the brake had failed released or with full pressure. I felt it was best to declare and have the trucks standing by and not need them. The only thing I would have done differently would have been to call Dispatch before talking to Maintenance. After discussing the event with the company it seems Dispatch was not aware of the issue until after the plane arrived at the gate. I usually call them first when we have maintenance issues but In this case since the flight was terminating I figured it would be best to go directly to Maintenance but I can see how the lack of communication can cause confusion with Dispatch.
ASRS:1798971.s: The Pilot Flying executed a go-around on final approach into ZZZ after receiving a right brake fault advisory. Following the QRH checklist, the crew landed with an extended rollout, using asymmetric braking to maintain centerline, and taxied to the gate with the right outboard brake confirmed inoperative.

ASRS:1799039.n: Due to the pandemic and the reduction in flight and passenger activity, many piers were closed. This led to packing more flights into fewer piers, while the passenger volume was low this did not have an effect on safety. The pier worker was able to work more flights simultaneously with a very low baggage volume.Many employees have expressed concerns to management and to their labor leaders.Today, the same piers are closed while the open piers are still working multiple flights and the baggage and passenger counts increasing. This is where the safety concern develops, there is limited space in the piers and the worker are forced to place bags on the ground waiting for future equipment to be placed in the pier. The main issue is that international destinations (bags) come down in advance of the ETD and other heavy volume flights cause the same hazard. The walking and working floor space is negligible. We have identified it as a serious tripping hazard. The majority of work place injuries come from 'Slips, Trips and Falls.' This has been identified and brought to operations leadership, no actions have taken place.Reopen closed piers and space out the work, as work volume has increased.
ASRS:1799039.s: Pier workers reported a serious tripping hazard caused by placing bags on the ground due to limited floor space in consolidated piers as passenger and baggage volumes increased. Despite identifying this risk to operations leadership, no corrective actions have been taken to reopen closed piers or space out the work.

ASRS:1799047.n: I was told to cross ZZZZZ at or above 12,300 feet and I was cleared for the RNAV (GPS) Approach. As I was descending past ZZZZZ I set my altitude at 10,000 feet. I should have set 11,800 feet per the approach chart, which is the altitude between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1. After ZZZZZ1 it is 10,000 feet until ZZZZZ2. About 10 to 15 miles from ZZZZZ1, Approach asked me to report ZZZZZ1. This seemed like an odd request, so I looked at the chart to make sure where ZZZZZ1 was and realized the error in altitude. As I started to initiate a climb, the TAWS (Terrain Alert Warning) activated and I got the terrain warning. The rest of the approach was normal after that.I think that I had 11,800 [ft.] set before ZZZZZ because the altitude I was descending from and my rate of descent was going to have me cross ZZZZZ well above 12,300 [ft.]. Then after crossing ZZZZZ I set 10,000 [ft.] because I was mentally one step ahead of where I actually was. While I was being proactive and efficient, I did not double check and confirm where I was on the approach. While I wasn't fatigued or distracted, I think complacency played a role due to the nice weather and the length of the flight.
ASRS:1799047.s: The pilot descended below the required 11,800 feet between waypoints ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 during an RNAV (GPS) approach, triggering a TAWS terrain warning. The pilot attributed the error to complacency and mentally anticipating the next altitude restriction without verifying the chart.

ASRS:1799051.n: While positioned on the ramp at FBO in ZZZ the aircraft I was operating came in contact with a parked aircraft.At brake release and at idle power I asked the pilot in the right seat if we had clearance from the winglet of the aircraft on our left which was on a tug. The pilot not flying told me that we had clearance and I released the brakes and rolled forward. The pilot not flying then told me to stop and I immediately applied brake pressure. My aircraft didn't move with the exception of the forward lurch from the brakes. I set the parking brake and then shut down both engines.I exited the aircraft and walked around to the right wing and observed the winglets of both aircraft in apparent contact with each other. Sometime later after the tugged aircraft was pushed back we observed no damage to my aircraft and that was further supported by four independent maintenance technicians and inspectors. There was however damage present to the Challenger that was still on the tug. The crew, including dispatch, notified the FBO of our departure time, and request to be online, in the several days leading up to our departure.Upon arrival, we requested the aircraft be fueled. Upon passenger arrival, the marshaller and wing walker escorted the passengers to our plane, they then subsequently left without informing the crew. We then proceeded to start engines normally, and contacted ground for our taxi clearance.Upon block out, the PIC asked if our right wingtip was clear of obstacles. As I looked up I determined there was not enough room for wing tip clearance, and called for an immediate left turn. The PIC then applied brakes, but it was too late and we made contact with a Challenger, wingtip to wingtip. Maintenance personnel inspected our plane and determined there was no damage, and a logbook entry was made.
ASRS:1799051.s: The flight crew operating a Challenger on the ramp at FBO ZZZ contacted a parked Challenger on a tug while taxiing after the pilot not flying incorrectly confirmed winglet clearance. Although the reporting aircraft sustained no damage, the parked Challenger was damaged, and the incident occurred after ground personnel left without informing the crew.

ASRS:1799059.n: We did night currency at our home airport. There was one Controller for Clearance [Delivery], Ground, and Tower. It was pretty busy with military aircraft doing night landings and airliners coming in. I had to ask the Controller to clear us to land each time. Usually they say report downwind or base and then will clear us to land or have us extend after we report. He was probably overwhelmed because he was constantly talking while working three frequencies. I wanted to report just in case it was unclear at any point if we were actually clear to land. The second landing he sounded annoyed when I asked if we were cleared to land - I had to ask because he had not cleared us. It didn't help that we were going 150 knots over the ground because of the 40 knot tail wind. It would help if there were separate people working Ground and Tower.
ASRS:1799059.s: A pilot conducting night currency landings reported that a single controller managing Delivery, Ground, and Tower frequencies failed to issue landing clearances, likely due to being overwhelmed. The situation was exacerbated by a 40-knot tailwind causing high ground speeds, leading to controller annoyance when the pilot requested clarification.

ASRS:1799076.n: Chain of events. ZZZ Ground cleared me to taxi from FBO. 'Taxi to Runway XX via Taxiway 1, Taxiway 2, Taxiway 3, cross Runway XY.' On Taxiway 3, approaching Runway YX/XY, I was looking down at my checklist, when I looked up, I was startled to see a regional jet on relatively short (1 mile?) final for Runway YX. After I crossed XY/XY, the regional jet landed without incident.Human Performance Considerations. First, when taxiing, one needs to be focused outside the airplane. When approaching a runway, slow to look for landing/departing traffic. If I had seen the regional jet earlier, I may have either increased taxi speed, determined no speed change was required or called Ground and advised that I would wait for landing traffic.With the pandemic, until recently, commercial air travel has been significantly reduced. Tower personnel may have been reduced as well. I believe one Controller was handling Ground and Tower. With activity picking up, ATC needs to be staffed appropriately as well.
ASRS:1799076.s: The pilot, while taxiing to Runway XX, looked down at a checklist and nearly missed a regional jet on final approach for Runway YX. The pilot attributed the near miss to distraction and noted that a single controller was likely handling both Ground and Tower duties.

ASRS:1799095.n: Before entering Runway XX I announced my intentions to depart and leave the area on a southeast heading. After my rollout about 400 feet down the runway I heard a helicopter pilot report his departure from the field left of Runway XX. He would be heading south. When I was airborne and climbing out I looked to my left and saw said helicopter about 100-150 feet off my left wing. I performed a hard climb and continued on runway heading until clear of the other aircraft.
ASRS:1799095.s: A fixed-wing pilot departing Runway XX encountered a helicopter departing left of the runway while climbing out. The helicopter was observed 100–150 feet off the pilot's left wing, prompting a hard climb to clear the other aircraft.

ASRS:1799097.n: Aircraft requested an RNAV Approach. The Radar Controller cleared the aircraft direct to the Initial Approach Fix. The route was updated in the computer to reflect. Aircraft was level at 13,000 feet and told to cross the Initial Approach Fix at 13,000 [ft.], cleared RNAV Approach. I was talking with the Radar Controller immediately before saying this was a common error point where aircraft descend below the 12,100 [ft.] MEA (Minimum Enroute Altitude) to the intermediate fix. We observed the aircraft cross the Initial Approach Fix and begin descending. The Radar Controller drew a circle around the next fix for reference. When I came back around on my scan I observed the aircraft already below the MEA of 12,100 feet. I do not recall the exact altitude but it was below 12,000 feet. I brought this to the attention of the Radar Controller. Immediately they transmitted 'Aircraft X WHAT ARE YOU DOING?...' The Radar Controller told the airplane they were below the 12,100 [ft.] MEA. The pilot immediately asked for a visual approach and the Radar Controller asked if they had the field in sight. Upon the affirmative response, the visual approach clearance was issued. I inbounded the aircraft to the Tower and a brasher statement was issued. A low altitude safety alert was never issued.First action should have been to issue a low altitude alert and verify they have surrounding terrain in sight. This approach has had multiple MEA violations and we have been briefed that issuing safety alerts is utmost priority. I should have told the Radar Controller to issue the alert but they responded quickly to the aircraft asking 'what are you doing?' and got them cleared for a visual approach. Perhaps the placement of the MEA step downs is not as apparent as required on the approach plate. The other transitions have both caused issues before on this approach.
ASRS:1799097.s: An air traffic controller observed an aircraft descend below the 12,100-foot MEA during an RNAV approach after crossing the Initial Approach Fix. The controller verbally alerted the pilot, who requested and received a visual approach clearance, though the reporter noted a low altitude safety alert was not issued.

ASRS:1799099.n: I was working a fairly busy session at the beginning of my mid shift. Aircraft X checked on to the NE of ZZZ and was given a heading of 280 and descended to 80, which they read back correctly. Aircraft Y was being vectored from the SW of ZZZ and was descended to 60, which they read back correctly. A little while after descending Aircraft Y I noticed that Aircraft X was at 60 just about to exit the NW corner of the 65 MVA entering the 60 MVA. When I realized that Aircraft X was at the unexpected altitude, there was not enough time to issue a safety alert before they entered the 60 MVA (which was fine for their current altitude).I talked to the pilot of Aircraft X and they indicated that they were sure that they had read back to descend to 60. I reviewed the incident multiple times and only heard Aircraft Y confirm that they were descending to 60. However, both aircraft were on separate frequencies and there could have been a 'stepped on issue' that caused Aircraft X's incorrect read back to not get through to me.There are a couple of things I will work on in the future:- The call signs of Aircraft X and Aircraft Y were similar enough that I should have informed them, that they were both on separate frequencies. I will work on making that a priority in the future.- Aircraft X descended 2,000 feet before I realized the deviation. I was fairly tired after a long work week and think under normal circumstances my scan would have caught the deviation. I should have recognized I was not operating at 100% and asked for an extra set of eyes from the ZZZ [TRACON] Controller. In the future I will work on recognizing this and ask for help.- I don't normally put in assigned altitudes on IFR aircraft data blocks but after this incident I will probably start. Keeping up with strip marking can be difficult when busy and take your eyes away from the scope. Maybe having the altitude in the data block may have helped me recognize Aircraft X was descending past their assigned altitude.- I don't normally come in for XA:15 mid shifts (Usually start at XC:15 or XB:15) and should have asked to work a slower position knowing I was fatigued and on my 6th day.From a technology standpoint there are a couple of issues:- I didn't ever see the Low Altitude (LA) alert go off when I reviewed the falcon replay. The LA indication would have definitely got my attention to issue a safety alert. In my experience working and training it seems like it rarely goes off when it is actually needed. That alert system needs to be revamped, it could be a very useful and a life saving tool!- I wish we could somehow keep everyone on one frequency when we are combined. I think there may have been some kind of 'stepped on' issue with this situation, that one frequency may have helped with.Our staffing has been really bad lately and controllers including myself have been working lots of overtime since last fall. I know management doesn't have many options to alleviate the problem and I don't mind helping out with working overtime. However, here are some recommendations that might help:- We have X supervisors that are certified and can work positions. With COVID vaccines going on they should absolutely be used as staffing until we get people through vaccines and some stability in our staffing. I feel like having well rested controllers that are working less overtime is way more beneficial to safety, then having a stand-alone supervisor in the operation as often possible. Once we get out of our current staffing slump, having stand-alone supervision is a great idea! However, it is currently NOT A GOOD use of our resources.- Plan ahead and be proactive. The entire facility was aware over a month ago that controllers were going to be eligible for COVID vaccines in March. However, there was nothing done to try and stay ahead of all the sick hits that we're going to be happening. There could have been COVID vaccine signup sheets back in January or February to find out who wanted it right away, who would wait, and who didn't want it at all, then plan the schedule based off of that. In addition, the union put a schedule together well ahead of the vaccine eligibility to help mitigate the problem, but it was not implemented for some reason. As a result of no planning or forward thinking, for the past few weeks staffing has been very unstable. There have been many last minute changes to controllers schedules with extra OT to make things work. This is not a safe way to run things and could have been avoided.
ASRS:1799099.s: An air traffic controller vectored Aircraft X and Y near ZZZ, but Aircraft X descended to 60 instead of the assigned 80, likely due to a misheard clearance or radio interference. The controller attributed the missed deviation to fatigue, staffing shortages, and a failure of the Low Altitude alert system.

ASRS:1799103.n: I was conducting training. Aircraft X was level at 12,000 feet. The trainee noticed Aircraft X was about to enter into a higher Minimum IFR Altitude (MIA) due to Minimum Safe Altitude Warning (MSAW) alert. Unfortunately a minute passed before he noticed due to handling a new VFR flight following on the other side of the scope. At the time I was on the information display looking up an approach plate. The nearest display was not configured for use so I was with my back to the scope on an adjacent sector. My trainee issued a 15 degree turn and climb to 13,000 feet and then issued a low altitude alert. The pilot unfortunately did not appear to begin his turn or climb for approximately 40 seconds. The turn is first seen on the radar right before the aircraft enters the 12,700 foot MIA at 12,100 feet and the trainee turned the aircraft an additional 30 degrees (45 total degrees) and the pilot complied immediately. Separation from the MIA was reestablished.With the help of the radar replay we identified that when the training team had pulled up the route to check the MIAs, the route line obscured the '27' of 127 and unfortunately we didn't notice and we both individually believed the route and altitude were safe. If either one of us had immediately observed the MSAW or if the pilot turned and climbed in a timely manner instead of delaying, I believe the aircraft wouldn't have entered the higher terrain box. As an aside, the event occurred before a position relief briefing had begun, but the relieving Controller was plugged into the position. I will use this as a reminder to carefully check routes for minimum safe altitudes and keep in mind that the route line can cover the text. I will and remind my CPCIT to use the phraseology 'immediately' for pressing clearances. I will remain vigilant, especially during times when I am training.
ASRS:1799103.s: An Air Traffic Controller and trainee issued a climb to 13,000 feet after a delayed MSAW alert caused Aircraft X to enter a higher Minimum IFR Altitude. The incident resulted from a route line obscuring the altitude text on the display and a 40-second pilot delay in complying with the clearance.

ASRS:1799109.n: On Date, ZZZ [TRACON] experienced a positive COVID-19 test that required facility cleaning. This cleaning required the facility to shut down radar operations, known as an ATC Zero event. ZZZ ARTCC contingency plan would then be put into place. Earlier discussions before I arrived at work discussed the options of how to work the ZZZ [TRACON] airspace. ZZZ [ARTCC] was advised that ZZZ [TRACON] would be working radar in the Tower, and the option of ZZZ [ARTCC] assuming the airspace did not become an option. The contingency plan states that ZZZ [ARTCC] clear the airspace and hold aircraft, not assume the airspace. [A telecom was] convened to discuss the plans for the closing and cleaning of ZZZ [TRACON]. It was clear to me and those listening at ZZZ [ARTCC] that the decision had been made for ZZZ [ARTCC] to take control of the airspace and continue operations at ZZZ [TRACON]. After the call, ZZZ [ARTCC] was given an hour to work through any issues and develop a plan to accomplish the mission. In conversations with the ATM, I advised him of what the Contingency plan stated, and even had a copy of the plan [sent] to him so he could read it. I also advised him we were creating a plan to work the airspace and we would be ready to go for the XC:00 deadline. I immediately brought together TMU, Tech OPs, FDCS, ZZZ [TRACON] ATM and area X staff to put a plan together to carry out the continuation of ATC services into and out of ZZZ [TRACON]. NOTAM was published closing the ZZZ [TRACON] airspace, TMU had instituted an X hour ground stop to slow the initial volume, I conferred the command center the request and they agreed and put in the ground stop. The plan was delayed for about XX minutes due to traffic volume at ZZZ [TRACON], and we assumed the airspace about XC:XX pm. I sat in the area during the entire event, just to ensure what procedures we had developed were followed. I also ensured correct phraseology was used concerning arrival traffic being cleared on the ILS [Runway] XXR. Overall, the professionalism of all involved provided for an orderly outcome of the event. We controlled the airspace for a little over an hour until the cleaning was complete. My only concern was that we did not follow published procedures during an ATC Zero event. I am filling this out today because I just received a call from another person at ZZZ [Center] concerned that I did not follow proper procedures concerning the ATC Zero event. I did not fill one out that night because I believed I was acting with approval from my ATM and District to assume the airspace and continue operations at ZZZ [TRACON].We proved that we could operate the airspace in a controlled manner for short periods. ZZZ [ARTCC] needs to develop basic procedures for all of our underlying 24 hour facilities in the case of an ATC Zero event. The controllers on the floor working the airspace need to have the basic information in front of them as they work through the basic issues during such events. While I know that all contingencies can't be covered, that list would be exhaustive, we could have a strong baseline to follow during a similar events in the future.
ASRS:1799109.s: An Air Traffic Controller at ZZZ ARTCC assumed control of ZZZ TRACON airspace during an ATC Zero event caused by a COVID-19 facility shutdown, deviating from the published contingency plan to clear and hold aircraft. The controller reported that while operations were orderly, the decision to assume airspace was made without following established procedures, highlighting a need for updated baseline guidance.

ASRS:1799118.n: While being radar vectored to the visual final for Runway XX at ZZZ, Approach Control issued a descent to 6,000 feet MSL. We read back the clearance and proceeded to descend to 6,000 feet MSL. The Captain did observe that we seemed closer to some radio Towers on a hill than what would appear normal, but we received no GPWS Alerts. We continued on vectors and flew an uneventful approach and landing. After a call from Tower a few hours later, it was explained that the descent clearance to 6,000 feet was issued to a (other carrier X) whose readback was on a different Approach Control frequency. Our readback to that clearance as Company A (very similar sounding call sign) must have occurred at the same moment as (other carrier's) reply. Since the (other carrier X) aircraft had been on a different approach frequency, we had yet to hear any other communications to or from that aircraft, and ATC had not issued a caution for the similar sounding call signs. Additionally, ATC did not issue a low altitude warning if we had gone below the Minimum Vector Altitude in the sector we were within.When managing multiple frequencies, ATC should ensure that aircraft with similar call signs are alerted to possible miss interpretations. Furthermore, ATC should minimize the use of simulcasting on multiple Approach frequencies and consolidate traffic to one radio frequency. We were being vectored for the visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ from the east. ZZZ Approach Control issued a clearance to 6,000 feet MSL. We were later contacted that the clearance was for (other carrier) X, on another frequency and not for Company A. The clearance apparently took us below the MVA for that sector. The Controller was controlling multiple frequencies (he was busy) and never advised us of similar sounding call signs. We did not receive any terrain cautions from the aircraft or Controller. The subsequent approach and landing were uneventful.Listening during communications is always the most important. Being advised of similar sounding call signs is an important step to help alleviate threats and for Crews to be more vigilant.
ASRS:1799118.s: Company A pilots received a descent clearance to 6,000 feet MSL while being vectored for a visual approach at ZZZ, which was intended for another carrier with a similar call sign. The error occurred due to simultaneous transmissions on different frequencies, taking the aircraft below the Minimum Vector Altitude without triggering GPWS or ATC warnings.

ASRS:1799131.n: After landing at night in ZZZ we taxied as instructed by Ground to a surface designated point. When we arrived, there was an outbound jet taxiing on the south line and another air carrier under tow on the north line. We advised ZZZ Ground of the conflict and they then instructed us to just take the south line after the outbound jet. The First Officer advised me that there was not a ramp frequency when there actually was. We thought we had been cleared in by Ground but by the time I taxied in I felt like something wasn't right due to the congestion on the ramp. I asked again ' Are you sure there isn't a ramp?'. He then found the frequency on the 10-7 after we had entered the ramp area. After parking at gate, I made contact with ramp and relayed our confusion. Contributing factors include, unfamiliar operations at ZZZ. First time operating there in over a year plus first time at the new terminal. New First officer fresh off OE and only my Xth flight segment in a year due to pandemic reductions.
ASRS:1799131.s: The crew experienced confusion while taxiing at night at ZZZ after landing, mistakenly believing no ramp frequency existed. This error, caused by unfamiliarity with the new terminal and a new First Officer, led to entering the ramp area before contacting Ramp Control.

ASRS:1799151.n: After being cleared for a visual approach to Runway XXL in ZZZ we received an EICAS 'E2 OIL LOW PRESS' red master warning message on the EICAS display. I cancelled the red warning and advised my First Officer (FO) to reduce the thrust lever to idle on engine number two. I observed the oil pressure for engine two indicating in the red at about 34 PSI, but fluctuating around the top of the red level, and with occasional fluctuations into the bottom on the green range, and which caused the EICAS warning to extinguish, but then reappear once again triggering another master warning for the same condition about 30 seconds to a minute later. Engine number one was still operating within normal engine parameters (green indications), however. The FO was the pilot flying the aircraft, with the autopilot coupled to the [Runway] XXL ILS. As engine number two was still operating at idle thrust, and as I deemed that there was insufficient time to safely compete the required QRH checklist items during the approach prior to landing, I advised the FO to continue the approach. Therefore, rather than perform a go around so as to provide an adequate amount of time to complete the QRH inflight engine shutdown checklist, I made a call to ZZZ Approach and advised the Controller of the situation - that the aircraft had low oil pressure on engine two and that engine failure was imminent. The Controller queried me if I [needed priority handling]? I replied in the affirmative, and subsequently advised the Controller that the we did not require immediate assistance [for the time being]. The ZZZ Approach controller requested the number of souls on board and approximate fuel. I advised the controller that we had XX passengers and X crew for a total of XX souls on board and that we had XXXX lbs of fuel, and approximately 2 hours fuel (endurance - at single engine burn). ZZZ Approach gave instructions to contact ZZZ Tower, who issued a landing clearance for Runway XXL. I advised the FO to disconnect the autopilot and continue to hand fly the approach to landing with the engine number two at idle thrust. The low oil pressure master warning occurred shortly after the glideslope intercept and normal thrust reduction at an altitude of approximately 10,000 MSL, at around the ZZZZZ fix, on approach to runway XXL. The aircraft configuration at the time of the first EICAS warning was flaps 9, gear up, with a speed of 200 KIAS. As we had already planned to make a normal flaps 22 approach and landing, I elected to continue the approach configure the aircraft for a flaps 22 landing as originally intended. I advised for the aircraft to be slowed to 190 KIAS and the approach to be continued. Landing gear down and flaps 22 was selected at ZZZZZ1 FAP and at which time the before landing items were completed. I then communicated with the flight attendant an abbreviated brief on the CABIN EMER intercom - that we had a low oil pressure indication on engine two, and that we had about 1 minute to go before landing, and to make sure to be seated. A normal landing was successfully carried out, and upon rollout I advised the FO to activate just the engine number one thrust reverser to aid slowing of the aircraft. I took control of the aircraft at the 80 knots and continued to slow the aircraft using moderate braking to a safe exit speed off the runway at the high speed taxiway exit 1. I taxied to a stop just after turning onto Taxiway M. I instructed the FO to advise the tower the we momentarily stopping on Taxiway M to perform checklist items. The tower advised us to contact ZZZ Ground. I then instructed the FO to shutdown engine two and back this up with the QRH and to then perform the after-landing checklist. A number of ZZZ rescue fire service trucks were approaching the aircraft. Cognizant that the close proximity of emergency service vehicles would cause some concern for the passengers, I made a PA announcement to the explaining the situation and that once the personnel hadperformed a visual check for any smoke emanating from the rear of aircraft fuselage, we would continue the taxi to the gate as normal. Once personnel confirmed that there was no visible fire or smoke present we requested to continue the taxi to the gate as normal. We then taxied to the gate as normal with the exception that I elected to not set the parking braking - due to a possible risk of smoke or fire developing, as the brake temperature on the left inboard brake was indicating in the amber caution range - but requested for the ground personnel to chock the wheels instead to give time for the brake temps to cool down. A normal shutdown check was performed and with normal passenger disembarkation. I immediately wrote up the discrepancy in the aircraft logbook and contacted the company dispatch to explain what had occurred and requested to speak with maintenance to discuss the write and the event. I advised Maintenance Control of the discrepancy details and what occurred. Maintenance Control then advised that they would need to place the call on hold while they checked if I needed to be transferred to the Maintenance Duty Manager or to receive a callback from a Maintenance Supervisor. I then performed the aircraft terminating checklist and went outside to inspect the aircraft exterior. I then received a call from a company Maintenance Supervisor to needed some additional information about the event. While on the phone call with maintenance I received a call from someone else in Maintenance (possibly the Duty Manager). As no voicemail or text was left by on my phone, I expected another callback from Maintenance Control, but which did not occur, however.In my view, appropriate decisions and actions were made by all crew members. And given the dynamics of the situation, that these decisions and actions were necessary to mitigate the safety risks, to the passengers, to the aircraft, and in the interests of other relevant aviation stakeholders, and which contributed to a safe resolution and satisfactory outcome. We were cleared for the visual approach to [Runway] XXL, when we received a master warning and EICAS message E2 OIL LOW PRESS. The Captain identified and cancelled the warning and we verified the oil pressure in the red on EICAS as well as checking the oil quantity on the to data page, where we saw only 4 quarts in the number two engine. I was instructed to bring the number two thrust lever to idle to prevent further damage. At this point we were between the IAF and FAF on the XXL around 190 knots with flaps 9. The Captain and I agreed due to the time available before touchdown and severity of the situation to leave the number two engine at idle thrust. The Captain called ATC and advised ATC of our situation, ultimately [requesting priority handling]. The Captain advised ATC of souls on board and remaining fuel onboard, stating we did not need immediate assistance. ATC handed us off to Tower where we got our landing clearance for XXL. The Captain then called the Flight Attendant and gave her a report to prepare for normal landing, advised the situation, gave her time till touchdown, the flight attendant stated cabin was secured. As we neared the FAF I called for gear down and flaps 22 for the final configuration with a landing checklist. We had already briefed to do a flaps 22 landing due to forecasted wind. The Captain had me disconnect the autopilot and hand fly the approach to maintain best control of the aircraft. We performed a normal landing with number two engine at idle thrust, which was successful. At 80 knots, we transferred controls and captain advised me to tell Tower we would need to stop once clear of the taxiway, which I promptly did. ZZZ Tower instructed us to contact Ground and cleared us to stop on the taxiway. The Captain instructed me to shutdown the number two engine, and promptly back it up with the QRH to verify all necessary steps were taken for the E2 OIL LOW PRESS master warning. We completed the QRH items and after landing checklist at this time. Operations vehicles contacted us and the Captain asked them to verify no smoke, fumes, flames etc., coming from the number two engine, which happened to have no indications. We then contacted ground control to taxi into the ramp area. Prior to movement we noticed the left hand inboard brake was in the yellow arc, in which the Captain elected to leave the parking brake released and have the wheels chocked at the gate. After parking, we accomplished the shutdown checklist, deplaned all passengers and cargo. I stepped outside to do the post flight walk around and found the bottom navel covered in oil, therefore verifying the oil leak. After returning to flight deck the captain was on the phone with Maintenance control, writing up the discrepancy, the Maintenance Duty Manager explaining the situation. We completed the terminating checklists to finish. I believe the decisions by the crew and actions performed, were the best course of action for the dynamics of the situation and time frame we worked with.
ASRS:1799151.s: The flight crew received an E2 OIL LOW PRESS warning on engine two during a visual approach to Runway XXL at 10,000 feet. They continued the approach with engine two at idle, landed safely, and shut down the engine on the taxiway after confirming no fire or smoke.

ASRS:1799156.n: Only upon my meeting with the chief pilot was I aware that I had a close range encounter with terrain. We never received any type of warning. The Ground Proximity Warning System (GPWS) did not notify us nor did we get a terrain alert from ATC. A previous report was submitted regarding this flight due to other reasons. I viewed the flight path in question as a go around (not anything to hide). The following is what I recall. We planned and briefed a Localizer Approach. When transferred to Approach we were informed the Localizer Approach was not available. We were left with the RNAV Approach. I requested the First Officer to brief the approach.The RNAV Approach was showing in the FMS. Approach gave us a clearance to a fix, the First Officer responded, but I did not understand the fix. A fix I was expecting to hear was not what I heard. I asked the First Officer to request the fix again. Approach replied and again I could not understand what was said. I am not seeing anything on the approach plate nor FMS what I am hearing. Approach mentioned that the fix is on the approach plate then spells it out. Now I understood and knew where to go. We are heading to ZZZZZ and at ZZZZZ I notice the aircraft is not turning. The FMS had a discontinuity then direct to ZZZZZ. I turned off the auto pilot and hand fly to get back on track.From ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1 the course was centering. Inside ZZZZZ1 was going IMC I wanted to go missed [approach]. Somewhere during this time, the flight in which I was following shifted. The First Officer tried twice to call Approach for a heading and altitude. No answer. I transferred the controls and called Approach. Approach responded. Approach said something about not to continue the descent and gave an altitude and heading. The second time around we landed. In reviewing the flight, I can see many errors. I allowed to many little errors become a larger error. With the little errors I allowed myself to become distracted.
ASRS:1799156.s: The pilot reported a close terrain encounter during an RNAV approach in IMC caused by communication misunderstandings, FMS discontinuities, and distraction. No GPWS or ATC warnings were received, but the crew eventually received a missed approach clearance and landed safely on a second attempt.

ASRS:1799163.n: Approximately midway through the pushback, the ground crew indicated that the tow bar had broken and requested that I set the brakes. It caught me off guard as I hadn't felt anything unusual, so I asked them to clarify that they indeed wanted me to set the brakes. They confirmed that they wanted [me to] set the brakes, so I complied. The push crew lead left the radio to retrieve an aircraft mechanic before I was able to obtain more information. The FO and I had a brief discussion as I had a vague recollection that broken tow bars might require a logbook entry, but the only reference we found was that it required a safety report. When the lead returned to the frequency, he indicated that the aircraft mechanic had inspected the nose gear and there was no damage (I witnessed a gentleman with an aircraft maintenance safety vest walk out from under the nose, but I did not speak to him). I asked him to please clarify the nature of the issue, and he indicated something to the effect that the bar had 'cracked where it hooked to the tug, not the airplane.' I asked the FO if he was satisfied with the response, which he indicated he was. They swapped the bar and we continued without further incident. I filed a report after the trip, and was contacted today by my union advising me that I failed to recognize that this event required a maintenance write-up and sign off.The biggest causal factor is my limited time in the seat, exacerbated by little flying during the pandemic. I had logged only XX hours since completing my upgrade in Month X of 2020, and that trip was the first live leg I'd flown in over five weeks. I remembered that a broken tow bar required additional acknowledgment, but I let myself be satisfied that I was compliant when we found the safety report reference. I think I also reasoned that since a mechanic knew what happened, he would have advised me if further action was required, and I see now that's not dependable logic. I will be spending more time reviewing my manuals in hopes of eliminating future oversights.The best suggestion in this case is the one I must make to myself- to know my company policies/procedures better, as well as striving to clearly understand how to access required information when I need it. I did search the FOM while we were stopped, but now know the reference I needed was actually in the OM. In the future, I will call the maintenance center as well, but this only provides another layer, not absolute protection, as they may not be certain of the policy either. Bottom line is that it's my job to know my manuals. I believe that the return of regular flying that looks to be unfolding over the coming months will help tremendously as we all get reacquainted to the tools of our profession. During push back the ground crew advised the Captain to set the parking brake. After setting the brake he was advised that the tow bar had malfunctioned. They then decided to get a new tow bar and push us out the remainder of the way. After the push back was complete the Captain discussed what happened to the tow bar. the ramp personnel said it was no big deal because it was broken on the tug side and not the aircraft side. I told my Captain that I think we have to do something for a malfunction of the tow bar so I looked in the FOM and told him he needed to file a safety report. It was later brought to my attention by a union safety representative that we should have returned to the gate and made an AML entry and had a maintenance inspection.I did a search in the FOM for tow bar and didn't see anything that would have led me to believe we needed a AML entry for our situation.Better training on this type of event.
ASRS:1799163.s: During pushback, the tow bar broke at the tug connection, prompting the crew to set brakes and replace the bar before continuing. The Captain later admitted that limited recent experience and searching the wrong manual caused a failure to log the event in the Aircraft Maintenance Log as required.

ASRS:1799188.n: I was so focused on no altitude restriction per tail number and dry ice restrictions due conversation with other Dispatcher about dry ice on his flight that ended in an ASAP event he experienced that I did not tell the ramp agent no lives allowed except on main deck. Lives were listed. Crickets coded AVI [live animal] in the ABK [aft bulkhead compartment]. Ramp insisted they are [US] Postal Perishables not lives. Told ramp to remove crickets. [I was] so focused on not making a mistake in one area of MEL that mistake was made in other area of same MEL. I will print and highlight areas of all MEL's that must be communicated prior to making phone calls to ramp agents.
ASRS:1799188.s: A flight dispatcher failed to instruct the ramp agent to exclude live animals from the main deck due to distraction regarding dry ice restrictions. Consequently, crickets were loaded into the aft bulkhead compartment, requiring the dispatcher to order their removal after the ramp agent disputed their classification.
