ASRS:1799193.n: SGU is notorious for near mid-air collisions and RA events. I was monitoring the CTAF while we were between ETIYR and PIETZ prior to being cleared for the GPS (Runway) 19. While monitoring I heard an aircraft state that they were having difficulty getting the runway lights to turn on via the CTAF. I heard multiple series of clicks on the frequency. After a minute the other plane said he saw the lights and all was normal. That plane made position reports and was doing a circle to land to a MAP (Missed Approach) for the HIVKA SID. Everything was uneventful until an aircraft at Mesquite Municipal began trying to cycle the lights at Mesquite. Hey, what do you know SGU and Mesquite share the same frequency along with Kanab or maybe 2 more fields. So, inside the FAF our Runway 19 lights cycle through all 3 settings of low, medium, high and turn off 3 times before we land. We landed with the lights on low with no incident. Too many airports on the same CTAF. Get a new CTAF for SGU that is it's own
ASRS:1799193.s: A pilot at St. George Municipal (SGU) reported that an aircraft at Mesquite Municipal cycled the shared CTAF frequency, causing SGU's runway lights to flash through all settings and turn off three times during the final approach to Runway 19. The pilot attributed this nuisance to multiple airports sharing one frequency and landed safely with lights on low.

ASRS:1799209.n: On pushback, the tow bar shear pin failed. Given the angle the tug was to the airplane it wasn't a surprise and no damage was suspected or reported. I recalled that we could do an information only write up in the logbook if no damage was suspected. Since this was the 737 MAX, I called maintenance control through dispatch to make sure we could still do that. Maintenance control said yes, we could do an information only write up. The fleet Captain contacted [me] today to let me know we can't do this on the MAX yet and that an inspection was required per our manual. I was used to the guidance for the NG and missed the note for the MAX requiring an inspection for shear pin failure. Since it was the MAX, I did take the extra step to obtain guidance from maintenance control but unfortunately that didn't trap this error. Perhaps a quick note or bulletin highlighting this change to the pilot group would help.
ASRS:1799209.s: During pushback of a 737 MAX, a tow bar shear pin failed. The pilot initially planned an information-only logbook entry based on 737 NG procedures, but a fleet Captain later clarified that the MAX manual requires a mandatory inspection for this event.

ASRS:1799210.n: We were assigned an aircraft to take from ZZZ to ZZZ1 that had the BLEED 1 system on MEL. The FO and I discussed before departure in our threat based briefing about how the BLEED 2 system would have a hard time pressurizing the entire aircraft all the way up to our cruise altitude of FL XX0 and how we should make the climb as shallow as we could without exceeding VMO or any airspeed restrictions in order to help the BLEED 2 system pressurize the aircraft.After takeoff the aircraft was pressurizing normally but then somewhere around approximately 7,000 feet on the climb we noticed that the cabin altitude was increasing at about the same rate as our actual altitude and there was only about a 2,500 foot difference between the two. Knowing that only one bleed system was trying to pressurize the aircraft we continued with the hopes that it would catch up and pressurize normally.At 12,500 we got the Cabin Press warning so we leveled off and asked ATC for the lowest altitude they could give us, we were over the [name] Mountains at this time so the lowest altitude they could give us was 12,000 feet. At 12,000 feet the cabin pressure was holding steady at about 9,500 feet but wasn't increasing or decreasing any further.The FO and I discussed running and looked at the pressurization fail checklist but both agreed that the checklist was designed for a 2 bleed operating system and that this was a unique situation.At this point I called Dispatch and Maintenance to discuss the best plan of action, after some discussion Dispatch told us that we needed to return to ZZZ because we didn't have drift down performance for our route of flight at 12,000 feet. By the time this was decided we were almost on the other side of the mountains and I could see the town of [name] about 30 miles to the southeast of our position. My decision was to not turn around and cross the mountain range again at 12,000 feet without drift down performance. When Dispatch became aware of our position we both decided that the best plan of action was to continue to ZZZ1.We landed in ZZZ1 without any further incidents.In hindsight there are two things I wish I would have done differently. The first thing I should have done was to not continue over the [name] mountains with the pressurization not adequately pressurizing the aircraft. I think my continuation was due to the fact that I was unfamiliar with how the pressurization of the aircraft performed with only one bleed system operative and it was my first time operating the aircraft with that particular MEL. If I had it to do over again I would have asked for delay vectors while we waited to see if the pressurization would catch up with our altitude and that way I could have avoided crossing the mountains at an altitude without drift down performance and just returned to ZZZ.The second thing I would have done was to at least run the unpressurized flight checklist, it was a short flight with a very high workload and even though we were still partially pressurized it would have been a good checklist to run just to see if there was anything else we were missing. Bleed 1 was consistently giving a #1 bleed hot caution on previous flights. Therefore, the bleed 1 source was placed on MEL. The only guidance from the MEL was that we shall not turn on the affected bleed valve. Climbing out of ZZZ, we were filed too FLXX0. Bleed 2 was on bleed 1 was off. Upon reaching 12,000 feet the cabin press master warning light appeared. We leveled off and descended to 10,000 feet. We contacted Maintenance Control and Dispatch. I took the radios and was already PF. Due to not having drift down performance and already being pass the mountains Dispatch and the pilots agreed that it was best to continue to ZZZ1 as we had a lot of fuel. We noticed the aircraft was very slow at pressurizing during the climb we attempted to help the system by reducing the rate of climb. This seemed to have little affect. It was almost expected by us that the master warning would go off. Once it went off we noticed the aircraft was at 12,000 feet. But the cabin pressure was at 10,000 feet. So there was a small pressure differential. We therefore decided that we would not put the masks on as this would make commutation more difficult with each other and there was no need for an emergency descent. We descend to 10,000 feet as soon as possible this allowed the cabin to descent to 8,000 feet which was much more normal. We contacted Maintenance Control first as we knew what caused the problem. They advised us to call Dispatch. Drift down performance was not available for our altitude so by the time we contacted Dispatch we had passed the mountains and we agreed with Dispatch that it was safest to continue to ZZZ1. Due to the aircraft not pressuring and knowing the issue causing the problem we did not run the cabin press checklist as this would have advised us to turn on bleed 1 which is specifically what we were told not to do in the MEL. By descending down to 10,000 the master warning went away. We continued to ZZZ1 with no further issues.1) It's important to continually monitor the pressurization panel. 2) Maybe contact [Dispatch during preflight for other options]. 3) Knowing that if the bleed source is on MEL, we should expect the aircraft to not pressurize.4) I would not feel comfortable flying an aircraft with this MEL again unless we were filed below 10,000 feet know the system would not pressurize.5) The MEL was not clear on what to expect with this system inop.
ASRS:1799210.s: Pilots operating an aircraft with Bleed 1 on MEL experienced inadequate pressurization during climb to FL XX0, triggering a Cabin Press warning at 12,000 feet. After descending to 10,000 feet and consulting Dispatch, they continued to ZZZ1 due to insufficient drift-down performance over mountains, noting the MEL lacked clear guidance for single-bleed operations.

ASRS:1799214.n: On the LIBER 3 arrival, ATC instructed 'after GLOWS fly heading 020 descend 4200 ft. for traffic, vectors for the approach.' Approximately 15 miles from the runway, ATC instructed '5 miles from CIGNI left turn to intercept the inbound course, maintain 4200 until established, cleared approach.' PF (Pilot Flying) tuned heading, drew a line out from WUNDU, set 1700 in the altitude alert and armed the approach.As course came alive and captured we noticed path continuing to drop below us on the vertical guide. As course came alive, PF pushed VS then VNAV. ALT turned to FLCH and the aircraft began to descend. Rather than capture, it descended through the path. PF pushed VS in attempt to regain the path. We heard 'Terrain warning.' PF turned off AP, began a climb and asked PM (Pilot Monitoring) to rest 4,200. ATC questioned the low altitude alert and asked us to confirm we were established on the approach due to the MSA of 4,200. We confirmed due to laterally established and visual contact with terrain. PF leveled at 4,200, engaged AP and we worked to re-engage the APP while continuing, landed and debriefed.After being vectored off the arrival, it may have been a better course of action to load the RNAV Y for 20R due to better altitude protections. Also need to wait for LNAV to be in magenta. Due to traffic we were on a heading and descended to 4,200. 5 miles from CIGNI turn left maintain 4,200 until established, cleared approach. I turned to the heading, pressed approach and spun the AA down to 1,700 and lined out from WUNDU, entered in the inbound course and activated.Waiting to intercept I noticed VNAV path was dropping below us. I as saw the course come alive I pressed VS and VNAV, ALT turned to FLCH. Aircraft began a descent to capture PATH but we went through it. My first reaction was to press VS and climb back to path. We heard a terrain warning, I clicked AP off and began a climb asked PM (Pilot Monitoring) to spin AA to 4,200. ATC notified us of a Low Altitude alert, he said if we were established we were okay, We were laterally established and had visual contact with all terrain. I leveled at 4,200 and engaged autopilot. We worked to re-engage APP and continued.We landed and debriefed. Mistake was lowering AA to 1,700 until fully magenta.
ASRS:1799214.s: During the LIBER 3 arrival, the crew descended below the 4,200 ft minimum safe altitude after prematurely arming the approach and setting the altitude alert to 1,700 ft. This triggered a terrain warning and ATC low altitude alert, requiring a manual climb to 4,200 ft before the crew re-engaged the autopilot and landed safely.

ASRS:1799238.n: During the landing roll out I took controls at 60 knots. We were instructed without delay to take the high speed taxiway due to landing traffic on short final. As I vacated the runway I saw an airport operations vehicle driving towards us and not showing signs of slowing down. I applied maximum breaking to avoid a collision with the vehicle and a few moments later the ops vehicle swerved into the grass. I asked Tower what the operations vehicle was doing on the taxiway, which ATC replied, 'I had no idea about any ops vehicles.' The driver came on the frequency and apologized, which clearly isn't good enough. There was no damage or injuries.
ASRS:1799238.s: During landing rollout, the pilot took controls at 60 knots and applied maximum brakes to avoid an airport operations vehicle on the high-speed taxiway. The vehicle swerved into the grass, and ATC admitted unawareness of its presence, resulting in no damage or injuries.

ASRS:1799300.n: I am a flight instructor at a 141 school. I am currently one of the instructors teaching the Private Pilot curriculum. The error I committed was sending one of my students on a solo flight without a current solo endorsement. Normally in our curriculum, a student pilot solo endorsement would not expire before the student earns their PPL. Due to COVID, our curriculum got pushed back and winter break put a pause on the private curriculum just a few flights before the check ride. The time added was enough for all student solo endorsements to expire. Knowing this, we added a reminder in our CFI guide that follows along with our Private Pilot Training Syllabus. The reminder was placed on the flight just before the solo flight. Due to the lost proficiency over winter break, I was not ready to give this student a new solo endorsement at the beginning of this spring semester.The issue began on the flight before the solo flight. This particular flight was the fourth time I had instructed this curricular period in the last 30 days so, I felt confident on the expectations of the flight. Because of this, I did not review the CFI guide before or after the flight and therefore missed the solo endorsement reminder. With my full permission, my student then flew solo the next day.I discovered the issue when I went to send that student on their next solo flight and I asked them to prove to me they had their required documents and endorsements. I then quickly gave a new solo endorsement.
ASRS:1799300.s: A flight instructor at a Part 141 school sent a student on a solo flight without a current endorsement after missing a syllabus reminder due to not reviewing the CFI guide. The instructor discovered the error during the next flight preparation and immediately issued the required endorsement.

ASRS:1799304.n: Approximately 30 nm north on the 340 radial from ZZZ at 3,000 feet MSL engine failure was experienced. Approximately 3 minutes prior to engine failure fuel tank selector was moved from both to left tank to compensate for uneven fuel burn. Before and at the time of engine failure aircraft was on flight following with ZZZ approach. Immediately upon experiencing engine failure ZZZ Approach was contacted and requested priority handling. At this time, aircraft pitched for best glide speed and made 180 degree turn to ZZZZ. Emergency procedures were followed, aircraft descended to 2,300 at 65 kts at which time fuel selector was placed back to both and engine power restored. ZZZ Approach was contacted and made aware of restored engine power. Aircraft climbed to 4,500 enroute to ZZZ to check and monitor systems circling over ZZZ. Once definitive evidence showed that engine failure was related to fuel tank selector in left position and that all other systems were functioning normally ZZZ Approach was contacted and aircraft resumed heading from ZZZ to ZZZ1 at 4,500 with no further system failures.
ASRS:1799304.s: The pilot experienced an engine failure at 3,000 feet while on flight following with ZZZ Approach after selecting the left fuel tank. Power was restored at 2,300 feet by returning the selector to both, and the flight resumed to ZZZ1 after confirming the failure was caused by the fuel tank selection.

ASRS:1799310.n: On VFR visual approach to Runway XXL at ZZZ, Second in Command (myself) was in communication with another flight which had just landed on Runway XXR. Pilot in command in left seat was pilot flying and I was pilot monitoring. Our selected course was direct to ZZZZZ for a GPS approach. Passing approximately 4,500 feet for selected altitude of 4,100 feet a 'terrain' advisory sounded. Descent was arrested and we temporarily returned to 4,500 feet. No further warnings, remainder of the flight was uneventful. I figured out that we were northeast of a mountain peak, whose highest obstacle is an antenna at 3,600 feet. Our lowest altitude above ground level was estimated 1,500 feet.
ASRS:1799310.s: During a VFR visual approach to Runway XXL, the Second in Command received a terrain advisory at 4,500 feet while northeast of a mountain peak. The crew arrested the descent and returned to 4,500 feet, maintaining an estimated 1,500 feet above ground level with no further warnings.

ASRS:1799323.n: I was the second in command on a charter into Bermuda Dunes airport in California. We landed on Runway 28, the aircraft was being flown by the PIC. After landing we exited the runway on a taxiway prior to the end of the runway. Once clear, I began to run the after landing checklist and was activating controls and switches as the pilot in command taxied the aircraft. As the PIC turned onto the parallel taxiway to proceed to the FBO, PIC started the turn slightly early and the left main landing gear departed the prepared surface into soft sand. We stopped the aircraft and evaluated the situation. It was determined that we needed assistance from airport personnel. Experts on the field in conjunction with our company determined the best plan of attack was to pull the aircraft back onto the prepared surface and tow it to the FBO. A plan was made with our Operations department, Maintenance, and the airport personnel who had experience pulling aircraft from the same location previously. The aircraft was safely returned to the asphalt and towed to the FBO where a qualified Maintenance Technician who was hired by our Maintenance department, inspected the aircraft and returned it to airworthiness status. Bermuda Dunes has a history of aircraft getting stuck turning onto the parallel taxiway and I was told that two other airplanes had already met the same fate in the sand this year that we were faced with. An evaluation should be made of the Bermuda Dunes airfield and notes placed in the Jeppesen plates, to alert aircrews of the hazardous situation that exists with narrow taxiways and a lack of turning fillet areas to prevent departing the prepared surface at Bermuda Dunes.
ASRS:1799323.s: The PIC and SIC of a charter aircraft departed the prepared surface into soft sand while turning onto a parallel taxiway at Bermuda Dunes after landing. The aircraft was recovered by airport personnel and towed to the FBO, where maintenance inspection returned it to airworthiness status.

ASRS:1799328.n: We were doing pattern operations at Leesburg with a student. We were on the left downwind for Runway 17 at Leesburg. It was busy with at least one other in the pattern and several aircraft waiting for takeoff and I believe two aircraft approaching for landing. About midfield I noticed on my portable ADS-B indicating an aircraft adjacent to us. Looking to the left there was an aircraft passing on our left just below and to our left. We were completely surprised by this. As far as I could tell the aircraft was doing a left downwind departure to the north which was unusual at Leesburg. I do not know if the aircraft had visual contact with us. Doubtful as we were in his blindspot. Most departures from 17 do a right hand departure to exit the pattern expeditiously. I heard nothing from the Tower that approved this and there was no warning from the Tower of the oncoming traffic. I confirmed with a fellow CFI in the pattern that I hadn't missed a call. The other CFI was about a half mile on downwind and witnessed the near collision. I called the Tower about the traffic and was just told he was departing to the North.
ASRS:1799328.s: A flight instructor and student in a pattern aircraft experienced a near collision at Leesburg while on left downwind for Runway 17. The incident involved an unexpected departure to the north that violated standard right-hand procedures, with no prior Tower warning or clearance issued.

ASRS:1799337.n: Arriving to OPF on the WAVUN5 [arrival] and leveled off at 6,000 feet a Cessna 182 0r 206 came out of nowhere from a small cloud opposite direction cleared our airplane by a 100 to 150 feet. We reported it to Miami Center and Miami Approach.
ASRS:1799337.s: A pilot arriving on the WAVUN5 arrival at 6,000 feet reported a Cessna 182 or 206 emerging from a cloud in the opposite direction, passing within 100 to 150 feet. The crew subsequently reported the near-midair collision to Miami Center and Miami Approach.

ASRS:1799442.n: During arrival into HPN, I noticed the PAPI seemed different. After a few moments I realized that the light indications were backwards. The PAPI for 16 is on the left hand side of the runway but the red lights began on the left (farthest two lights from the runway were red). The FAA requirements per FAA AC150/5340-30G Chapter 7.4 (d) are that the 'light housing assemblies nearest the runway (inboard) must be seen as red and the two farthest from runway (outboard) must be seen as white.' The VGSI (visual glideslope indicator) was at a corresponding angle to the ILS glideslope which we were using as a backup, despite the red and white being 'flipped'. I wasn't sure the reference and didn't want to address my concern without being certain and without a reference so I did not immediately notify operations. In addition to my hesitation that evening, the Tower closed just a few minutes after we parked at the gate. The next morning when I arrived to the aircraft, I asked for a contact number for the Tower and gave them a call. The Controller who answered seemed helpful and keen on ensuring that the issue would be resolved. Controller said they would send OPS out to check on the system. Address with HPN operations to resolve the PAPI indications.
ASRS:1799442.s: A pilot reported reversed PAPI light indications during arrival at HPN, where outboard lights appeared red instead of white. The pilot contacted the tower the next morning, and a controller agreed to dispatch operations to inspect and resolve the system error.
